parts.q: TCA seizures: first drug, and the one to avoid?
parts.a: **Benzodiazepines** first (then phenobarbital or propofol); **avoid phenytoin** — another sodium-channel blocker.

TOX-15.sub: Toxicology → Antidotes → Lipid emulsion for local anaesthetic toxicity
TOX-15.intro: Bupivacaine and other local anaesthetics are lipophilic and bind tightly to cardiac sodium channels; an accidental intravascular dose can cause seizures and then cardiac arrest that resists standard resuscitation. A 20% lipid emulsion creates a fat phase in the blood into which the drug moves out of the heart, and also gives the myocardium fuel. The doses are by weight, with a ceiling, and resuscitation itself is modified.
why: a
**Bolus: 20% lipid 1.5 mL/kg over 2–3 minutes (100 mL if over 70 kg).** The bolus quickly builds a lipid sink in plasma so the drug can partition out of the heart.
b

**Infusion: 0.25 mL/kg/min (200–250 mL over 15–20 minutes if over 70 kg). If still unstable, repeat the bolus once or twice and double the rate.** The infusion keeps the lipid level up while the drug is redistributed and cleared.
c
**Maximum dose: 12 mL/kg.** Larger lipid loads risk pancreatitis, fat overload, lung injury and interference with laboratory tests.
d

**Changes to resuscitation: adrenaline boluses ≤1 µg/kg; avoid vasopressin, calcium-channel blockers, beta-blockers and lidocaine; benzodiazepines for seizures, avoiding large doses of propofol.** Large adrenaline doses worsen arrhythmia and blunt the lipid response. Lidocaine is another local anaesthetic. Calcium-channel blockers and beta-blockers depress a heart that is already failing, and large propofol doses do the same.
e
**Monitoring: 4–6 hours after a cardiovascular event; 2 hours after a CNS-only event.** As the lipid is cleared, the drug can move back from fat into plasma and the heart, so toxicity can recur.
mimic: LAST resuscitation vs standard ACLS
Smaller adrenaline doses, no vasopressin, and no lidocaine for the arrhythmia.
traps: “Standard 1 mg adrenaline boluses”
Use small boluses, ≤1 µg/kg.
“Lidocaine for the ventricular arrhythmia”
It is another local anaesthetic and adds to the toxicity.
“Patient stable after lipid — discharge to the ward at once”
Monitor 4–6 hours after a cardiovascular event: toxicity can recur.
decode: Which drugs are avoided in LAST resuscitation?
TOX-15.punch: Lipid soaks the fat-soluble drug out of the heart, so it is dosed by weight with a ceiling of 12 mL/kg — and resuscitation changes with it: small adrenaline doses and no extra local anaesthetic.

parts.q: Lipid emulsion beyond local anaesthetics?
parts.a: Rescue for **lipophilic cardiotoxins** — propranolol, verapamil/diltiazem, TCAs — after standard antidotes fail; **VA-ECMO** is the next step.

TOX-16.intro: This card tests the deck’s key distinctions. Each statement is either true or turns on one detail from an earlier card; the reason for each answer is the mechanism you met there.
why: a
**False — anticholinergic skin is dry.** Sweat glands work through muscarinic receptors, so blocking them stops sweating (TOX-03).
b
**True — bitter almonds suggest cyanide** (TOX-06), though many people cannot smell it.
c
**False — lithium is not bound by charcoal; use whole bowel irrigation.** Charcoal binds organic molecules; ions such as lithium and iron slip through (TOX-09).
d
**True — urine alkalinisation is used for salicylates.** A weak acid is ionised and trapped in alkaline urine (TOX-10).
e
**False — a tricyclic wide QRS is treated with bicarbonate; avoid class Ia drugs such as procainamide.** Procainamide is itself a sodium-channel blocker (TOX-07).
f
**True — octreotide treats sulfonylurea overdose** by stopping insulin release (TOX-14).
g
**True — the maximum lipid emulsion dose is 12 mL/kg** (TOX-15).
h
**True — methanol raises the osmolal gap,** early, before it is metabolised to formic acid (TOX-08).
traps: “Charcoal binds everything”
Not metals, ions or alcohols.
“Any anti-arrhythmic will do for a toxic wide QRS”
Class Ia and Ic deepen sodium-channel block.
decode: Check sweat: wet sympathomimetic, dry anticholinergic.
Ask whether charcoal can bind the toxin.
TOX-16.punch: Every statement here turns on a mechanism from earlier in the deck — the sweat gland’s muscarinic receptor, what charcoal can bind, ion trapping, and sodium-channel block.

topups.q:
**Drug-induced long QT:**
**a** Which SSRIs?
**b** Which antipsychotics most?
**c** Several QT drugs at once: stop which first?
**d** Then correct
a: **a** **Citalopram, escitalopram**.
**b** **Thioridazine, ziprasidone**; IV haloperidol is dangerous at high doses.
**c** The one that also **blocks CYP3A4** (erythromycin, fluconazole) — it raises the others’ levels.
**d** **Potassium and magnesium**.

x.sub: Toxicology → Cardiac toxicity → Drug-induced long QT
x.intro: Many common ICU drugs block the cardiac potassium channel (hERG) that ends the action potential. Repolarisation is delayed, the QT lengthens, and an early afterdepolarisation can set off torsades de pointes. The risk is cumulative: each extra drug, a low potassium or magnesium, bradycardia or a raised drug level adds to it.
why: a

**Citalopram and escitalopram.** Among the SSRIs these two prolong the QT in a dose-dependent way, which is why their maximum doses were lowered, especially in the elderly. Sertraline is the usual choice when cardiac risk is a concern.
b

**Thioridazine and ziprasidone; IV haloperidol is dangerous at high doses.** Thioridazine causes the greatest QTc prolongation of the commonly used antipsychotics (pimozide and sertindole are also high-risk). Haloperidol by mouth carries modest risk, but large intravenous doses for agitated delirium have caused torsades, so the ECG is monitored when it is given that way.
c

**The one that also blocks CYP3A4 (erythromycin, fluconazole) — it raises the others’ levels.** Such a drug prolongs the QT itself and also slows the clearance of other QT drugs metabolised by CYP3A4, so their levels and effect climb. Removing it removes two sources of risk at once.
d

**Potassium and magnesium.** Low potassium reduces the repolarising current and enhances hERG block; low magnesium makes afterdepolarisations more likely. Correcting both raises the threshold for torsades, and intravenous magnesium is also the first treatment once torsades occurs.
mimic: Torsades vs polymorphic VT from ischaemia
Torsades arises from a long QT, often pause-dependent; ischaemic polymorphic VT occurs with a normal QT and is treated as ischaemia.
traps: “All SSRIs carry the same QT risk”
Citalopram and escitalopram stand out; sertraline is preferred in cardiac patients.
“Oral and IV haloperidol are equally risky”
The danger is mainly with high intravenous doses.
“Correcting potassium is enough”
Magnesium must be corrected too; it stabilises the membrane against afterdepolarisations.
decode: Patient on a QT drug starts erythromycin or fluconazole, then torsades
The CYP3A4 inhibitor raised the other drug’s level — stop it first.
Delirious patient, large IV haloperidol doses, then polymorphic VT
Drug-induced torsades: stop haloperidol, give magnesium.
x.punch: QT risk adds up, so remove the drug that multiplies the others first, then correct potassium and magnesium.

topups.q:
**Carbon monoxide vs methaemoglobin:**
**a** SpO₂ in CO
**b** SpO₂ in MetHb, and why
**c** Common drug causes of MetHb
**d** Treatment of MetHb, and its contraindication
**e** Hyperbaric oxygen in CO: when?
a: **a** **Falsely normal** — COHb looks like oxyhaemoglobin; PaO₂ normal.
**b** **Drifts toward ~85%** as MetHb rises — it absorbs equally at 660 and 940 nm.
**c** **Benzocaine/prilocaine** before endoscopy, dapsone, nitrites/nitrates, primaquine, rasburicase.
**d** **Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg** if symptomatic or MetHb >20–30%; **never in G6PD deficiency**.
**e** COHb **>25%** (>15% in pregnancy), loss of consciousness, ischaemia or neurological signs.

x.sub: Toxicology → Gases and haemoglobin → Carbon monoxide vs methaemoglobin
x.intro: A pulse oximeter estimates saturation from the ratio of light absorbed at two wavelengths, 660 and 940 nm, and assumes only oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin are present. Carbon monoxide and methaemoglobin both add a third haemoglobin that carries no oxygen. The oximeter misreads them in opposite directions, and that difference is what the exam tests.
why: a

**Falsely normal — COHb looks like oxyhaemoglobin; PaO₂ normal.** Carboxyhaemoglobin absorbs red light much as oxyhaemoglobin does, so it is counted as saturated. PaO₂ measures dissolved oxygen, which is normal. Only co-oximetry measures COHb.
b

**Drifts toward ~85% as MetHb rises — it absorbs equally at 660 and 940 nm.** An equal absorption ratio corresponds to a reading of about 85%, so the SpO₂ settles there however high the MetHb climbs. A low SpO₂ with a normal PaO₂ that does not respond to oxygen is the ‘saturation gap’.
c

**Benzocaine/prilocaine before endoscopy, dapsone, nitrites/nitrates, primaquine, rasburicase.** These oxidise haem iron from the ferrous to the ferric state, which cannot bind oxygen. Topical anaesthetic sprays are the classic ICU cause.
d

**Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg if symptomatic or MetHb >20–30%; never in G6PD deficiency.** Methylene blue is reduced to leucomethylene blue by NADPH-dependent reductase, and this reduces methaemoglobin back to haemoglobin. The NADPH comes from G6PD; without it the drug does not work and can cause haemolysis. It is also an MAO inhibitor, so it can precipitate serotonin syndrome in a patient on an SSRI or SNRI.
e

**COHb >25% (>15% in pregnancy), loss of consciousness, ischaemia or neurological signs.** Hyperbaric oxygen shortens the COHb half-life and is given to reduce delayed neurological sequelae. Fetal haemoglobin binds CO more tightly, hence the lower threshold in pregnancy.
mimic: CO vs cyanide
Both give a normal SpO₂ with tissue hypoxia; cyanide gives a very high lactate and high venous oxygen.
Methaemoglobinaemia vs sulfhaemoglobinaemia
Both cause cyanosis; sulfhaemoglobin does not respond to methylene blue.
traps: “A normal SpO₂ excludes CO poisoning”
COHb reads as oxyhaemoglobin; send a co-oximetry sample.
“A normal PaO₂ excludes hypoxia”
PaO₂ measures dissolved oxygen, not how much haemoglobin can carry.
“Methylene blue works in everyone”
It needs NADPH from G6PD; in deficiency it fails and haemolyses.
decode: Cyanosis after endoscopy spray, SpO₂ 85% unchanged on oxygen, PaO₂ normal
Headache in a family sharing a heater, SpO₂ 99%
Methylene blue given, cyanosis worse, haemolysis
x.punch: The oximeter cannot see what it was not built for: carbon monoxide reads as normal, methaemoglobin as about 85%, and only co-oximetry tells the truth.

topups.q:
**Toxic alcohol: block or dialyse?**
**a** When to give fomepizole
**b** Does a normal osmolal gap exclude it?
**c** Why ethanol lets fomepizole wait
**d** When to dialyse
a: **a** **Empirically** when a toxic alcohol is suspected and the level is delayed.
**b** **No** — in a late presenter the alcohol is already metabolised to acid.
**c** Ethanol **≥100 mg/dL** saturates alcohol dehydrogenase (10–20× higher affinity).
**d** **Visual signs, AKI or severe acidosis**.

x.sub: Toxicology → Toxic alcohols → Block or dialyse
x.intro: Methanol and ethylene glycol are not very toxic themselves. Alcohol dehydrogenase converts them to formic acid and glycolic and oxalic acids, which cause the acidosis, blindness and renal failure. Treatment therefore has two parts: stop the enzyme before acid forms, and remove the alcohol and acid once harm has started.
why: a

**Empirically when a toxic alcohol is suspected and the level is delayed.** Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase, so no new acid forms while waiting. Toxic alcohol levels are rarely available quickly, and every hour of delay lets more acid form.
b

**No — in a late presenter the alcohol is already metabolised to acid.** The osmolal gap reflects the unmetabolised alcohol; as it is converted, the osmolal gap falls and the anion gap rises. A normal osmolal gap with high anion gap acidosis is consistent with late poisoning. The normal range is also wide, so a small toxic amount can hide inside it.
c

**Ethanol ≥100 mg/dL saturates alcohol dehydrogenase (10–20× higher affinity).** The enzyme prefers ethanol, so while ethanol is at this level the toxic alcohol is hardly metabolised. Fomepizole becomes necessary as the ethanol level falls.
d

**Visual signs, AKI or severe acidosis.** These show that acid has already formed and is causing organ damage. Haemodialysis removes both the parent alcohol and the toxic acids, which fomepizole cannot do.
mimic: Toxic alcohol vs alcoholic ketoacidosis
Both give high anion gap acidosis in a drinker; ketoacidosis has ketones, often low glucose, and a small osmolal gap.
Isopropanol
Raises the osmolal gap but makes acetone, a ketone, not an acid — no acidosis.
traps: “Normal osmolal gap, so not a toxic alcohol”
A late presenter has converted the alcohol to acid.
“Wait for the level before fomepizole”
Give it on suspicion; delay lets acid form.
“Fomepizole is enough once the patient is blind”
Established acid and organ damage need dialysis.
decode: Drinker, blurred vision, high anion gap acidosis, normal osmolal gap
Alcohol dehydrogenase is occupied; fomepizole can follow as ethanol falls.
x.punch: Block the enzyme early, while there is still alcohol to block; dialyse once the acid or the damage is already there.

topups.q: **Spot it:** hallucinations, BP 190/110, HR 129, sweating — urine drug screen **negative**.
a: **Synthetic cathinones** (bath salts, mephedrone) or **synthetic cannabinoids** — routine immunoassays miss them.
Benzodiazepines, cooling, fluids; watch hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, hyponatraemia.

x.sub: Toxicology → Toxidromes → Sympathomimetic with a negative screen
x.intro: A patient is agitated, hallucinating, hypertensive, tachycardic and sweating — a sympathomimetic toxidrome. The urine screen is negative for amphetamines and cocaine. That does not exclude a drug; it shows the limits of the test.
why: a

**Synthetic cathinones (bath salts, mephedrone) or synthetic cannabinoids — routine immunoassays miss them.** A urine immunoassay detects only the molecules its antibodies were made against. These new psychoactive substances are structurally different enough to escape the amphetamine and cannabinoid assays, and their structures keep changing. The diagnosis is clinical.
b

**Benzodiazepines, cooling, fluids; watch hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, hyponatraemia.** Benzodiazepines reduce central sympathetic drive, which lowers heart rate, blood pressure and heat production. Agitation and muscle activity cause hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis, which are the main causes of death. Hyponatraemia is reported with mephedrone, as with MDMA, and can cause seizures.
mimic: Sympathomimetic vs anticholinergic
Both are hot, agitated and tachycardic; the sympathomimetic patient sweats, the anticholinergic patient has dry skin and urinary retention.
Serotonin syndrome
Also hot and agitated, but with clonus and hyperreflexia, worse in the legs, after a serotonergic drug.
traps: “Negative screen, so not drug-induced”
Immunoassays miss most new psychoactive substances; treat the toxidrome.
“A β-blocker for the tachycardia”
Sedation with benzodiazepines comes first; it treats the cause of the tachycardia and hypertension.
decode: Festival-goer, agitation, hypertension, sweating, screen negative
Same picture with dark urine and high CK
Same picture with a seizure and sodium 122
x.punch: A urine screen finds only what it was built to find; a sympathomimetic picture with a negative screen is still a sympathomimetic, and it is treated with sedation and cooling.

topups.q: **Spot it:** coma, pinpoint pupils, slow breathing, bradycardia — **no response to naloxone**.
a: **Clonidine** (central α₂ agonist).
Supportive care; atropine for bradycardia. Naloxone response is inconsistent.

x.intro: Coma, pinpoint pupils and slow breathing look like opioid poisoning, so naloxone is given. When it fails, the question becomes which drug produces the same picture through a different receptor.
why: a

**Clonidine (central α₂ agonist).** Clonidine stimulates α₂ receptors in the brainstem, which reduces sympathetic outflow: miosis, sedation, respiratory depression, bradycardia and hypotension. Children are often poisoned by a single tablet or by imidazoline eye or nasal drops, which act the same way. Early transient hypertension can occur from peripheral α stimulation.
b

**Supportive care; atropine for bradycardia. Naloxone response is inconsistent.** Most patients recover within 24–48 hours with airway and circulatory support. Atropine treats symptomatic bradycardia, and fluids or vasopressors treat hypotension. Naloxone helps some patients, possibly through an indirect opioid link, but its effect cannot be relied upon.
mimic: Clonidine vs opioid
Same picture; clonidine adds marked bradycardia and hypotension, and naloxone often fails.
Clonidine vs pontine haemorrhage
Pontine haemorrhage also gives coma with pinpoint pupils; CT separates them.
traps: “Pinpoint pupils and apnoea mean opioid”
Clonidine, imidazolines and pontine haemorrhage give the same picture.
“If naloxone fails, give more until it works”
Clonidine response is inconsistent; supportive care is the treatment.
“Early hypertension excludes clonidine”
A brief hypertensive phase can precede hypotension.
decode: Toddler, coma, miosis, HR 50, naloxone no response
Father’s antihypertensive tablets at home, child drowsy and bradycardic
x.punch: Clonidine copies the opioid picture through a different receptor, so the opioid antidote is unreliable and care is supportive.

topups.q: **Spot it:** unconscious house-fire victim, lactate 12, SpO₂ 99%.
a: **Cyanide plus carbon monoxide**.
**Hydroxocobalamin 5 g** with 100% O₂ (intubate if GCS ≤8); **avoid nitrites** — their methaemoglobin worsens oxygen carriage.

x.sub: Toxicology → Smoke inhalation → Cyanide and carbon monoxide
x.intro: Burning wool, silk, plastics and foam release hydrogen cyanide as well as carbon monoxide. A house-fire victim can therefore have two poisons that both stop oxygen use, and neither lowers the pulse oximeter reading. The blood lactate is the clue.
why: a

**Cyanide plus carbon monoxide.** COHb reads as oxyhaemoglobin, so SpO₂ is normal. Cyanide blocks cytochrome oxidase, so cells cannot use oxygen and switch to anaerobic metabolism; venous blood stays oxygenated and lactate rises. In smoke inhalation a lactate of about 8–10 mmol/L or more strongly suggests cyanide.
b

**Hydroxocobalamin 5 g with 100% O₂ (intubate if GCS ≤8); avoid nitrites — their methaemoglobin worsens oxygen carriage.** Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, which is excreted in urine; it is given intravenously over 15 minutes and can be repeated. Nitrites work by creating methaemoglobin, which binds cyanide, but with CO already blocking haemoglobin this further reduces oxygen delivery. 100% oxygen speeds removal of CO.
mimic: Smoke victim vs simple CO poisoning
CO alone rarely gives a very high lactate; a lactate of 12 with shock points to cyanide.
traps: “SpO₂ 99%, so oxygenation is fine”
COHb reads as oxyhaemoglobin and cyanide stops oxygen use, not delivery.
“Use the standard cyanide kit with nitrites”
Nitrite-induced methaemoglobin adds to the CO deficit in carriage; hydroxocobalamin is safe.
“Wait for the cyanide level”
The level takes hours; treat on the clinical picture and lactate.
decode: Fire victim, coma, high lactate, normal SpO₂
Cyanide with CO → hydroxocobalamin and 100% oxygen.
Which cyanide antidote to avoid in smoke inhalation?
x.punch: In a fire victim with a normal SpO₂, the lactate gives cyanide away: give hydroxocobalamin and oxygen, never nitrites.

topups.q:
**Heavy metals in the ICU:**
**a** Arsenic: how it poisons
**b** Arsenic: the neuropathy and its mimic
**c** Arsenic: the test before treating ‘GBS’, and the chelator
**d** Lead encephalopathy: chelation order
**e** Mercury: swallowed vs inhaled
a: **a** Binds **sulfhydryl** groups (blocks pyruvate dehydrogenase); garlic odour, rice-water diarrhoea, QT prolongation.
**b** At 1–3 weeks an ascending **axonal** neuropathy that **mimics GBS**; Mees lines.
**c** **24-h urine arsenic** (blood clears in days); chelate with **dimercaprol**, then DMSA or DMPS.
**d** **Dimercaprol first, then CaNa₂EDTA 4 h later**; avoid LP and routine hyperventilation.
**e** Swallowed elemental (thermometer): **harmless**. Inhaled vapour: **pneumonitis, ARDS**, neurotoxicity.

x.sub: Toxicology → Heavy metals → Arsenic, lead, mercury
x.intro: Heavy metals poison enzymes by binding their sulfhydryl groups. In the ICU they appear as an unexplained gastroenteritis with arrhythmia, a neuropathy that looks like Guillain–Barré syndrome, or an encephalopathy. Chelators treat them by offering the metal a partner it binds more tightly, which is then excreted.
why: a

**Binds sulfhydryl groups (blocks pyruvate dehydrogenase); garlic odour, rice-water diarrhoea, QT prolongation.** Blocking pyruvate dehydrogenase stops aerobic energy production in cells. Damage to capillaries in the gut causes profuse watery diarrhoea and fluid loss, and potassium-channel effects prolong the QT, leading to torsades.
b

**At 1–3 weeks an ascending axonal neuropathy that mimics GBS; Mees lines.** The neuropathy is sensorimotor, often painful, and can progress to weakness and respiratory failure. Mees lines are white transverse bands across the nails; they appear weeks later as the nail grows out.
c

**24-h urine arsenic (blood clears within hours to days); chelate with dimercaprol, then DMSA or DMPS.** Arsenic leaves the blood quickly, so a blood level taken at the neuropathy stage is often normal while urine still shows it. Dimercaprol is given intramuscularly in the acute, unwell patient; oral DMSA or DMPS follows when the gut works.
d

**Dimercaprol first, then CaNa₂EDTA 4 h later; avoid LP and routine hyperventilation.** EDTA given alone mobilises lead from tissues and can move it into the brain, worsening encephalopathy; dimercaprol first prevents this, and both then continue together. Lead encephalopathy causes cerebral oedema, so lumbar puncture risks herniation.
e

**Swallowed elemental (thermometer): harmless. Inhaled vapour: pneumonitis, ARDS, neurotoxicity.** Elemental mercury is almost not absorbed from the gut. Heated or vaporised, it is absorbed well through the lungs and damages lung and brain.
mimic: Arsenic neuropathy vs GBS
Both ascend; arsenic follows a gastrointestinal illness with QT prolongation and later Mees lines — check urine arsenic before treating as GBS.
traps: “Normal blood arsenic excludes poisoning”
Blood clears in days; 24-hour urine is the test.
“EDTA alone for lead encephalopathy”
It can move lead into the brain; dimercaprol goes first.
“A swallowed thermometer needs chelation”
Elemental mercury is not absorbed from the gut.
decode: Vomiting and diarrhoea, then 2 weeks later ascending weakness
Child with pica, seizures, raised ICP
Heated mercury in a closed room, then ARDS
x.punch: Metals poison by binding sulfhydryl groups and chelators offer them a better partner — but the route and the order of chelation decide whether that helps or harms.

topups.q:
**Iron poisoning:**
**a** Stage 1 (0–6 h)
**b** Stage 2 (6–24 h)
**c** Stage 3 (24–48 h)
**d** Late stages
**e** Decontamination and chelation
a: **a** **Corrosive GI**: vomiting, haematemesis, shock.
**b** **Latent** — apparent recovery while iron enters cells: the dangerous reassurance.
**c** **Shock, high anion gap acidosis**, hepatic necrosis, coagulopathy.
**d** Hepatic failure; **gastric outlet stricture** at 2–6 weeks.
**e** Not bound by charcoal (an ion) → **whole bowel irrigation**; tablets are radio-opaque; **deferoxamine** up to 15 mg/kg/h (vin-rosé urine), usually stopped by ~24 h (ARDS).

x.intro: Iron tablets are common in homes, and in children they are a classic cause of death from overdose. Iron first damages the gut directly, then enters the circulation and cells, where free iron damages mitochondria. The stages follow that path, and the quiet middle stage is where patients are wrongly sent home.
why: a

**Corrosive GI: vomiting, haematemesis, shock.** Iron is directly corrosive to the gut lining. Vomiting and diarrhoea, sometimes bloody, with fluid loss can cause early hypovolaemic shock. A patient with no gastrointestinal symptoms by 6 hours is unlikely to develop serious toxicity.
b

**Latent — apparent recovery while iron enters cells: the dangerous reassurance.** Gut symptoms settle, but iron is moving into tissues. In severe poisoning this stage may be short or absent, and a persistent acidosis or tachycardia shows that toxicity is still progressing.
c

**Shock, high anion gap acidosis, hepatic necrosis, coagulopathy.** Free iron disrupts mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, so cells make lactate; iron also causes vasodilatation and capillary leak. The liver receives the iron first through the portal circulation.
d

**Hepatic failure; gastric outlet stricture at 2–6 weeks.** Survivors of the early stages may develop liver failure. The early corrosive injury heals with scarring, which can obstruct the pylorus weeks later.
e

**Not bound by charcoal (an ion) → whole bowel irrigation; tablets are radio-opaque; deferoxamine up to 15 mg/kg/h (vin-rosé urine), usually stopped by ~24 h (ARDS).** Charcoal does not bind charged metals, so tablets seen on X-ray are flushed through with polyethylene glycol. Deferoxamine binds free iron to form ferrioxamine, which colours urine red-orange. Infusions beyond about 24 hours are associated with ARDS.
mimic: Iron vs lithium
Both are not bound by charcoal and are treated with whole bowel irrigation; iron tablets are radio-opaque and give a corrosive gastroenteritis.
traps: “Symptoms have settled at 12 hours, so discharge”
That may be the latent stage; check acidosis and serum iron.
“Give activated charcoal”
Iron is an ion and is not bound.
“Continue deferoxamine until the urine clears”
Long infusions cause ARDS; usually stopped by about 24 hours.
decode: Child, mother’s tablets, vomiting, then well, then shock at 30 h
x.punch: Iron burns the gut, then hides in cells: a quiet middle stage is not recovery, so judge by the acidosis, not by how the patient looks.

topups.q:
**Caustic ingestion with hoarseness and drooling:**
**a** First step
**b** Then
**c** What not to do
**d** Steroids?
a: **a** **Secure the airway early** (fibreoptic or awake): laryngeal oedema worsens over hours.
**b** **Endoscopy within 12–24 h** for Zargar grading.
**c** No emesis, no charcoal, no neutralisation, no blind NG tube.
**d** No overall benefit; only a deep circumferential **grade IIb** burn may benefit — never grade III (masks perforation).

x.intro: A patient has swallowed a strong acid or alkali. The burn to the pharynx and larynx swells over the following hours, so a patient who is talking now can obstruct later. Hoarseness, stridor and drooling show that the larynx is already involved.
why: a

**Secure the airway early (fibreoptic or awake): laryngeal oedema worsens over hours.** Intubation becomes harder as the oedema grows, so it is done while it is still possible. Paralysing a patient with a swollen, distorted airway risks a can’t-intubate, can’t-oxygenate crisis, so spontaneous breathing is kept (awake fibreoptic), and blind nasal intubation is avoided because it can perforate burned tissue.
b

**Endoscopy within 12–24 h for Zargar grading.** Grading the depth of the burn predicts stricture and perforation and guides feeding and steroid decisions. Beyond about 48 hours the healing wall softens, and it is weakest from roughly day 5 to day 15, when endoscopy carries the highest risk of perforation.
c

**No emesis, no charcoal, no neutralisation, no blind NG tube.** Vomiting re-exposes the oesophagus and airway to the caustic. Charcoal does not bind caustics and obscures endoscopy. Neutralisation produces heat and adds thermal injury, and a blind tube can perforate a burned oesophagus.
d

**No overall benefit; only a deep circumferential grade IIb burn may benefit — never grade III (masks perforation).** Trials have not shown that steroids reduce strictures overall. In grade IIb burns, some data suggest a reduction; in grade III necrosis, steroids add infection risk and hide the signs of perforation.
mimic: Alkali vs acid
Alkali causes liquefactive necrosis, penetrating deeply, mainly in the oesophagus; acid causes coagulative necrosis, often worse in the stomach.
traps: “No mouth burns, so no oesophageal injury”
The oesophagus can be burned without visible oral injury; symptoms guide endoscopy.
“Neutralise the alkali with a weak acid”
The reaction produces heat and worsens the burn.
“Steroids prevent strictures”
No overall benefit, and harmful in grade III.
decode: Drooling, hoarseness after drinking drain cleaner
x.punch: A caustic burn of the larynx swells while the patient still looks well, so the airway is secured first and the endoscopy grades everything else.

topups.q:
**SJS/TEN vs DRESS:**
**a** SJS vs TEN
**b** Timing after the drug
**c** The feature that marks DRESS
**d** Mucosa
**e** Treatment
a: **a** One spectrum by detachment: **SJS <10% · overlap 10–30% · TEN >30%** BSA.
**b** SJS/TEN **4–28 days**; DRESS **2–8 weeks**.
**c** **Eosinophilia** with fever, facial oedema, nodes and organ involvement (liver most).
**d** SJS/TEN: involved. DRESS: usually **spared**.
**e** SJS/TEN: stop the drug, burn-unit care (ciclosporin or IVIG may help). DRESS: stop the drug, **steroids with a slow taper**.

x.sub: Toxicology → Drug reactions → SJS/TEN vs DRESS
x.intro: Two severe drug reactions can bring a patient to the ICU with a rash and fever. SJS/TEN is widespread death of the epidermis and mucosa, behaving like a burn. DRESS is a delayed systemic hypersensitivity reaction in which the internal organs, not the skin, carry the risk.
why: a

**One spectrum by detachment: SJS <10% · overlap 10–30% · TEN >30% BSA.** Both are caused by cytotoxic T cells killing keratinocytes. The name depends only on the area of skin that detaches, and mortality rises with it.
b

**SJS/TEN 4–28 days; DRESS 2–8 weeks.** The latency is a key clue. DRESS appears later than almost any other drug rash, so a recently started drug may not be the cause — the causative drug is often one started a month or more before.
c

**Eosinophilia with fever, facial oedema, nodes and organ involvement (liver most).** DRESS is a systemic hypersensitivity, so blood and organs are affected. Hepatitis is the commonest organ injury; kidney, lung and heart can be involved.
d
**SJS/TEN: involved. DRESS: usually spared.** Mucosal erosions of the mouth, eyes and genitals are part of SJS/TEN, usually from the start. In DRESS they are absent or mild.
e

**SJS/TEN: stop the drug, burn-unit care (ciclosporin or IVIG may help). DRESS: stop the drug, steroids with a slow taper.** SJS/TEN is managed like a burn: fluids, wound care, eye care, infection control. In DRESS the immune reaction drives organ damage, so systemic steroids are used, tapered slowly because it relapses.
mimic: TEN vs staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
SSSS splits more superficially, spares mucosa and affects mainly children.
traps: “The rash began 5 weeks after the drug, so it is not drug-induced”
DRESS typically appears at 2–8 weeks.
“Stop steroids once the rash fades”
DRESS relapses; taper slowly over weeks.
decode: Started carbamazepine 5 weeks ago, fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia, raised ALT
10 days after a new drug, blisters, oral erosions, 40% detachment
x.punch: Timing and blood separate them: early skin and mucosal necrosis is SJS/TEN and is treated as a burn; late fever, eosinophils and organ injury is DRESS and is treated with a slow steroid taper.

topups.q:
**Quinine overdose:**
**a** First symptoms
**b** The classic exam feature
**c** ECG and treatment
**d** Glucose
**e** Elimination
a: **a** **Cinchonism**: tinnitus, deafness, nausea, headache.
**b** **Blindness** at 6–12 h, fixed dilated pupils.
**c** **Na⁺-channel block**: wide QRS, VT → **bicarbonate**.
**d** **Hypoglycaemia** (quinine releases insulin).
**e** **Multi-dose charcoal**; dialysis does not help.

x.intro: Quinine is still used for malaria and, in some places, for cramps. In overdose it behaves like other sodium-channel blockers on the heart, but it also damages the retina and stimulates insulin release. These two features make it recognisable.
why: a

**Cinchonism: tinnitus, deafness, nausea, headache.** These appear even at high therapeutic levels and are the first sign of toxicity. They come from toxicity to the inner ear and the central nervous system.
b
**Blindness at 6–12 h, fixed dilated pupils.** Quinine is directly toxic to the retina. Vision may recover partly over weeks, but permanent loss can occur.
c

**Na⁺-channel block: wide QRS, VT → bicarbonate.** Like tricyclics, quinine slows conduction through sodium channels, widening the QRS and causing ventricular arrhythmias. Sodium bicarbonate raises extracellular sodium and pH, which reduces drug binding to the channel. It also blocks potassium channels, so the QT lengthens.
d
**Hypoglycaemia (quinine releases insulin).** Quinine stimulates insulin secretion from pancreatic β cells. Low glucose can add to coma and seizures, so it is checked repeatedly.
e

**Multi-dose charcoal; dialysis does not help.** Repeated charcoal binds quinine in the gut and draws it from the circulation, shortening its half-life. Quinine is widely distributed in tissues and protein-bound, so little is in the blood for dialysis to remove.
mimic: Quinine vs tricyclic overdose
Both widen the QRS and respond to bicarbonate; quinine adds blindness, tinnitus and hypoglycaemia.
Quinine vs salicylate
Both cause tinnitus; salicylate gives respiratory alkalosis with metabolic acidosis, not wide QRS and blindness.
traps: “Dialyse to remove quinine”
Its large distribution volume makes dialysis ineffective; use multi-dose charcoal.
“Coma in quinine overdose is only cardiac”
Hypoglycaemia from insulin release can cause or worsen it.
decode: Overdose with tinnitus, then sudden blindness
Recurrent low glucose in a malaria patient on quinine
x.punch: Quinine is a sodium-channel blocker with two extras: it blinds and it releases insulin, so give bicarbonate for the QRS, glucose for the sugar, and charcoal, not dialysis.

topups.q:
**Lamotrigine or carbamazepine overdose:**
**a** Why they can CAUSE seizures
**b** ECG
**c** Seizure treatment
**d** QRS >100 ms
a: **a** At toxic levels the Na⁺ block silences **inhibitory interneurons** → paradoxical seizures.
**b** **Wide QRS** — the same block in the heart.
**c** **Benzodiazepines**, then phenobarbital or propofol.
**d** **Bicarbonate**; lipid if refractory.

x.sub: Toxicology → Sodium-channel blockers → Antiseizure drug overdose
x.intro: Lamotrigine and carbamazepine control seizures by blocking neuronal sodium channels. In overdose the same block appears in the heart, and, paradoxically, the brain can start seizing. Treating these seizures means choosing drugs that do not add more sodium-channel block.
why: a

**At toxic levels the Na⁺ block silences inhibitory interneurons → paradoxical seizures.** The proposed explanation: inhibitory interneurons fire rapidly and depend heavily on sodium channels, so they may be suppressed first. With less inhibition, excitatory neurons are released and seizures follow.
b

**Wide QRS — the same block in the heart.** Cardiac sodium channels conduct the impulse through the ventricles. Blocking them slows conduction and widens the QRS, with risk of ventricular arrhythmia and hypotension.
c

**Benzodiazepines, then phenobarbital or propofol.** These work on GABA-A receptors and do not depend on sodium channels. Phenytoin is avoided because it is itself a sodium-channel blocker and adds to cardiac toxicity.
d

**Bicarbonate; lipid if refractory.** Raising extracellular sodium and pH reduces drug binding to the channel and narrows the QRS. Intravenous lipid emulsion is a rescue therapy for lipophilic drugs when the patient does not respond.
mimic: Antiseizure drug vs tricyclic overdose
Both cause wide QRS and seizures and both respond to bicarbonate; carbamazepine is structurally similar to tricyclics and also anticholinergic.
traps: “Seizures in overdose mean the antiseizure level is low”
In toxicity the drug itself can cause seizures.
“Phenytoin for the seizures”
It is another sodium-channel blocker and worsens cardiac toxicity.
“A wide QRS needs procainamide or flecainide”
Class Ia and Ic add sodium-channel block; give bicarbonate (lidocaine is only a second-line option after bicarbonate).
decode: Carbamazepine overdose, seizures — which anticonvulsant to avoid?
Refractory hypotension and wide QRS despite bicarbonate
x.punch: Too much sodium-channel block silences the brain’s brakes and slows the heart, so treat with GABA drugs and bicarbonate, never another sodium-channel blocker.

topups.q: **Spot it:** seizures that continue after a benzodiazepine, high anion gap acidosis, coma — on TB treatment.
a: **Isoniazid** — give **pyridoxine** with the benzodiazepine: gram for gram, or **5 g IV** if the amount is unknown.
Phenytoin does not work.

x.intro: A patient on tuberculosis treatment is seizing, and the seizures do not stop with a benzodiazepine. Isoniazid in overdose depletes the vitamin the brain needs to make its main inhibitory transmitter. Until that vitamin is replaced, the usual anticonvulsants have little to act on.
why: a

**Isoniazid — give pyridoxine with the benzodiazepine: gram for gram, or 5 g IV if the amount is unknown.** Isoniazid depletes pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6, which is the cofactor for glutamic acid decarboxylase, the enzyme that makes GABA. With low GABA the brain seizes, and benzodiazepines, which enhance GABA, have too little GABA to work with. Pyridoxine restores GABA synthesis, and the two drugs together stop the seizures. The acidosis is lactic, mainly from the seizures, and isoniazid also slows lactate clearance.
b
**Phenytoin does not work.** Phenytoin acts on sodium channels and does nothing to correct the GABA deficit. The seizures are corrected only by replacing pyridoxine.
mimic: Isoniazid vs other causes of refractory seizures in overdose
Tricyclics, bupropion and tramadol also cause seizures; the clue to isoniazid is TB treatment and failure of benzodiazepines.
Isoniazid vs toxic alcohol
Both give coma and high anion gap acidosis; isoniazid has seizures from the start and a TB history.
traps: “More benzodiazepine will eventually work”
Without pyridoxine there is too little GABA to enhance.
“Load phenytoin for refractory seizures”
It does not act on GABA synthesis and fails.
“Pyridoxine replaces the benzodiazepine”
They are given together; they work as a pair.
decode: TB patient, refractory seizures, high anion gap acidosis
Unknown amount of isoniazid ingested — pyridoxine dose?
x.punch: Isoniazid takes away the vitamin B6 that GABA synthesis depends on, so GABA drugs fail until pyridoxine is replaced.

topups.q:
**Acute radiation syndrome — dose to syndrome:**
**a** >1 Gy
**b** >6 Gy
**c** ≥20 Gy
**d** Early clue to a high dose
a: **a** **Haematopoietic**: marrow nadir at 2–4 weeks; the 48-h lymphocyte count estimates the dose.
**b** **Gastrointestinal**: vomiting, diarrhoea, sepsis within days.
**c** **Neurovascular** (signs from ~20 Gy, full syndrome >~50 Gy): collapse within hours; uniformly fatal.
**d** **Vomiting within 1 hour**.

x.sub: Toxicology → Physical agents → Acute radiation syndrome
x.intro: After whole-body radiation exposure, cells that divide rapidly die first, because radiation damages DNA and the damage shows when a cell tries to divide. The dose therefore decides which tissue fails: marrow at the lowest dose, then gut lining, and at very high doses the nervous system and blood vessels. Estimating the dose early guides who needs intensive care.
why: a

**Haematopoietic: marrow nadir at 2–4 weeks; the 48-h lymphocyte count estimates the dose.** Marrow stem cells are very sensitive, but mature blood cells already in circulation survive their normal lifespan, so counts fall over weeks. Lymphocytes are the exception: they die directly from radiation, and the fall in the absolute lymphocyte count over the first 48 hours tracks the dose.
b

**Gastrointestinal: vomiting, diarrhoea, sepsis within days.** The crypt cells that replace the gut lining are destroyed, so the lining sloughs within days. Fluid loss, bleeding and bacterial translocation follow, made worse by the falling neutrophil count.
c

**Neurovascular (signs from ~20 Gy, full syndrome >~50 Gy): collapse within hours; uniformly fatal.** At these doses damage to blood vessels and neurons causes oedema, confusion, hypotension and collapse within hours. Death follows within days, and care is palliative.
d

**Vomiting within 1 hour.** The prodrome of nausea and vomiting comes earlier with higher doses. Vomiting within an hour suggests a dose of roughly 4 Gy or more, which means significant marrow failure is likely.
mimic: Radiation sickness vs gastroenteritis
Early vomiting after a known exposure, followed by falling lymphocytes, marks radiation injury.
traps: “The patient feels well after the prodrome, so the dose was low”
A latent phase follows the prodrome; the marrow nadir comes weeks later.
“Platelets and neutrophils fall first”
Lymphocytes fall first, within 48 hours; they estimate the dose.
decode: High dose — expect marrow failure, possibly GI syndrome.
Best early lab estimate of dose
Collapse and confusion within hours of exposure
x.punch: The faster a tissue divides, the lower the dose that kills it: marrow first, then gut lining, then nerves and vessels, and how soon the patient vomits shows how high the dose was.

APAP-01.intro: Paracetamol is safe at therapeutic doses because the liver has more than enough capacity to make it harmless. Toxicity is a matter of dose per kilogram: once the ingested amount outruns that capacity, a toxic metabolite starts to accumulate. The thresholds below mark where the risk begins, where it becomes near-certain, and how severe injury is defined.
why: a

**Maximum therapeutic dose 4 g/day in adults; 75 mg/kg/day in children.** At these doses glucuronidation and sulfation handle almost all of the drug, and the small oxidised fraction is mopped up by glutathione without depleting it.
b

**Toxic single dose: >150 mg/kg, or 7.5–10 g in an adult.** Above this the conjugation pathways saturate, so a larger share of the dose is diverted to oxidation, and the resulting NAPQI begins to use up glutathione faster than the liver can make it (APAP-02).
c

**Liver failure almost certain above 350 mg/kg (untreated).** At this dose glutathione is exhausted early and NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins in large amounts; without N-acetylcysteine severe hepatotoxicity is the rule rather than the exception.
d

**Severe hepatotoxicity: peak AST or ALT >1000 U/L.** Transaminases leak from necrotic hepatocytes, so a peak above 1000 marks substantial necrosis. It is the standard end-point used in the studies behind the nomogram and NAC timing.
e

**Peak level at 1.5–2 h normally; within 4 hours in overdose — later with opioids, anticholinergics or food.** Paracetamol is absorbed quickly from the small intestine, so a level taken 4 hours after ingestion has usually captured the peak. Anything that slows gastric emptying (opioid or anticholinergic co-ingestion, food, large tablet masses) delays the peak, which is why a 4-hour level is the earliest valid one (APAP-06).
mimic: Hepatotoxicity vs hepatic failure
Hepatotoxicity is a laboratory definition (AST/ALT >1000); hepatic failure adds coagulopathy and encephalopathy. Most patients with hepatotoxicity recover.
traps: “A 2-hour level can show the peak”
Absorption may not be complete before 4 hours, and later still with opioids or anticholinergics.
“Toxicity is set by the number of tablets”
It is set by mg/kg — 10 g is far more dangerous in a 45 kg woman than in a 90 kg man.
“ALT 600 meets severe hepatotoxicity”
The definition is a peak above 1000 U/L.
decode: Peak AST or ALT above 1000 U/L.
APAP-01.punch: Paracetamol is dosed by the liver’s capacity: above 150 mg/kg the safe pathways saturate and the toxic metabolite starts to win, and above 350 mg/kg it almost always wins unless N-acetylcysteine is given.
fix: WATCH: pesticides “dominate”
Pesticides dominate poisoning deaths in India, but acute liver failure in India is mostly viral hepatitis (HEV, HBV) and anti-TB drug injury.

APAP-02.sub: Toxicology → Dose & Mechanism → Metabolism and injury
APAP-02.intro: Paracetamol itself does not damage the liver; one of its metabolites does. Normally that metabolite is made in small amounts and neutralised at once by glutathione. Injury happens when the dose is large enough to use up glutathione, and it happens where the metabolite is made — in the hepatocytes around the central vein.
why: a

**90% glucuronidation and sulfation (non-toxic); 1–2% unchanged in urine; 5–9% oxidised (your notes’ text says 5–7%).** Conjugation attaches a water-soluble group so the drug can be excreted; the products are inert. Only the oxidised fraction is dangerous, and in overdose this fraction grows because the conjugating pathways saturate.
b

**NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine), made by CYP2E1.** NAPQI is a highly reactive electrophile: it attacks the sulphydryl groups of cell proteins. CYP2E1 is the main enzyme, with contributions from CYP3A4 and CYP1A2.
c

**Conjugation with glutathione to cysteine and mercapturic acid conjugates.** Glutathione donates its sulphydryl group to NAPQI, making a harmless conjugate that is processed and excreted in urine. Each molecule of NAPQI uses up glutathione, so the store falls as the dose rises.
d

**Injury begins when glutathione stores fall by 70–80%: NAPQI binds cell proteins (adducts), mitochondria fail, and the cell necroses.** While glutathione is available, NAPQI is captured before it reaches proteins. Once stores are below about a quarter of normal, NAPQI binds mitochondrial proteins, causing oxidative stress, loss of ATP and necrosis. The protein–paracetamol adducts that leak out are the basis of the adduct test (APAP-07).
e

**Centrilobular (zone 3), where CYP450 is concentrated.** NAPQI is made where CYP2E1 is most abundant, around the central vein; zone 3 also receives the least oxygenated blood. So the necrosis is centrilobular, and periportal (zone 1) cells are relatively spared.
mimic: Paracetamol vs ischaemic hepatitis
Ischaemic hepatitis is also centrilobular (zone 3, least oxygen). Paracetamol injury follows an ingestion with a timed rise in transaminases; ischaemic injury follows shock.
traps: “The toxic metabolite is made by glucuronidation”
Glucuronidation makes inert conjugates; NAPQI comes from CYP2E1 oxidation.
“Paracetamol injury is periportal”
It is centrilobular, zone 3 — where CYP2E1 is concentrated.
“NAPQI injures the liver from the first tablet”
It is harmless while glutathione lasts; injury starts after a 70–80% fall.
decode: Zone of necrosis in paracetamol poisoning
APAP-02.punch: Paracetamol is poisonous only through NAPQI, which glutathione neutralises until about three-quarters of the store is gone — and because CYP2E1 sits around the central vein, that is where the liver dies.

APAP-03.intro: Two things decide how much harm a given dose does: how fast NAPQI is made, and how much glutathione is there to meet it. Anything that speeds CYP oxidation or lowers glutathione raises the risk; anything that slows oxidation or boosts conjugation lowers it. Every item on this list fits one of those two levers.
why: a

**Raises: chronic alcohol.** Long-term drinking induces CYP2E1, so more NAPQI is made from the same dose, and the poor nutrition that goes with it lowers glutathione. Both levers move against the patient.
b

**Raises: CYP inducers — anticonvulsants, antitubercular drugs — and tobacco.** Enzyme inducers increase oxidative metabolism. Isoniazid acts on CYP2E1; phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital and rifampicin induce other CYP isoforms that can also make NAPQI. Smoking induces CYP1A2 and has been linked to worse outcomes after overdose.
c

**Raises: fasting and malnutrition.** Glutathione is built from amino acids, chiefly cysteine; a starved or malnourished patient has smaller stores and less capacity for glucuronidation, so NAPQI overwhelms the defence sooner.
d

**Raises: age over 40, Gilbert syndrome, repeated supratherapeutic dosing.** Older patients have less hepatic reserve and worse outcomes. Gilbert syndrome reduces UGT1A1 activity, so in theory less drug is glucuronidated and more is left for oxidation; the clinical evidence for this is weak. Repeated dosing wears glutathione down over days (APAP-04).
e

**Lowers: childhood — more glutathione, more conjugation.** Young children clear paracetamol mainly by sulfation, which they do efficiently, and they make glutathione readily, so a smaller fraction becomes NAPQI and it is neutralised faster.
f

**Lowers: acute alcohol co-ingestion — it competes for CYP2E1.** Ethanol drunk at the same time occupies CYP2E1, so less paracetamol is oxidised to NAPQI while the alcohol is present. The same enzyme, once induced by chronic drinking, has the opposite effect.
mimic: Acute vs chronic alcohol
Acute alcohol competes for CYP2E1 and protects; chronic alcohol induces CYP2E1 and depletes glutathione, and harms.
traps: “Alcohol always increases paracetamol toxicity”
Acute co-ingestion is protective; only chronic use increases risk.
“Children are at higher risk because they are smaller”
Dosed per kg, children are at lower risk: more sulfation and glutathione.
“Risk factors mean a lower nomogram line in the UK”
The UK abolished its separate high-risk line in 2012; everyone is treated above the single 100 line (APAP-06).
decode: Chronic alcoholic, fasting, takes 6 g over a day
High risk: induced CYP2E1 and low glutathione.
Paracetamol taken with a bottle of whisky at a party
Acute alcohol — protective while it lasts.
Why do toddlers tolerate accidental ingestions better?
More sulfation and glutathione, less NAPQI.
APAP-03.punch: Every risk factor either makes more NAPQI or leaves less glutathione to meet it — which is why chronic alcohol harms and acute alcohol, competing for the same enzyme, protects.

parts.q: Children under ~10: main clearance route?
parts.a: **Sulfation** (adults mainly glucuronidation), with more glutathione — so less NAPQI. The nomogram and NAC rules still apply.

fix: Anticonvulsants listed as CYP2E1 inducers

Only isoniazid and alcohol act mainly on CYP2E1; phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital and rifampicin induce other CYP isoforms. The evidence that inducers raise risk is weak (the UK dropped its high-risk line in 2012).

APAP-04.sub: Toxicology → Dose & Mechanism → Repeated supratherapeutic ingestion
APAP-04.intro: Not every paracetamol poisoning is a single deliberate overdose. A patient in pain — a toothache, a fever, a hangover — may take a little more than the maximum dose, several times a day, for several days. Each dose is small, but glutathione is never allowed to recover, and the patient does not see a doctor until the liver is already injured.
why: a

**More dangerous: presents late with established injury, so severe hepatotoxicity and death are more frequent.** There is no dramatic event to bring the patient in, so the treatment window passes unnoticed. These patients are also often the ones with risk factors — fasting through illness, chronic alcohol — so glutathione is low before the excess even begins (APAP-03).
b

**The nomogram does not apply: levels do not correlate with toxicity.** The nomogram reads a level against the time since one ingestion. With many doses there is no single time zero, and much of the drug has already been metabolised, so a low level can coexist with severe injury.
c

**NAC if more than 7.5 g in 24 h (4 g with risk factors), symptoms, a level above 20 µg/mL, or raised transaminases (>50) whatever the level.** Because the level cannot be plotted, the decision rests on the amount taken and on two simple markers: a level above 20 µg/mL means enough drug is still circulating to keep making NAPQI, and a raised ALT means injury has already begun. The exact dose thresholds differ between guidelines (Australia–NZ, for example, uses 10 g or 200 mg/kg in 24 h, 6 g or 150 mg/kg a day for 48 h or more, and 4 g or 100 mg/kg in 24 h with risk factors), but the level and ALT triggers are shared. Either one is a reason to start NAC (APAP-14 watch: 12 hours of IV NAC, then repeat the tests).
mimic: Repeated ingestion vs staggered overdose
Both lack a single time zero, so neither can be plotted. A staggered overdose is several large doses over hours; repeated supratherapeutic ingestion is over-dosing for pain over days.
traps: “Plot the level and treat only if it is above the line”
The nomogram is invalid for repeated ingestion; treat on dose, level >20 or raised ALT.
“A low level means low risk”
The drug has already been metabolised; ALT tells you about injury.
decode: Repeated supratherapeutic ingestion — start NAC; the nomogram does not apply.
Repeated ingestion, level 25 µg/mL, ALT normal
Treat — a level above 20 is an indication.
APAP-04.punch: With repeated dosing there is no time zero to plot, the level understates the danger, and the patient comes late — so treatment is triggered by the dose, any meaningful level, or a rising ALT.
fix: Repeated ingestion: 7.5 g, or 4 g with risk factors, in 24 h

Guidelines use ≥10 g or 200 mg/kg in 24 h, or ≥6 g or 150 mg/kg a day for ≥48 h (US consensus 2006, Australia–NZ); Australia–NZ adds ≥4 g or 100 mg/kg in 24 h with risk factors. The level >20 µg/mL and ALT >50 triggers are right.

APAP-05.intro: Paracetamol poisoning unfolds over days, and the time course follows the mechanism. In the first day NAPQI is depleting glutathione and binding proteins, but cells have not yet died, so the patient looks almost well. Necrosis declares itself on days 2 to 4, and those who survive the peak regenerate their liver.
why: a

**Stage I, 0.5–24 h: nausea, vomiting, pallor, sweating; laboratory tests usually normal.** The symptoms are non-specific gastrointestinal upset. Injury is under way inside the hepatocyte, but transaminases have not yet leaked — which is exactly why a level is sent in every overdose (TOX-02).
b

**Stage II, 24–72 h: symptoms settle; right upper quadrant pain; transaminases rise; oliguria.** Hepatocytes are now dying, so ALT and AST rise and the swollen liver causes right upper quadrant pain. Oliguria is the first sign of the renal tubular injury that paracetamol can cause independently of the liver.
c

**Stage III, 72–96 h: peak injury — AST/ALT above 10,000, coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia, encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, AKI.** The failing liver cannot make clotting factors (INR rises), cannot release glucose (hypoglycaemia), cannot clear ammonia (encephalopathy) or lactate (lactic acidosis). Death in this stage is from cerebral oedema, multi-organ failure, haemorrhage or sepsis.
d

**Stage IV, beyond 5 days: recovery, usually complete by day 7.** The liver regenerates from surviving cells and survivors usually recover without chronic liver disease. Biochemical recovery is often under way by the end of the first week, but Goldfrank’s places stage IV from about day 4 to 2 weeks, and histological recovery can take up to 3 months; the AKI recovers over 1–4 weeks.
mimic: Stage I vs stage II
Nausea and sweating with normal enzymes is stage I; right upper quadrant pain with rising enzymes is stage II.
traps: “She feels better on day 2, so she can go home”
Stage II is the deceptive one: symptoms settle while the liver worsens. Decide on ALT and INR.
“Normal LFTs at 12 hours exclude poisoning”
Stage I labs are normal; the level, not the LFTs, decides treatment.
“Survivors of paracetamol liver failure develop cirrhosis”
Survivors usually regenerate fully; chronic liver disease is not the expected outcome.
decode: RUQ pain, rising enzymes at 48 h
Jaundice, INR 3 and AKI at 36 h
Severe poisoning reaching stage III early — fulminant hepatic failure.
Leading causes of death in fulminant paracetamol failure
APAP-05.punch: The stages track the mechanism: silent glutathione depletion on day 1, necrosis that the patient does not feel on day 2, liver failure by days 3–4, and regeneration in those who survive — so a well patient on day 2 is not a safe patient.

parts.q: Severe poisoning: can stage III come early?
parts.a: **Yes** — jaundice, INR 3 and AKI at 36 h already mean fulminant hepatic failure; the killers are **cerebral oedema** and dysrhythmias with **multi-organ failure**.

fix: Stage IV usually complete by day 7
Recovery runs from about day 4–5 to 2 weeks; the liver tissue takes up to 3 months to heal (Goldfrank’s).

APAP-06.intro: After a single overdose the paracetamol level falls steadily once absorption is complete. If the level at a known time is high, more drug is reaching CYP2E1 and the risk of injury is higher. The nomogram turns that into a line: plot one level against the hours since ingestion, and treat if the point lies above the line.
why: a

**It plots serum paracetamol against time since a single acute ingestion.** The line is drawn on a log scale and falls by half every 4 hours — a deliberately long half-life (the drug’s own is 2–3 hours, longer in overdose), so the line stays conservative. It only works when there is one known time zero.
b
**Earliest valid level: 4 hours after ingestion.** Before 4 hours absorption may not be complete, so the level is still rising and a low value can be falsely reassuring (APAP-01).
c

**Original line: 200 µg/mL at 4 h. Treatment line, 25% lower: 150 at 4 h.** Rumack and Matthew drew the 200 line from patients who developed hepatotoxicity. US practice lowered it by 25% to 150 to allow for errors in the timing and the assay — a deliberate safety margin.
d

**Revised UK line (2012): a single line from 100 at 4 h to 15 at 15 h, with no risk stratification.** After a Commission on Human Medicines review in 2012, the UK regulator (MHRA) moved everyone to the 100 line and dropped the separate high-risk line, because risk factors could not be judged reliably at the bedside (APAP-03). The price is that many more patients receive NAC.
e

**Not usable: staggered or repeated ingestion, unknown time; with sustained-release, take 4- and 8-hour levels and treat if either is above the line.** Without a single time zero the point cannot be placed. Sustained-release tablets may produce a late or second peak, so one level can understate the exposure.
mimic: µg/mL vs mg/L vs µmol/L
µg/mL and mg/L are the same number (150 µg/mL = 150 mg/L). Laboratories reporting in µmol/L multiply by about 6.6, so the 150 line is about 990 µmol/L and the UK 100 line about 660 µmol/L.
traps: “A 2-hour level above the line can be plotted”
The nomogram starts at 4 hours.
“Plot a level after a staggered overdose”
There is no single time zero; treat instead.
“The treatment line is 200 at 4 hours”
200 is the original line; the US treatment line is 150 and the UK line 100.
decode: 100 mg/L at 4 h, one line for all.
Below the 150 line, above the UK 100 line — the answer depends on which line the question names.
APAP-06.punch: The nomogram reads one level against one time, so it needs a single ingestion at a known time and a level at 4 hours or later — then the only question is which line the question names: 200, 150 or 100.

parts.q: More than 150 mg/kg taken, level will not be back before 8 hours: wait?
parts.a: **No** — start NAC on the dose and stop it if the level returns below the line (APAP-14).

APAP-07.intro: Some patients arrive in liver failure days after an overdose they do not mention. By then the paracetamol has been cleared, so the level is undetectable and cannot prove the cause. But the injury leaves a fingerprint: when NAPQI binds liver proteins and the cells die, the bound fragments leak into the blood and persist for days.
why: a

**They establish paracetamol as the cause of liver injury when the level is already undetectable.** Adducts form only when NAPQI binds cysteine groups on proteins (APAP-02), so they are specific to paracetamol toxicity. Their half-life in blood is far longer than the drug’s, so they remain measurable after the parent drug is gone.
b

**Above 1 nmol/mL (with ALT above 1000), measured by HPLC.** A high adduct level together with severe hepatotoxicity indicates that paracetamol caused the injury; therapeutic dosing produces only low adduct levels.
c

**AcetaSTAT: a competitive immunoassay giving a positive or negative result only.** It is a rapid strip test designed for the bedside where HPLC is not available; it answers ‘has paracetamol injured this liver?’ but does not give a number.
mimic: Paracetamol level vs adducts
The level measures drug still in the blood and guides NAC early; adducts measure injury already done and identify the cause late.
traps: “An undetectable level excludes paracetamol as the cause of liver failure”
The drug is cleared within a day; adducts persist and can prove the cause.
“Adducts are raised in anyone taking therapeutic paracetamol”
Therapeutic dosing gives only low levels; the high cut-off with ALT >1000 is what matters.
decode: Acute liver failure, denies overdose, paracetamol undetectable
APAP-07.punch: When the drug has gone but the liver has failed, adducts are the fingerprint NAPQI left on the dead cells — proof of cause, not a guide to NAC dosing.

APAP-08.intro: The liver cannot take up glutathione given from outside, but it can make its own from cysteine. N-acetylcysteine delivers that cysteine, so it refills the store that NAPQI is draining. Its effect is greatest before glutathione runs out and NAPQI starts binding proteins — but it still helps after that, by other means.
why: a

**Replenishes glutathione; enhances sulfation; antioxidant and anti-inflammatory.** NAC is deacetylated to cysteine, the rate-limiting building block of glutathione, so NAPQI is captured before it reaches proteins. Its sulphur also supports the sulfation pathway, so less drug goes to oxidation. Once injury has started, its antioxidant action and improved microcirculation limit further damage — the reason it helps even in liver failure.
b

**Within 8 hours of ingestion: near-complete protection.** In the first 8 hours glutathione has not yet fallen to the point at which NAPQI binds proteins (APAP-02), so refilling it prevents almost all injury. After that, protein binding has begun and each hour of delay allows more necrosis.
c

**Activated charcoal 1 g/kg (maximum 50 g) within 4 hours of a single ingestion; not with altered sensorium unless the airway is protected.** The usual window is 1 hour (TOX-09); some guidelines extend it for paracetamol because large or modified-release overdoses keep absorbing for hours — Australia–NZ, for example, uses 2 hours for an ordinary toxic dose and up to 4 hours for very large (over 30 g) or modified-release ingestions. As with all charcoal, aspiration is the danger, hence the airway condition.
mimic: NAC before vs after 8 hours
Before 8 hours it prevents injury by refilling glutathione; after 8 hours it limits injury that has already begun, so it is still given.
traps: “After 8 hours NAC is useless”
It is still given late and in established liver failure; it improves outcome.
“A patient arriving at 7 hours should wait for the level before NAC”
If the level will not be back by 8 hours and the dose is over 150 mg/kg, start NAC now (APAP-14).
“NAC works by binding paracetamol”
It replenishes glutathione, which binds NAPQI.
decode: Presents 30 hours after overdose with ALT 4000
Give NAC — late treatment still improves outcome.
APAP-08.punch: NAC refills the glutathione that NAPQI drains: given within 8 hours it prevents injury almost completely, and given later it still limits the damage — so it is never withheld for being late.
fix: Charcoal within 4 hours
The usual window is 1 hour; Australia–NZ uses 2 hours for a toxic dose and up to 4 hours only for >30 g or modified-release tablets.

APAP-09.intro: NAC can be given intravenously over about a day or by mouth over three days. Both regimens aim at the same thing — enough cysteine to keep glutathione ahead of NAPQI until the paracetamol has been cleared — and they differ in route, length and side effects.
why: a

**IV 21-hour protocol: bag 1 150 mg/kg in 200 mL 5% dextrose over 60 min; bag 2 50 mg/kg in 500 mL over 4 h; bag 3 100 mg/kg in 1000 mL over 16 h — 300 mg/kg in total.** The large first dose refills glutathione quickly while NAPQI production is at its peak; the smaller later bags (12.5 then 6.25 mg/kg/h) keep it topped up while the remaining paracetamol is cleared. Bag 1 was originally run over 15 minutes; lengthening it to 60 minutes was meant to reduce reactions, though trials showed little difference.
b

**Oral protocol: 140 mg/kg, then 70 mg/kg every 4 h for 17 doses (72 hours).** The oral route delivers NAC straight to the liver through the portal vein, but its systemic bioavailability is low (about 10%) and the sulphurous taste and vomiting make doses hard to keep down. The 72-hour length comes from the original US protocol design rather than from proof that so long a course is needed.
c

**IV is chosen for vomiting, no oral route, pregnancy and liver failure.** In all of these the oral dose may not be absorbed or tolerated, and in liver failure and pregnancy reliable delivery matters most.
d

**Main adverse effect of IV: an anaphylactoid reaction — rate-related, not IgE — so slow or pause, give an antihistamine, then restart.** NAC releases histamine directly, most often during the high-concentration first bag, giving flushing, rash, wheeze and sometimes hypotension. Because no antibody is involved, it is not true allergy and not a contraindication; the infusion is restarted once the reaction settles.
mimic: Anaphylactoid vs anaphylactic reaction
Anaphylactoid is direct histamine release related to rate and concentration; it does not need prior exposure and allows NAC to be restarted.
traps: “A rash on bag 1 means NAC must be stopped for good”
It is anaphylactoid: pause, antihistamine, restart.
“The first IV bag is 150 mg/kg over 15 minutes”
The original protocol used 15 minutes; your notes print 60 minutes, which is current practice in the three-bag regimen.
“The oral course lasts 21 hours”
Oral is 72 hours (loading dose plus 17 doses); IV is 21 hours.
decode: Flushing and wheeze 30 minutes into NAC
APAP-09.punch: Both regimens refill glutathione — IV front-loads it over 21 hours, oral spreads it over 72 — and the IV reaction is anaphylactoid, so it means slowing down, not stopping.

parts.q: Newer IV regimens with fewer reactions?
parts.a: **Two-bag** (Australia–NZ): 200 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h. **SNAP** (Scottish, Bateman, Lancet 2014): 100 mg/kg over 2 h, then 200 mg/kg over 10 h — 12 hours. Both give 300 mg/kg but avoid the high-concentration first bag: in its trial SNAP cut both vomiting and anaphylactoid reactions, and the two-bag regimen mainly reduces reactions.

APAP-10.intro: The 21-hour protocol is a fixed course, but the patient may not be finished when the bags are. NAC is needed for as long as paracetamol is still being turned into NAPQI or the liver is still being injured. So, at the end of the course, the decision to stop rests on three blood tests rather than the clock.
why: a

**Stop when paracetamol is undetectable, ALT is falling, and INR is below 2.** An undetectable level means no more NAPQI is being made. A falling ALT means necrosis has stopped. An INR under 2 means synthetic function is preserved. Together they show that the poison has gone and the liver is recovering.
b

**If not met at 21 hours, continue at 6.25 mg/kg/h — the third-bag rate — and repeat the tests 12-hourly.** The third bag gives 100 mg/kg over 16 hours, which is 6.25 mg/kg/h; continuing at that rate maintains the protection without a new loading dose.
c
**In established liver failure, continue until transplant or resolution.** NAC still improves survival once the liver is failing (APAP-08), so it is continued for as long as the failure lasts.
mimic: Falling ALT: recovery vs burnout
A falling ALT with a falling INR means recovery; a falling ALT with a rising INR means too few hepatocytes are left — a bad sign (APAP-11).
traps: “The 21-hour course is complete, so stop NAC”
Stop only if the level is undetectable, ALT falling and INR below 2.
“Restart with a new 150 mg/kg loading bag”
Continue at the third-bag rate, 6.25 mg/kg/h.
decode: End of 21 h: level undetectable, ALT rising, INR 2.4
Continue NAC at 6.25 mg/kg/h, repeat tests in 12 hours.
APAP-10.punch: NAC is stopped by the blood tests, not the clock: when no drug is left, the ALT is falling and the INR is under 2 — otherwise it continues at the third-bag rate.

APAP-11.sub: Toxicology → Transplant & Sweep → King’s College criteria
APAP-11.intro: Most patients with paracetamol liver failure recover with NAC and intensive care, but some will die without a transplant, and the liver must be found in time. King’s College criteria pick out the group most likely to die, using markers of how much liver function is left. Transaminases are not among them: they measure how many cells died, not how many survive.
why: a

**Arterial pH below 7.30 after fluid resuscitation; OR all three of creatinine above 3.4 mg/dL, grade 3 or 4 encephalopathy and INR above 6.5 (PT above 100 s).** A persistent acidosis despite fluids means the liver can no longer clear lactate and other acids. INR measures loss of synthetic function, encephalopathy loss of detoxification, and creatinine the hepatorenal and direct renal injury. Each limb is a measure of what the liver can no longer do.
b

**Specificity 90%, sensitivity only 60%: it misses patients who will die.** When the criteria are met, death without transplant is very likely, so listing is justified. But a large share of patients who die never meet them, so failing to meet the criteria is not reassurance.
c

**Lactate modification: above 3.5 after 1 hour of fluid resuscitation, or above 3.0 after adequate fluids.** Lactate rises early because the necrotic liver both fails to clear it and produces it. In the original study (Bernal, Lancet 2002) the units are mmol/L, the early value was measured about 4 hours after admission and the later one at about 12 hours, after full fluid resuscitation; adding the post-resuscitation lactate raised the sensitivity of King’s criteria from 76% to 91% and identified non-survivors hours earlier.
mimic: Paracetamol vs non-paracetamol King’s criteria
Non-paracetamol criteria use INR >6.5 alone, or three of five (age, aetiology, jaundice-to-encephalopathy interval, INR >3.5, bilirubin); pH and creatinine are the paracetamol limbs.
traps: “ALT is the prognostic marker”
ALT measures injury, not outcome; pH, INR, creatinine, encephalopathy and lactate predict death.
“Not meeting King’s criteria means the patient will survive”
Sensitivity is only about 60%.
“A falling ALT means recovery”
With a rising INR it means too little liver is left.
decode: pH 7.25 after fluids in paracetamol liver failure
Meets King’s criteria — list for transplant.
Best prognostic marker among options including ALT
Creatinine, pH, INR or lactate — not ALT.
APAP-11.punch: King’s College criteria measure what the liver can no longer do — clear acid, make clotting factors, protect the brain and the kidneys — so they predict death well when met, but miss many who will still die.

APAP-12.sub: Toxicology → Transplant & Sweep → Adjuncts in massive overdose
APAP-12.intro: In a massive overdose NAC alone may not keep up. Enormous levels can also poison mitochondria directly, giving coma and lactic acidosis within hours, before the liver injury of stage III. Adjuncts aim either to stop NAPQI being made or to remove the paracetamol itself — but each sits on top of NAC, never in place of it.
why: a

**Fomepizole: a CYP2E1 inhibitor, an emerging adjunct to NAC (case reports).** Blocking CYP2E1 reduces NAPQI formation at its source, which is attractive when the drug load is too large for glutathione to cope with. In mice it also blocks JNK-mediated mitochondrial injury, which may explain benefit even after metabolism. The human evidence is limited to case reports, and no guideline yet sets a dose or threshold for it.
b

**Haemodialysis clears paracetamol; it is used in massive ingestion with severe lactic acidosis, and is never a substitute for NAC.** Paracetamol is a small molecule with low protein binding and a modest volume of distribution, so dialysis removes it efficiently. The EXTRIP workgroup (2014) recommends it — intermittent haemodialysis preferred — for a level above 1000 mg/L without NAC, or for signs of mitochondrial dysfunction (altered mental status, metabolic acidosis, raised lactate) with a level above 700 mg/L without NAC or above 900 mg/L with NAC. It corrects the acidosis and lowers the drug load, but NAC must continue — at a higher rate, because dialysis also removes NAC.
c
**Cimetidine worked in animals but gave no benefit in humans.** It is a CYP inhibitor and in theory should reduce NAPQI formation; in clinical use it did not improve outcome, so it has no role.
mimic: Early vs late acidosis in paracetamol poisoning
Early (hours), with coma and a massive level, is mitochondrial toxicity — dialysis is considered. Late (days 3–4) is from liver failure — a King’s College criterion (APAP-11).
traps: “Dialysis can replace NAC in massive overdose”
It is always added to NAC, never instead of it.
“Cimetidine is a useful CYP inhibitor adjunct”
It showed no benefit in humans.
“Fomepizole is only for toxic alcohols”
It also inhibits CYP2E1 and is an emerging adjunct here.
decode: Massive paracetamol ingestion, comatose, severe lactic acidosis, level 950 mg/L on NAC
Haemodialysis (EXTRIP) plus NAC at an increased rate.
CYP2E1 inhibitor as an adjunct to NAC
APAP-12.punch: In a massive overdose the adjuncts attack the same problem from two ends — fomepizole stops NAPQI being made, dialysis removes the drug — but NAC stays the treatment throughout.

APAP-13.sub: Toxicology → Transplant & Sweep → True or false
APAP-13.intro: This card tests the deck’s key distinctions. Each statement either holds or turns on one detail from an earlier card; the reason is the mechanism you met there.
why: a
**False — the toxic metabolite is formed by CYP2E1 oxidation.** Glucuronidation makes inert conjugates; NAPQI comes from the small oxidised fraction (APAP-02).
b
**False — injury is centrilobular.** CYP2E1 is concentrated in zone 3, so NAPQI is made, and cells die, around the central vein (APAP-02).
c
**False — the level must be taken at 4 hours or later.** Before 4 hours absorption may be incomplete and the level still rising (APAP-06).
d
**False — acute alcohol is protective; chronic alcohol harms.** Acute ethanol competes for CYP2E1; chronic use induces it (APAP-03).
e
**True — the US treatment line starts at 150 at 4 hours,** 25% below the original 200 line as a safety margin (APAP-06).
f
**True — the first IV NAC bag is 150 mg/kg,** to refill glutathione quickly (APAP-09).
g
**True — NAC is stopped when INR is below 2 and ALT falling, with an undetectable level.** All three are needed: no drug left, necrosis over, function preserved (APAP-10).
h
**True — pH below 7.30 after fluids meets King’s criteria** on its own (APAP-11).
traps: “Alcohol increases toxicity”
Only chronic alcohol; acute co-ingestion protects.
“INR <2 and falling ALT are enough to stop NAC”
The level must also be undetectable.
decode: Ask which pathway makes NAPQI — CYP2E1, not conjugation.
Check the time (≥4 h) and which line (200, 150, 100).
APAP-13.punch: Every statement here turns on a mechanism from earlier in the deck — CYP2E1 making NAPQI in zone 3, absorption complete by 4 hours, and stopping or listing decided by what the liver can still do.

APAP-14.sub: Toxicology → Transplant & Sweep → Indications for NAC
APAP-14.intro: NAC is safe and the cost of missing paracetamol toxicity is a dead liver, so the indications are deliberately broad. They follow one logic: treat whenever the nomogram says the dose is toxic, whenever the nomogram cannot be used but toxicity is possible, and whenever the liver is already injured.
why: a
**Single ingestion with a level at 4 hours or later above the treatment line.** This is the nomogram doing its job: a known time and a valid level place the patient in the risk zone (APAP-06).
b

**More than 150 mg/kg (7.5 g) with no level available within 8 hours.** Protection is near-complete only if NAC starts within 8 hours (APAP-08), so waiting for a delayed result throws away the window. Start on the dose and stop if the level returns below the line.
c
**Unknown dose or time with a level above 10 µg/mL.** Without a time the level cannot be plotted, so any measurable paracetamol means drug is still present to form NAPQI.
d
**Any ingestion with evidence of liver injury.** A raised ALT shows that NAPQI has already overwhelmed glutathione, whatever the level or the history; NAC limits further injury.
e
**Presentation after 24 hours with liver injury.** The nomogram ends at 24 hours, but NAC still improves outcome in late presenters and in liver failure (APAP-08).
mimic: Acute single vs repeated supratherapeutic ingestion
Acute: these five indications and the nomogram. Repeated: dose, level >20 or raised ALT (APAP-04).
traps: “No paracetamol in the history, so no level”
Send a paracetamol level in every deliberate overdose: co-ingestion is common, histories are unreliable and stage I looks harmless.
“Wait for the level even if it will take 10 hours”
Over 150 mg/kg with no result by 8 hours — start NAC.
“Presented at 30 hours, beyond the nomogram, so NAC is pointless”
Late NAC still improves outcome when the liver is injured.
decode: Took 12 g, level will not be available for 9 hours
Found with empty strips, time unknown, level 18 µg/mL
Treat — unknown time with a detectable level.
Combination analgesic overdose with vomiting, other drug named
APAP-14.punch: NAC is given whenever toxicity is shown, cannot be ruled out in time, or has already begun — because the drug is safe and the window is short.

PEST-01.sub: Toxicology → Pesticides → Scale and WHO hazard classes
PEST-01.intro: Organophosphates are the single biggest cause of fatal poisoning in the developing world, because they are cheap, sold without control and kept in the house where farming families live. Most deaths are deliberate self-poisoning, and most happen before or soon after the patient reaches hospital. The WHO grades the compounds by how little of them kills a rat, which is the only practical way of saying in advance how dangerous a bottle on a shelf is.
why: a

**About 3 million people exposed and up to 300,000 deaths a year; the commonest poisoning in developing countries.** The case fatality is high — of the order of 10–20% in South Asian series — not because the drug is exotic but because the dose swallowed is large, the hospital is far and ventilation is scarce. In Indian ICU practice organophosphates compete only with aluminium phosphide (PEST-18) for the top place.
b

**Class Ia extremely hazardous, oral LD50 <5 mg/kg; Ib highly hazardous 5–50; II moderately hazardous 50–2000; III slightly hazardous >2000; U unlikely to be hazardous ≥5000.** The LD50 is the single oral dose that kills half of a group of rats, so a smaller number means a more toxic compound.
