The classes therefore run the opposite way to the numbers: the lower the LD50, the higher the hazard class. The grading is of the technical compound, not of the diluted product in the bottle, so the formulation strength and the solvent still matter at the bedside.
mimic: LD50 vs lethal dose in a patient
LD50 is a population statistic in rats; it ranks compounds but does not predict what a given swallow will do to one person.
WHO hazard class vs clinical severity
Class reflects intrinsic toxicity. Severity in the patient is set by the amount, the formulation and the delay to treatment, and is graded by RBC cholinesterase activity (PEST-09).
traps: “A high WHO class number means a more dangerous pesticide”
It is the reverse: Ia is the most hazardous and III the least, because the class is defined by a low LD50.
“Organophosphate poisoning is mainly occupational”
In South Asia the great majority is deliberate ingestion of a concentrated formulation; occupational exposure is usually mild and dermal.
“Deaths are falling because antidotes have improved”
The fall where it has happened followed bans on the most hazardous compounds — supply, not antidote, drives mortality.
decode: Commonest cause of fatal poisoning in a developing country
Approximate annual global deaths from organophosphates
PEST-01.punch: The WHO class is only the compound’s intrinsic toxicity read backwards from its LD50 — the reason organophosphates kill 300,000 people a year is availability and dose, not subtlety.
fix: Up to 300,000 deaths a year from organophosphates
About 250,000–370,000 deaths a year are from all pesticide self-poisoning, organophosphates the largest share.

PEST-02.intro: All organophosphates do the same thing to acetylcholinesterase, so the class matters for two other reasons: what the two alkyl side groups are, which decides how quickly the enzyme–poison bond becomes permanent, and how fat-soluble the compound is, which decides how long the illness lasts. Carbamates sit alongside them with the same clinical picture but a different chemistry. Nerve agents are the military members of the same family.
why: a

**Dimethyl: dichlorvos, fenthion, malathion, methamidophos.** Two methyl groups are attached to the phosphorus. The bound enzyme loses one of them fast, so ageing takes only about 3 hours (PEST-03) and the window for an oxime is short.
b

**Diethyl: chlorpyrifos, diazinon, parathion, quinalphos.** The bulkier ethyl groups are lost far more slowly, so ageing takes about 33 hours and oximes still work the next day. Several of these (chlorpyrifos, parathion, diazinon) are thions, which must be converted in the liver to their active oxon, so the onset of the cholinergic crisis may be delayed by hours and then prolonged — a feature of the thion chemistry rather than of the ethyl group itself.
c

**Atypical: profenofos.** Its side chains do not fit the dimethyl or diethyl pattern, and the enzyme it inhibits is poorly reactivatable — the rescuable window is effectively absent, which is why oximes do little for it.
d

**Nerve agents: sarin, tabun, soman, VX.** Chemical-warfare organophosphates, far more potent per milligram and absorbed through intact skin. Soman ages within minutes, which is why pretreatment with pyridostigmine and immediate antidote autoinjectors are used in that setting rather than oximes alone.
e

**Carbamates: carbaryl, aldicarb, methomyl, propoxur.** They carbamylate the same esteratic site but the bond hydrolyses spontaneously, so there is no ageing, the illness is shorter and central features are fewer (PEST-03).
mimic: Dimethyl vs diethyl compound
Chemistry you must read off the bottle; it changes only one decision — how much an oxime can still achieve.
Lipophilic vs water-soluble organophosphate
Fenthion, dichlofenthion and malathion are stored in fat and leach back out, so cholinergic features relapse for weeks; water-soluble agents give one defined illness.
traps: “Malathion is harmless because it is used domestically”
It is of low mammalian toxicity per milligram but highly lipophilic, so a large ingestion gives prolonged and relapsing illness.
“Nerve agents need different antidotes”
The antidotes are the same — atropine and an oxime — but ageing is so fast with soman that the oxime must be given within minutes.
“Carbamates are mild”
Aldicarb and methomyl are WHO class Ia and can kill quickly; what differs is the duration, not the severity.
decode: Chlorpyrifos ingestion, pralidoxime at 20 hours — any point?
Yes: diethyl, ageing half-life about 33 h.
Recurrent cholinergic crises over three weeks
A lipophilic agent such as fenthion leaching from fat.
Profenofos (then dimethyl compounds; soman among nerve agents).
PEST-02.punch: The subclass tells you nothing new about the toxidrome and everything about the clock: dimethyl ages in hours, diethyl in a day and a half, carbamates never — and the fat-soluble agents simply refuse to end.

PEST-03.intro: Acetylcholinesterase sits in the synapse and splits acetylcholine the instant it is released. An organophosphate attacks its catalytic (esteratic) site and leaves a phosphate group stuck there, so transmitter accumulates everywhere acetylcholine is used — muscarinic, nicotinic and central synapses. At first that phosphate can still be pulled off; after a chemical rearrangement it cannot. That rearrangement, ageing, is the whole reason oxime treatment is a race.
why: a

**Phosphorylates the esteratic site of acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates at muscarinic, nicotinic and CNS synapses.** The enzyme is normally the only route of acetylcholine removal, and it is fast enough to clear a synapse between impulses. With it inhibited the transmitter lingers, and every cholinergic receptor is stimulated continuously — which is why the picture is a sum of three receptor groups rather than one organ (PEST-04).
b

**Loss of an alkyl group from the bound enzyme: the bond becomes irreversible and oximes no longer work.** The phosphorylated enzyme can spontaneously shed one of its alkyl side chains, leaving a stable, negatively charged mono-alkyl phosphate on the active site. An oxime cannot attack that; recovery then depends on synthesis of new enzyme, which takes weeks.
c

**Dimethyl about 3 hours; diethyl about 33 hours.** These are half-lives of ageing: time for half the inhibited enzyme to pass the point of rescue. The smaller methyl group leaves far more readily than the ethyl group, hence the tenfold difference.
d

**A dimethyl patient arriving at 3 hours already has half the enzyme aged, so oximes work far better in diethyl poisoning; profenofos ages faster still.** This is why pralidoxime trials have been largely negative in populations dominated by dimethyl agents, and why an oxime is still worth giving a day later after chlorpyrifos. The oxime also slows further ageing, so it is started while the compound is unknown.
e

**Carbamylation is reversible, with no ageing; shorter illness; little CNS penetration.** A carbamate forms a carbamyl–enzyme bond that hydrolyses by itself within hours, so the enzyme recovers without any antidote. Carbamates are also less lipophilic and more ionised, so they cross the blood–brain barrier poorly and cause fewer convulsions and less coma.
mimic: Ageing vs enzyme regeneration
Ageing is loss of rescuability within hours. Regeneration of aged enzyme is synthesis of new protein — RBC cholinesterase recovers at roughly 1% a day, so weeks.
Organophosphate vs carbamate at the bedside
Identical cholinergic syndrome; carbamate illness resolves in a day or two, rarely shows the intermediate syndrome, and needs atropine but not an oxime.
traps: “Ageing is faster with diethyl compounds”
The opposite: dimethyl ~3 h, diethyl ~33 h — the smaller alkyl group is lost more easily.
“Pralidoxime can be given at any time”
Once the enzyme has aged an oxime does nothing; its value falls with every hour and is near zero for profenofos.
“Carbamates need no treatment”
They need atropine and often ventilation; what they do not need is an oxime, because there is nothing to rescue.
decode: “Oximes would be least useful in poisoning with…”
Normal enzyme activity only after 4–6 weeks
Aged enzyme — recovery depends on new synthesis.
Cholinergic crisis that resolves fully in 24 hours
PEST-03.punch: Inhibition is reversible for a few hours and then permanent, so everything in treatment is timed against ageing — fast in dimethyl and profenofos, slow in diethyl, and never in carbamates.

parts.q: Why does RBC cholinesterase take weeks to normalise after severe poisoning?
parts.a: Aged enzyme cannot be reactivated; the red cell cannot make new enzyme, so activity returns only as new erythrocytes appear — about **1% a day**.

PEST-04.intro: Everything in cholinergic poisoning follows from where acetylcholine receptors sit. Muscarinic receptors are on glands, smooth muscle and the heart’s pacemaker; nicotinic receptors are at the neuromuscular junction and in autonomic ganglia, including the sympathetic ones; and both types are in the brain. So the patient shows glandular flooding and bradycardia from one group, weakness and sometimes tachycardia and hypertension from another, and confusion, fits and loss of respiratory drive from the third. Death is respiratory, from all three at once.
why: a

**Muscarinic — salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, GI cramps, emesis; bradycardia, bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm; miosis.** Muscarinic stimulation turns on every exocrine gland and contracts smooth muscle, so secretions pour out at both ends and the airway narrows and fills. The vagus slows the sinus node, and the pupil constrictor contracts to a pinpoint. These are the effects atropine blocks, which is why atropine is titrated to a dry chest (PEST-10).
b

**Nicotinic — fasciculation, weakness, paralysis; tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis from ganglionic stimulation.** At the neuromuscular junction persistent acetylcholine first makes muscle twitch and then depolarises the end-plate into a block, so fasciculation gives way to flaccid weakness, including the diaphragm. In autonomic ganglia the same receptor sits on the sympathetic pathway, so the patient may be tachycardic, hypertensive and even dilated in the pupils. Atropine does nothing here; only an oxime addresses it (PEST-11).
c

**CNS — confusion, coma, convulsions; central respiratory depression.** Lipophilic organophosphates cross into the brain, where cholinergic excess causes agitation, seizures and finally depression of the brainstem respiratory centre. Carbamates do this much less (PEST-03).
mimic: Organophosphate vs opioid coma
Both give small pupils and a failing respiratory effort; the organophosphate patient is wet, wheezy and fasciculating, the opioid patient dry (TOX-04).
Nicotinic weakness vs the intermediate syndrome
Early weakness accompanies the cholinergic crisis and improves with it; weakness appearing at 24–96 hours after the crisis has settled is the intermediate syndrome (PEST-06).
Bilateral infiltrates: bronchorrhoea vs ARDS
Both are non-cardiogenic with a normal CVP. Secretion flooding clears with suction and atropine; if the picture fits the Berlin timing and P/F it is ARDS and needs lung-protective ventilation.
traps: “Tachycardia excludes organophosphate poisoning”
Ganglionic nicotinic stimulation, hypoxia, pain and bronchospasm all raise the rate; a substantial minority of patients are tachycardic rather than bradycardic on arrival.
“Dilated pupils rule it out”
Ganglionic sympathetic stimulation can dilate the pupil, and atropine already given will too.
“Atropine will stop the fasciculations and the weakness”
Those are nicotinic; atropine has no action at the neuromuscular junction.
decode: Pinpoint pupils, wet patient, wheeze, fasciculations
Still organophosphate; nicotinic ganglionic effect — do not withhold atropine.
Bilateral infiltrates, normal CVP, after organophosphate ingestion
Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from bronchorrhoea, permeability and aspiration; call it ARDS when the stem gives Berlin criteria.
PEST-04.punch: Read the patient receptor by receptor: glands and airway are muscarinic and answer to atropine, muscle and ganglia are nicotinic and answer only to an oxime, and the brain adds coma and apnoea — which is why these patients die of their airway, not their heart.

table.title: Three receptor groups, three sets of signs
head: Receptor
Signs
Antidote

parts.q: Why does the ECG sometimes show a long QTc?
parts.a: Organophosphates prolong repolarisation and are associated with **QTc prolongation and torsade**; a long QTc marks more severe poisoning and worse outcome.

parts.q: What is the actual mode of death?
parts.a: **Respiratory** — bronchorrhoea and bronchospasm, nicotinic failure of the diaphragm, and central apnoea together; hence airway, suction and ventilation rank with atropine.

PEST-05.intro: Weakness in organophosphate poisoning comes in three separate waves with different mechanisms, so the same patient can be weak on day one, recover, become weak again on day three, and develop a quite different weakness three weeks later. Keeping them apart matters because only the first responds to atropine, the second needs a ventilator and nothing else, and the third is a neuropathy that no antidote touches.
why: a

**Type I — acute cholinergic crisis: minutes to hours, generalised weakness with fasciculation, responds to atropine.** This is the cholinergic flood itself (PEST-04): muscarinic secretions and bronchospasm alongside nicotinic fasciculation and depolarising block. Atropine reverses the muscarinic half, which is what saves the airway.
b

**Type II — intermediate syndrome: 24–96 hours, neck flexors, proximal limb, cranial nerve and respiratory muscles, no response to atropine.** It appears after the cholinergic crisis has settled, in a patient who looked to be recovering, and is a post-synaptic nicotinic problem — persistent stimulation with receptor down-regulation (PEST-06). Atropine cannot help because no muscarinic receptor is involved.
c

**Type III — delayed neuropathy (OPIDN): 1–3 weeks, distal muscles, legs first, ascending, no response to atropine.** This is a dying-back axonopathy from inhibition of a different enzyme, neuropathy target esterase, not acetylcholinesterase at all (PEST-07) — hence the different timing, the distal pattern and the uselessness of cholinergic antidotes.
mimic: Intermediate syndrome vs Guillain–Barré
Both give ascending or proximal weakness with respiratory failure; the intermediate syndrome follows a documented cholinergic crisis by 1–4 days, spares sensation and has normal CSF.
OPIDN vs intermediate syndrome
Distal and sensory at 1–3 weeks versus proximal, neck-flexor and respiratory at 24–96 hours.
Type II weakness vs prolonged suxamethonium block
Suxamethonium given to such a patient is metabolised by the inhibited plasma enzyme and paralyses for hours (PEST-12); the history separates them.
traps: “Intermediate syndrome affects distal muscles first”
It is neck flexors and proximal muscles; distal, ascending weakness is the delayed neuropathy.
“More atropine will fix the weakness on day three”
Type II is nicotinic; extra atropine only adds delirium and tachycardia.
“Recovery from the cholinergic crisis means the patient can be extubated and discharged”
The intermediate syndrome begins exactly then — keep the patient where ventilation is available for 4 days.
decode: Day 3, cannot lift head off the pillow, atropine not helping
Three weeks later, distal leg weakness with absent ankle jerks
PEST-05.punch: Three waves, three mechanisms: the cholinergic flood answers to atropine, the intermediate syndrome answers only to a ventilator, and the delayed neuropathy belongs to a different enzyme altogether.

PEST-06.intro: The dangerous moment in organophosphate poisoning is not always the first day. In a substantial minority the cholinergic crisis settles, atropine is weaned, and then over a few hours the patient cannot hold the head up, cannot cough and stops breathing adequately. Nothing prevents it, nothing shortens it, and the only thing that matters is that a ventilator is ready when it happens.
why: a

**10–40% of patients; 24–96 hours after exposure, after the cholinergic crisis has resolved.** The wide range reflects how it is defined and which agents dominate a given series. The timing is the point: it begins when the muscarinic features have gone and the patient appears to be improving.
b

**Neck flexion weakness (cannot lift the head off the pillow), proximal limb weakness, cranial nerve palsies, reduced reflexes, respiratory failure.** The muscles affected are those with the least reserve against a failing neuromuscular junction — neck flexors, shoulder and hip girdle, the bulbar muscles and the diaphragm. Distal strength and sensation are preserved, which separates it from the delayed neuropathy (PEST-07).
c

**Highly fat-soluble agents; possibly inadequate oxime dosing.** Lipophilic compounds such as fenthion and dichlofenthion keep releasing poison from fat, so the junction never gets a clean interval (PEST-02). Whether too little oxime contributes is debated, which is one argument for a sustained infusion rather than boluses (PEST-11).
d

**Persistent nicotinic over-stimulation with receptor down-regulation and muscle necrosis.** Continuous acetylcholine at the end-plate causes post-synaptic receptor down-regulation and desensitisation, and calcium entry damages the muscle fibre itself — a myopathy with a raised creatine kinase. The mechanism is still not settled, but all the proposed ones are post-synaptic and structural, which is why neither atropine nor an oxime alters the course.
e

**Supportive ventilation; no treatment prevents it.** Recovery takes days to two or three weeks as receptors are restored and muscle repairs. The clinical task is anticipation: watch head lift, single-breath count and vital capacity, and intubate before the patient tires rather than after.
mimic: Intermediate syndrome vs recurrent cholinergic crisis
A relapse of secretions, wheeze and miosis is cholinergic and needs atropine again; pure weakness with a dry chest is the intermediate syndrome.
Intermediate syndrome vs myasthenic crisis
Same pattern of proximal, bulbar and respiratory weakness; the poisoning history and the preceding cholinergic phase decide it.
traps: “It is a late cholinergic relapse, so give more atropine”
It is nicotinic and post-synaptic; atropine does not treat it.
“The patient is well at 24 hours, so discharge”
This is precisely the window in which the syndrome begins; observe for at least 4 days after a significant ingestion.
“It means the poisoning was mild if the pupils are normal”
Pupils and secretions are irrelevant by then — the sign to follow is whether the head can be lifted off the pillow.
decode: Weakness of neck flexion 48 hours after chlorpyrifos
Intermediate syndrome — nothing prevents or shortens it.
A highly fat-soluble agent such as fenthion.
PEST-06.punch: The intermediate syndrome is the trap of the second and third day: the cholinergic storm is over, the antidote is being weaned, and the only treatment for the weakness that follows is a ventilator you decided on early.

PEST-07.intro: Weeks after the poisoning is over, some patients return with numb feet and a slapping gait. This has nothing to do with acetylcholinesterase: certain organophosphates inhibit another esterase in the axon, and the long nerves degenerate from their tips backwards. Because the mechanism is separate, so is everything else — the timing, the pattern and the fact that the severity of the acute illness predicts nothing.
why: a

**Inhibition of neuropathy target esterase, not acetylcholinesterase.** The compound phosphorylates this axonal enzyme and then undergoes its own ageing reaction; the modified enzyme, rather than simple loss of its function, triggers a dying-back degeneration of the longest axons. Cholinergic antidotes are therefore irrelevant.
b

**Stocking-and-glove paraesthesia, then distal flaccid weakness of the legs ascending to the arms; absent ankle jerks.** The longest fibres fail first, so symptoms begin in the feet and hands, sensory before motor, with wasting and loss of the ankle jerk. It is a peripheral axonopathy, so there is no sphincter or cranial involvement, and some patients are left with spasticity from an associated central component.
c

**Chlorpyrifos is the typical agent.** Among the compounds in common agricultural use it is the one most often reported; the classic historical examples were triorthocresyl phosphate (contaminated cooking oil and ‘ginger jake’ paralysis) and mipafox.
d

**Independent of the severity of the acute poisoning: it can follow a mild acute illness.** The two enzymes are different proteins with different sensitivities, so a compound can inhibit neuropathy target esterase appreciably while causing only modest cholinergic symptoms. A patient who never needed much atropine may still develop the neuropathy at three weeks.
e

**Carbamates only rarely cause it.** Carbamates inhibit neuropathy target esterase weakly and their bond does not age in the way required to trigger degeneration, so the syndrome is exceptional with them.
mimic: OPIDN vs Guillain–Barré syndrome
Both ascend; OPIDN starts 1–3 weeks after a known exposure, progresses over days to weeks rather than hours, and has normal CSF protein.
OPIDN vs critical illness polyneuropathy
Indistinguishable electrically at times; the exposure history and onset after recovery rather than during sepsis separate them.
traps: “Delayed neuropathy follows only severe poisoning”
It is independent of acute severity, because a different enzyme is involved.
“Pralidoxime given early prevents it”
Oximes act on acetylcholinesterase; they do not protect neuropathy target esterase.
“Weakness at 10 days is the intermediate syndrome”
That window has passed: at 1–3 weeks with distal sensory loss this is OPIDN (PEST-05).
decode: Three weeks after chlorpyrifos: numb feet, foot drop, absent ankle jerks
Does a mild acute illness exclude it?
PEST-07.punch: OPIDN is organophosphate poisoning in a different enzyme: a dying-back axonopathy of the longest nerves that arrives weeks later, ignores how ill the patient was, and has no antidote.

PEST-08.sub: Toxicology → Pesticides → Delayed manifestations by time
PEST-08.intro: Organophosphate poisoning is not one illness but a sequence spread over three weeks, and most of the sequence appears after the patient has been declared out of danger. The order follows the mechanisms: continuing absorption first, then the neuromuscular junction, then the brain, and last the peripheral axon. Knowing when each is due is what sets the length of observation.
why: a

**Delayed-onset cholinergic phase at 40–48 hours.** Seen with lipophilic compounds and with thion compounds needing hepatic conversion to their active oxon (chlorpyrifos, parathion, fenthion, malathion), so poison keeps arriving at the synapse and secretions and miosis return after an apparent recovery. This phase does respond to atropine.
b
**Intermediate syndrome at 24–96 hours.** Post-synaptic nicotinic failure of neck flexors, proximal, bulbar and respiratory muscles, needing ventilation and nothing else (PEST-06).
c

**Late-onset intermediate syndrome at about 114 hours.** The same syndrome appearing beyond the usual four days, again typically with fat-soluble agents whose release from adipose tissue is still going on.
d

**Delayed encephalopathy or coma at 4–6 days.** A central cholinergic and possibly hypoxic-metabolic effect appearing after the acute phase, with confusion, drowsiness or coma and no new muscarinic signs.
e
**Cerebellar ataxia at about 8 days.** Transient cerebellar dysfunction with gait and limb ataxia, usually self-limiting over weeks.
f
**Extrapyramidal syndrome at 5–15 days.** Dystonia, rigidity and tremor, attributed to striatal cholinergic–dopaminergic imbalance; generally reversible.
g
**Delayed neuropathy at 1–3 weeks.** The neuropathy target esterase axonopathy — distal, sensory then motor, ascending (PEST-07).
mimic: Delayed cholinergic phase vs intermediate syndrome
Secretions, wheeze and miosis returning means cholinergic and needs atropine; pure weakness with a dry chest does not.
Delayed encephalopathy vs hypoxic brain injury
Overlapping; a patient who was never hypoxic and has normal imaging points to the toxic encephalopathy.
traps: “Everything happens in the first 24 hours”
Most of the syndromes begin after 24 hours, which is why observation runs for at least four days and follow-up for weeks.
“Movement disorder after organophosphate means permanent brain injury”
The extrapyramidal and cerebellar syndromes are usually transient.
“A patient asymptomatic at 12 hours after a fat-soluble agent can go home”
Fenthion and relatives can declare themselves at 40–48 hours or later.
decode: Ataxia at one week after poisoning
PEST-08.punch: The poisoning unfolds for three weeks, and the order is mechanistic: continuing absorption, then the junction, then the brain, then the axon — so observation is measured in days and follow-up in weeks.

PEST-09.sub: Toxicology → Pesticides → Diagnosis: cholinesterases and the atropine challenge
PEST-09.intro: The diagnosis is clinical, but two blood enzymes are often measured and they answer different questions. One is the same enzyme as in the synapse and tracks how poisoned the patient is; the other is a liver protein that merely proves exposure. Where neither assay is available, a small dose of atropine can be used as a test: a patient with real cholinergic excess barely responds to it.
why: a

**RBC cholinesterase is true (acetyl) cholinesterase: it mirrors the synaptic enzyme and correlates with severity.** It is the identical enzyme on the red cell membrane, so its inhibition reflects inhibition at the junction. Severity grades with activity: roughly 20–50% of normal is mild, 10–20% moderate and under 10% severe, with coma, flaccid paralysis, bronchorrhoea or pulmonary oedema at the severe end. Because red cells cannot resynthesise it, recovery is slow — about 1% a day.
b

**Plasma cholinesterase is pseudo (butyryl) cholinesterase, made in the liver: a simple marker of exposure with no correlation with severity.** It is inhibited earlier and more readily, so it is a sensitive screen, but its baseline varies widely and falls in liver disease, pregnancy, malnutrition and genetic variants. It also recovers within days as the liver makes more, which can mislead. Its one practical use is a warning that suxamethonium will be prolonged (PEST-12).
c

**Atropine challenge: a rise in heart rate of more than 20–25/min with flushing after a small dose means no significant cholinergic poisoning.** A test dose of around 1–2 mg is given. In a genuinely poisoned patient the muscarinic receptors are swamped with acetylcholine, so a small competitive antagonist dose produces little change; an unpoisoned patient shows the expected tachycardia, dry mouth and flush. It is a bedside substitute where assays are unavailable, not a substitute for clinical judgement.
mimic: Low plasma cholinesterase from poisoning vs other causes
Liver disease, pregnancy, malnutrition and genetic variants all lower it; only the clinical picture and the RBC enzyme confirm poisoning.
Atropine challenge vs atropine loading
The challenge is one small diagnostic dose; loading is 2–5 mg doubled every 5 minutes to an end-point (PEST-10).
traps: “Plasma cholinesterase correlates with severity”
It does not — the RBC enzyme does; plasma activity only shows exposure.
“A normal cholinesterase excludes poisoning”
Baselines vary several-fold between people, so an individual’s ‘normal’ value may already represent a large fall; treat the patient.
“Wait for the assay before giving atropine”
Treatment is clinical and immediate; the assay is confirmatory and often retrospective.
decode: RBC (true) acetylcholinesterase — severe under 10% of normal.
Heart rate rises 30/min after 1 mg atropine
PEST-09.punch: The red cell enzyme is the synapse in a tube and grades severity; plasma cholinesterase only says the patient met the poison — and if neither is available, a patient who shrugs off a test dose of atropine is the one who needs it.

parts.q: Severity bands by RBC acetylcholinesterase activity?
parts.a: **Mild 20–50%**, moderate 10–20%, **severe <10%** of normal; severe poisoning shows coma, flaccid paralysis, bronchorrhoea or pulmonary oedema and pinpoint pupils.

PEST-10.intro: Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist, so it must outnumber the acetylcholine piling up in the synapse — which means the dose is whatever it takes, not a number from a book. The thing it is competing for is the airway: secretions and bronchospasm are what kill these patients in the first hours. So the dose is escalated fast and judged by the chest, not by the pupils or the pulse.
why: a

**2–5 mg IV, doubling every 5 minutes until atropinised.** Fixed small doses given slowly lose the race against a synapse flooded with transmitter, so the dose is doubled rather than repeated — 2, 4, 8, 16 mg and beyond — until the end-points are met. Published protocols open with 1.8–3 mg and then double in the same way, so the card's 2–5 mg is the same practice. Total requirements from about 10 mg up to 100 mg or more in the first day are usual, and giving too little is the commoner error.
b

**End-points: a clear chest with no wheeze or secretions, heart rate above 80, systolic pressure above 80, dry axillae, and pupils no longer pinpoint.** The chest is the one that matters, because bronchorrhoea and bronchospasm are the lethal muscarinic effects; the others confirm that enough has been given to reach the whole muscarinic system. Pupils are the least reliable end-point — they respond late and may be affected by continuing absorption.
c

**Maintenance by infusion of 10–20% of the total loading dose per hour.** Atropine’s effect lasts a few hours while the organophosphate persists for days, so stopping after loading lets the patient relapse. Running a fraction of the dose that worked keeps the chest dry and allows titration up or down against the same end-points.
d

**If atropine toxicity occurs, stop, then restart at 70–80% of the previous rate.** Over-atropinisation gives agitation, delirium, hyperthermia, ileus, urinary retention and tachyarrhythmia — and because it is a hot, dry, confused patient, it mimics worsening poisoning. Brief interruption and a modest reduction keep the airway protected without the delirium.
e

**It does not treat the nicotinic effects: weakness and paralysis.** There are no muscarinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction, so fasciculation, weakness and respiratory muscle failure are untouched; they need an oxime and often a ventilator (PEST-11, PEST-05).
mimic: Atropine toxicity vs continuing poisoning
Both give a confused, tachycardic patient; atropine excess has a dry chest, absent bowel sounds and a full bladder, continuing poisoning a wet, wheezy chest.
Atropine vs glycopyrrolate
Glycopyrrolate does not cross into the brain, so it dries secretions with far less delirium but cannot treat central effects (PEST-12).
traps: “Atropinisation is judged by dilated pupils”
The end-point is a dry chest; pupils are slow and unreliable.
“Tachycardia is a reason to withhold atropine”
Tachycardia is usually hypoxia, bronchospasm or ganglionic stimulation; a wet chest still needs atropine.
“A fixed 0.6 mg dose repeated as needed”
Too small and too slow — the dose is doubled every 5 minutes until the chest is clear.
decode: Agitated, hot, dry patient with absent bowel sounds on day 2
Which effects does atropine not treat?
PEST-10.punch: Atropine is titrated against the airway and nothing else: double the dose until the chest is clear and the axillae dry, keep an infusion going because the poison outlasts the drug, and accept that weakness is not its business.

PEST-11.intro: Atropine blocks the receptor; an oxime attacks the problem one step upstream by taking the phosphate off the enzyme and giving the synapse its acetylcholinesterase back. That is the only way the nicotinic effects — fasciculation, weakness, respiratory muscle failure — can be treated at all. It works only while the bond is still rescuable, which is why it is started at once and given in a way that keeps the plasma level up.
why: a

**Pralidoxime, obidoxime, trimedoxime.** All are quaternary oximes; pralidoxime is the one available in India (as the chloride or iodide), obidoxime is used mainly in Europe and is somewhat more potent against some compounds.
b

**They bind the anionic site and pull the phosphate off the esteratic site, reactivating cholinesterase before ageing; they also slow further ageing.** The charged oxime docks onto the enzyme’s anionic subsite, which positions its nucleophilic oxime group next to the phosphorus; it then strips the phosphate off as a phosphoryl-oxime. Reactivated enzyme clears acetylcholine again, so fasciculation and weakness improve — the effects atropine cannot reach.
c

**Pralidoxime 1–2 g over 30 minutes, repeated in 1 hour if weakness persists, or given as an infusion.** Weight-based WHO dosing is a 30 mg/kg bolus (about 2 g) over 30 minutes followed by 8 mg/kg/h (about 500 mg/h), continued until atropine is no longer needed. The reasoning for an infusion rather than intermittent boluses is that a plasma concentration above roughly 4 mg/L has to be sustained to outpace re-inhibition from drug still being absorbed and released from fat. The clinical evidence is thin and conflicting: a small Indian trial of a sustained high-dose regimen (1 g every hour for 48 hours against 1 g every four hours) found fewer deaths and a shorter time on the ventilator, whereas a placebo-controlled trial of the WHO regimen in Sri Lanka showed no clinical benefit and a trend towards harm despite reactivating blood cholinesterase.
d

**Not recommended in carbamate poisoning, but do not withhold it when the agent is unknown.** Carbamylated enzyme hydrolyses by itself within hours, so there is nothing to rescue, and with carbaryl there is old experimental evidence of worse outcome. In practice the bottle is often unidentified and a mixed or organophosphate exposure cannot be excluded, so the oxime is given.
e

**Useless once the enzyme has aged; no CNS effect; rapid injection causes laryngospasm, hypertension and vomiting.** Aged enzyme offers no bond for the oxime to attack (PEST-03). Being permanently charged, pralidoxime scarcely crosses the blood–brain barrier, so it does nothing for coma or convulsions. Given as a fast push it causes laryngospasm, muscle rigidity, hypertension and vomiting — hence a 30-minute infusion.
mimic: Atropine vs pralidoxime
Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and treats secretions; pralidoxime restores the enzyme and is the only treatment for nicotinic weakness. They are always given together.
Oxime failure from ageing vs from under-dosing
Dimethyl or profenofos poisoning ages past rescue within hours; under-dosing shows as weakness that improves when a proper infusion is started.
traps: “Oximes are recommended in carbamate poisoning”
They are not — carbamylated enzyme recovers spontaneously; but an unknown agent is still treated.
“Pralidoxime instead of atropine if secretions are heavy”
It has no muscarinic action; secretions need atropine.
“Give the 1 g dose as a bolus to save time”
Rapid injection causes laryngospasm and hypertension; infuse over 30 minutes.
“Trial evidence settles the question either way”

It does not: the Cochrane review concludes the evidence is insufficient to show oximes are beneficial or harmful, and the trials were dominated by dimethyl compounds and late presentation. An oxime is still started early, when the compound is unknown and the bond may still be rescuable, but it cannot be relied on to change the outcome.
decode: Which effects do oximes treat that atropine cannot?
30 mg/kg (~2 g) over 30 min, then 8 mg/kg/h (~500 mg/h) until atropine is no longer needed.
Is the WHO regimen proven to save lives?
No — a placebo-controlled trial of it showed no clinical benefit; the evidence overall is insufficient either way.
Hypertension and laryngospasm during the antidote
PEST-11.punch: An oxime is the only drug that gives the enzyme back, so it is the only treatment for nicotinic weakness — started early, infused rather than pushed, and worthless once the bond has aged.

parts.q: Why an infusion rather than repeated boluses?
parts.a: A plasma level above about **4 mg/L** has to be sustained to outrun re-inhibition from drug still being absorbed and released from fat, before ageing fixes the bond.

fix: Pralidoxime works if given in time

The evidence is insufficient either way (Cochrane): the Sri Lankan placebo-controlled trial of the WHO regimen showed no benefit, a small Indian trial of 1 g/h for 48 h showed fewer deaths. WHO regimen: 30 mg/kg (~2 g) over 30 min, then 8 mg/kg/h.

PEST-12.intro: Beyond atropine and an oxime, management is airway, decontamination and avoiding harm. Two details are specific to this poisoning: the muscle relaxant used for intubation is cleared by the very enzyme the poison has inhibited, and the poison is still on the patient’s skin and in the vomit, so it keeps being absorbed — by the patient and by the staff. A long list of plausible-sounding extras has no benefit and one is harmful.
why: a

**Avoid succinylcholine: it is metabolised by plasma cholinesterase, so paralysis is prolonged.** With the plasma enzyme inhibited, a standard dose can paralyse for hours rather than minutes. Use a non-depolarising agent — rocuronium — recognising that higher doses may be needed since acetylcholine is competing at the junction.
b

**Remove clothes and wash the skin; activated charcoal 1 g/kg within 1 hour; no forced emesis.** Organophosphates are absorbed through intact skin and evaporate from soaked clothing, so undressing and washing with soap and water stops further absorption — and protects the team, who need gloves, gown, eye protection and a ventilated space, since vomit and clothing release the agent. Charcoal binds any that remains in the gut if given early. Induced emesis is dangerous in a patient who may convulse or lose airway control within minutes, and gastric lavage has no proven benefit.
c

**Glycopyrrolate does not cross the blood–brain barrier: added to atropine it caused far less confusion and hallucination (30% versus 90%) and less tachyarrhythmia, with the same outcome. Dose 7.5 mg in 200 mL, infused until the mucous membranes are dry.** Being a quaternary amine it is excluded from the brain, so it dries secretions peripherally without central antimuscarinic delirium. It cannot replace atropine entirely, because central respiratory depression and seizures need a drug that does get in.
d

**Fresh frozen plasma is harmful; haemodialysis and bicarbonate have no role; magnesium has no scientific data, and clonidine and vitamin E rest on animal studies only.** FFP has been proposed as a source of butyrylcholinesterase to scavenge circulating poison. The one randomised pilot trial (FFP against albumin against saline, in India) did raise plasma cholinesterase but produced no improvement in deaths or ventilator days, with a numerically longer time ventilated in the FFP arm — so the honest position is no benefit rather than proven harm, and it is not recommended. Organophosphates are lipophilic with a large volume of distribution and are not meaningfully cleared by dialysis, and the acidosis in these patients is from hypoxia and shock, so bicarbonate treats nothing. Magnesium is better described as unproven than undocumented: several small trials exist and pooled together they hint at lower mortality, but they are too small and too heterogeneous to recommend, and the higher doses caused hypotension.
mimic: Glycopyrrolate vs atropine
Glycopyrrolate dries without delirium but has no central action; atropine remains the drug for central effects and the one titrated to the chest (PEST-10).
Rocuronium vs succinylcholine here
Succinylcholine depends on the inhibited plasma enzyme; rocuronium does not, though its dose may need to be higher.
traps: “Give fresh frozen plasma to replace cholinesterase”
It raises the plasma enzyme without improving survival or ventilator days in the one randomised trial, and carries the usual transfusion risks; it is not a treatment for organophosphate poisoning.
“Dialyse the organophosphate”
Large volume of distribution and high lipid solubility — dialysis removes nothing useful.
“Decontamination is only for the patient”
Staff are exposed through vomit and soaked clothing; gloves, gown, eye protection and ventilation are part of the procedure.
“Induce vomiting to get the poison out”
Forced emesis risks aspiration and convulsion; use early charcoal instead.
decode: Intubating drug to avoid in organophosphate poisoning
Glycopyrrolate, 7.5 mg in 200 mL to dry mucous membranes.
Which listed therapy is the one to answer as harmful?
Fresh frozen plasma (the trial evidence shows no benefit).
PEST-12.punch: The extras are mostly about not adding harm: no succinylcholine, no forced emesis, no dialysis or bicarbonate, never FFP — while the things that do work are washing the patient, protecting the team and keeping the chest dry.
fix: FFP: harmful
The only randomised pilot (Vellore 2010) showed no benefit, not proven harm: FFP is not recommended. For the exam’s ‘which is harmful’ it is still the intended answer.
Magnesium: no scientific data
There are four small randomised trials and cohorts with a possible mortality benefit (Brvar 2018), but the evidence is still insufficient to recommend it.

PEST-13.intro: These eight statements are the deck’s key discriminations, and each one turns on a mechanism met earlier: which alkyl group ages faster, which enzyme is the synapse’s own, which receptor each antidote reaches, and which muscles fail when.
why: a

**False — dimethyl compounds age in about 3 hours, diethyl in about 33.** The smaller methyl group is shed far more readily from the phosphorylated enzyme, so it is the dimethyl patient whose window for an oxime has closed (PEST-03).
b
**False — the RBC (true) enzyme correlates with severity.** Plasma butyrylcholinesterase is a liver protein with a wide normal range; it shows exposure only (PEST-09).
c
**False — the intermediate syndrome affects neck flexors and proximal muscles first.** Distal, ascending weakness at 1–3 weeks is the delayed neuropathy instead (PEST-05, PEST-07).
d
**False — delayed neuropathy is independent of acute severity.** It follows inhibition of neuropathy target esterase, a different enzyme, so it can follow a mild cholinergic illness (PEST-07).
e
**False — fasciculation is nicotinic, and atropine is purely antimuscarinic.** There are no muscarinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction; only an oxime addresses it (PEST-10, PEST-11).
f

**False — oximes are not recommended in carbamate poisoning.** Carbamylated enzyme hydrolyses spontaneously, so there is nothing to reactivate; they are still given when the agent is unknown (PEST-11).
g

**True — atropinisation is judged by a dry chest.** Clear lungs and dry axillae, not dilated pupils or a particular heart rate, are the end-point, because bronchial secretions are what kill (PEST-10).
h
**False — tachycardia does not exclude organophosphate poisoning.** Nicotinic ganglionic stimulation, hypoxia and bronchospasm all raise the rate (PEST-04).
mimic: Dry chest vs dilated pupils as the atropine end-point
The chest is the lethal muscarinic target; pupils respond late and unreliably.
RBC vs plasma cholinesterase
Same words, different enzymes: one is the synaptic enzyme and grades severity, the other a liver marker of exposure.
traps: “Pinpoint pupils are needed to make the diagnosis”
Pupils may be normal or dilated from ganglionic stimulation or atropine already given.
“Atropine covers the whole syndrome”
It covers only the muscarinic part; nicotinic weakness and central effects need an oxime and a ventilator.
decode: Check which alkyl group — dimethyl is the fast one.
Ask which receptor the drug reaches: atropine muscarinic, oxime the enzyme itself.
PEST-13.punch: Every statement here comes back to three questions: which alkyl group is on the phosphorus, which enzyme is being measured, and which receptor the antidote can actually reach.

PEST-14.intro: A rodenticide has to kill a rat that eats only a small amount of bait, so many of them are poisons of the most basic machinery of the cell. Toxicity in humans depends on two things: how potent the chemical is and how much is in the bait. In India three groups account for most poisonings — yellow phosphorus paste, metal phosphide tablets and the long-acting anticoagulants — and they sit in very different places on this scale.
why: a

**Highly toxic: yellow phosphorus, metal phosphides, strychnine, arsenic, sodium monofluoroacetate.** Each attacks something every cell needs. Yellow phosphorus is a protoplasmic poison that causes fatty degeneration of the liver (PEST-15). Phosphides release phosphine, which blocks cytochrome c oxidase and stops oxidative phosphorylation (PEST-18). Monofluoroacetate is converted in the body to fluorocitrate, which blocks aconitase and halts the citric acid cycle. Strychnine blocks inhibitory glycine receptors in the spinal cord, and arsenic binds the thiol groups of many enzymes. Small amounts are lethal, and there is no specific antidote for most of them.
b

**Moderately toxic: alpha-naphthyl thiourea (ANTU), cholecalciferol.** ANTU increases pulmonary capillary permeability, causing pulmonary oedema and pleural effusion; rats are far more sensitive to it than humans. Cholecalciferol (vitamin D₃) acts slowly, by raising calcium absorption and bone resorption, so the danger is hypercalcaemia over days, treated as any other hypercalcaemia.
c

**Less toxic: superwarfarins, red squill, bromethalin.** Superwarfarin baits contain very little drug (typically 0.005%), so a single accidental mouthful rarely matters — although a deliberate large ingestion causes weeks of coagulopathy (PEST-17). Red squill contains a cardiac glycoside but is also a strong emetic; rats cannot vomit, humans can, so most of the dose comes back up. Bromethalin uncouples oxidative phosphorylation in nerve cells and causes cerebral oedema, but human poisoning is rare.
mimic: Strychnine vs tetanus

Both give spasms with a clear sensorium. Strychnine starts within minutes to an hour and the muscles relax completely between spasms; tetanus starts days after a wound with rigidity persisting between spasms.
Yellow phosphorus vs metal phosphide
Both smell of garlic; phosphorus kills the liver over days, phosphide kills the circulation within hours (PEST-15).
traps: “Superwarfarins are less toxic, so a large ingestion can be sent home”
‘Less toxic’ refers to the small dose in a bait. A deliberate ingestion of many packets causes coagulopathy that lasts weeks to months.
“Red squill is dangerous because it is a cardiac glycoside”
It is, but it makes humans vomit, which limits the dose absorbed; rats cannot vomit, which is why it works on them.
“Cholecalciferol rodenticide acts within hours”
Vitamin D acts through calcium absorption and bone resorption, so hypercalcaemia develops over days.
decode: Yellow phosphorus — watch the liver on day 3.
Rat poison cake, bleeding gums a few days later
PEST-14.punch: The most toxic rodenticides poison what every cell needs — the mitochondria, the citric acid cycle, inhibitory synapses — while the least toxic are either dilute in the bait or make the patient vomit.

parts.q: Strychnine poisoning: the airway trap?
parts.a: Strychnine blocks glycine receptors, giving painful spasms with a clear sensorium. Treat with **benzodiazepines** in a quiet room, then paralysis and ventilation if needed — but **avoid suxamethonium**: rhabdomyolysis brings hyperkalaemia; use a non-depolarising agent.

PEST-15.sub: Toxicology → Rodenticides → Yellow phosphorus vs metal phosphide
PEST-15.intro: Both poisons contain phosphorus and both smell of garlic, but they kill in completely different ways and on different clocks. Yellow phosphorus is absorbed and poisons the liver cell itself, so the patient may look well for a day before liver failure sets in. A metal phosphide releases a gas, phosphine, that switches off cellular respiration everywhere at once, so the heart and circulation fail within hours.
why: a

**Form: yellow phosphorus as a paste (Ratol); metal phosphide as tablets (Celphos) or zinc phosphide powder.** Ratol is a paste spread on bait. A Celphos tablet weighs 3 g and releases about 1 g of phosphine on contact with moisture — far more than a lethal dose.
b

**Mechanism: yellow phosphorus is a protoplasmic toxin causing fatty degeneration of liver, kidney and brain; phosphide releases phosphine with acid or water, which blocks mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.** Phosphorus disrupts protein synthesis and the export of fat from the hepatocyte, so fat accumulates and the cell dies. Phosphide reacts with water and stomach acid to form phosphine, which inhibits cytochrome c oxidase; without the last step of the respiratory chain cells cannot make ATP, and those with the highest demand — myocardium and vascular smooth muscle — fail first.
c

**Course: yellow phosphorus mild on day 1, transaminitis on day 2, liver failure on day 3; phosphide shock and multi-organ failure within 30 minutes.** The delay with phosphorus is the time it takes for liver cells to accumulate fat and die, which is why an early ‘well’ patient must still be admitted. Phosphine acts as soon as it is formed, so collapse is early.
d

**Clue: luminescent faeces and garlic odour with yellow phosphorus; garlic odour with phosphide.** Elemental phosphorus glows in the dark as it oxidises in air, so vomit or stool may glow or smoke. The garlic smell comes from phosphorus compounds in both.
e

**Death: yellow phosphorus by liver failure; phosphide by circulatory failure.** Phosphine causes myocardial depression, arrhythmias and vasodilatation together, so the shock does not respond well to fluids or vasopressors (PEST-18).
f
**Antidote: none for either.** Treatment is decontamination and support; for yellow phosphorus, liver support up to transplantation (PEST-16).
mimic: Yellow phosphorus vs paracetamol
Both look mild at first and cause liver failure around day 3; paracetamol has NAC as an antidote and a treatment nomogram, phosphorus has neither.
Phosphide shock vs septic shock
Phosphide shock comes within hours of a tablet, with severe acidosis and myocardial dysfunction, in a patient who was well that morning.
traps: “The Ratol patient is well on day 1, so discharge”
The liver injury is still developing; transaminases rise on day 2 and failure comes on day 3.
“Luminescent faeces suggest phosphide”
It is yellow phosphorus — the elemental form glows as it oxidises.
“Phosphide shock responds to fluids”
It is largely myocardial and mitochondrial, so it is often refractory.
decode: Garlic odour, glowing stool, jaundice on day 3
Garlic odour, BP 70/40 two hours after a tablet
PEST-15.punch: Same element, two clocks: yellow phosphorus slowly poisons the liver cell and kills on day 3, while phosphine shuts down mitochondria everywhere and kills the circulation within hours.
fix: Shock and multi-organ failure within 30 minutes
Vomiting starts within minutes, but shock usually develops over 1–6 hours and most deaths come within 24 hours.

PEST-16.intro: There is no antidote to yellow phosphorus, so treatment follows the course of the poisoning: limit absorption early, support the failing liver and its clotting factors, and, if the liver does not recover, replace it. Because the patient may look well for a day, the window for decontamination is easily missed.
why: a

**Lavage with potassium permanganate, which oxidises phosphorus; avoid oily or fatty food, which increases absorption.** Permanganate is an oxidising agent that converts elemental phosphorus into less toxic, less absorbable phosphates. Phosphorus dissolves in fat, so a fatty meal or oil carries it across the gut wall.
b

**Vitamin K, FFP or prothrombin complex for bleeding, electrolytes, N-acetylcysteine.** The damaged liver cannot make clotting factors, so the INR rises; vitamin K helps only as far as the liver can still use it, and FFP or prothrombin complex replaces the factors directly when the patient bleeds. N-acetylcysteine is used as in other non-paracetamol acute liver failure, to support glutathione and reduce oxidative injury; it is not a specific antidote here.
c

**Plasma exchange in liver failure lowered INR and transaminases significantly; bilirubin was unchanged.** Exchange removes toxin and inflammatory mediators and replaces the missing clotting factors with donor plasma, so the INR falls. Bilirubin behaves differently: the failing liver still cannot conjugate and excrete it, and much of it sits in the tissues, so an exchange lowers the plasma level only briefly — a likely reason it did not change. It buys time for the liver to regenerate or for a transplant.
d

**Liver transplant as the last resort.** When the liver fails and does not recover — worsening encephalopathy, coagulopathy and acidosis, judged by criteria such as King’s College — transplantation is the only definitive treatment.
mimic: Plasma exchange vs liver transplant
Exchange corrects the INR and buys time; only a transplant replaces the failed liver.
traps: “Give vegetable oil to bind the phosphorus”
Phosphorus dissolves in fat, so oils and fatty food increase absorption.
“A normal INR after plasma exchange means the liver has recovered”
Exchange replaces clotting factors temporarily; follow encephalopathy, acidosis and the trend once exchange stops.
“N-acetylcysteine is the antidote, as in paracetamol”
There is no antidote; NAC is supportive here.
decode: Ratol poisoning with rising INR on day 3, bridge to recovery
Ratol poisoning with grade III encephalopathy
PEST-16.punch: Without an antidote, yellow phosphorus is treated by its timeline: oxidise and avoid fat early, replace clotting factors as the liver fails, exchange plasma to buy time, and transplant if the liver does not come back.
fix: WATCH: vegetable oil lavage
Digestible oils increase phosphorus absorption; older texts used liquid paraffin (not absorbed). Gastric lavage of any kind is not routine now.

PEST-17.intro: Rats learn to avoid a bait that makes them ill at once, so anticoagulant rodenticides were designed to work slowly. The second-generation ‘superwarfarins’ were made after rats became resistant to warfarin: they bind the same enzyme far more tightly and stay in the liver for weeks. In a human that means a coagulopathy that starts late and lasts long.
why: a

**Brodifacoum, bromadiolone, difenacoum, chlorophacinone.** The first three are 4-hydroxycoumarins like warfarin; chlorophacinone is an indandione, a different chemical class with the same action. All are fat-soluble and concentrate in the liver, which gives them half-lives of weeks.
b

**Inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase, so no active factors II, VII, IX and X are made.** These factors need vitamin K to become functional; once used, vitamin K is turned into its epoxide and must be recycled by this reductase. Block the reductase and the liver keeps releasing factors that cannot work. Proteins C and S are also vitamin K dependent.
c

**Bleeding begins at 24–48 hours, once the existing factors fall below 30%.** The drug stops new factors being made but does not destroy those already circulating, so nothing happens until they are used up. Factor VII has the shortest half-life (about 6 hours), so the INR rises first, and bleeding follows once levels fall far enough.
d

**Confirmation by 4-hydroxycoumarin level on mass spectrometry.** A long INR with low II, VII, IX and X and a normal fibrinogen fits, but the level confirms the agent and, repeated, shows when it has cleared.
e

**Vitamin K1 in high doses for weeks to months; FFP or prothrombin complex for active bleeding.** Large doses of vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) drive an alternative reductase that is not blocked, so some active factor is made despite the poison. The drug lasts weeks, so treatment does too, guided by the INR. Vitamin K takes hours to act, so a bleeding patient also needs the factors replaced directly.
mimic: Superwarfarin vs warfarin overdose
Same mechanism, but warfarin wears off in days; a superwarfarin coagulopathy lasts weeks to months.
Superwarfarin vs liver failure
Both raise the INR, but in liver failure fibrinogen and factor V also fall; superwarfarin spares them.
traps: “Normal INR on the day of ingestion — safe to discharge”
The existing factors have not yet run out; repeat the INR at 48 hours.
“A single dose of vitamin K reverses it”
The drug outlasts the vitamin K; high doses are needed for weeks to months.
“Bleeding starts within 6 hours”
Stored factors must be used up first — 24–48 hours.
decode: Unexplained high INR with bleeding, no warfarin prescribed, normal liver
Superwarfarin ingestion (check the history of rat poison).
INR recurs after vitamin K is stopped
Long-acting anticoagulant still in the liver — restart high-dose vitamin K1.
Factors II, VII, IX, X low, V and fibrinogen normal
PEST-17.punch: Superwarfarins stop new clotting factors being made but leave the old ones, so the INR is normal until they run out at 24–48 hours — and because the drug stays in the liver for weeks, so must the vitamin K.
fix: A 4-hydroxycoumarin level covers the superwarfarins
Chlorophacinone is an indandione, not a 4-hydroxycoumarin. The INR rises at 24–48 h, but bleeding may only appear days later.

PEST-18.intro: Aluminium phosphide is sold as a grain fumigant, cheap and freely available in rural North India, and it is one of the commonest suicidal poisons there. Each tablet releases phosphine gas in the moist, acid stomach. Phosphine stops the cell’s final step of energy production, so the organs with the highest energy demand — the heart and blood vessels — fail first.
why: a
**26% of pesticide poisonings in a North Indian series (PGI Chandigarh).** It matters because it is common where grain is stored, and mortality is high.
b

**Phosphine, which inhibits cytochrome c oxidase.** This is complex IV, the last enzyme of the respiratory chain. With it blocked, oxygen cannot accept electrons, ATP production collapses and free radicals form. Cells switch to anaerobic metabolism, which is why lactate rises.
c

**Vomiting, refractory shock, myocarditis and arrhythmias, severe metabolic acidosis, within minutes to hours.** The shock combines a failing myocardium with vasodilatation, so neither fluids nor vasopressors restore pressure easily. Myocardial injury shows as ST changes, conduction block and arrhythmias. The acidosis is lactic, from cells unable to use oxygen. ARDS can follow.
d

**Supportive only; magnesium sulphate is used but unproven.** There is no antidote. Support means early ventilation, careful fluids, vasopressors and inotropes, and correction of acidosis; VA-ECMO has been used to carry the heart through the first 24–48 hours, after which survivors usually recover. Magnesium is given as a membrane stabiliser against arrhythmias, and low magnesium has been reported in some series, but small trials have given conflicting results and no survival benefit has been established.
mimic: Aluminium phosphide vs organophosphate

Both are pesticides with a garlic smell, but the organophosphate patient has cholinergic signs — miosis, bronchorrhoea, bradycardia, fasciculations (TOX-04); the phosphide patient is in shock with severe acidosis but no cholinergic toxidrome.
Phosphide cardiac shock vs acute MI
ST changes and troponin rise in both, but phosphide comes with a tablet history, severe acidosis and vasodilatation.
traps: “Phosphide has a specific antidote”
None exists; care is supportive.
“Magnesium is proven to lower mortality”
It is widely used, but the small trials conflict and benefit has not been established.
“Shock is hypovolaemic, so give large volumes of fluid”
The heart is failing; large volumes worsen pulmonary oedema. Guide fluids by echo and use inotropes.
decode: Grain-storage tablet, refractory shock and severe acidosis
Toxic gas in phosphide poisoning, and its target
PEST-18.punch: Phosphine blocks the last step of the respiratory chain, so the heart and vessels fail first and the shock resists treatment — and with no antidote, survival depends on supporting the circulation through the first day.

PEST-19.intro: Paraquat is a contact herbicide that destroys green plant tissue by generating free radicals. It is cheap, widely used and, swallowed, one of the deadliest poisons in agricultural regions of Asia. A small volume of the concentrate is enough to kill, and there is no antidote — which is why so many countries have banned it.
why: a

**Bipyridyl herbicide.** Two linked pyridine rings form a molecule that accepts and gives away electrons easily. That chemistry is the basis of its toxicity (PEST-20). Diquat is the other member of the group.
b
**10–20 mL of the 20% concentrate.** That is 2–4 g, or roughly 30–60 mg/kg in a 70 kg adult — inside the moderate-to-fulminant range (PEST-21). A single mouthful can therefore be fatal.
c

**Ingestion is dangerous; inhalation and skin contact are not life-threatening.** Spray droplets are too large to reach the alveoli, and intact skin absorbs little. Swallowed paraquat is absorbed from the gut and carried to the lungs and kidneys, where it concentrates.
d
**Case fatality up to 70%.** Death comes either quickly, from multi-organ failure after a large dose, or slowly, over weeks, from pulmonary fibrosis after a moderate one.
mimic: Paraquat vs diquat
Both bipyridyls; diquat spares the lung (no active alveolar uptake) and injures the kidney and brain instead.
Paraquat vs a corrosive
Both burn the mouth and oesophagus; only paraquat goes on to lung fibrosis.
traps: “The patient only swallowed a mouthful, so it is minor”
10–20 mL of the concentrate is a lethal dose.
“Farmers who spray paraquat die of lung fibrosis”
Inhaled droplets do not reach the alveoli; serious poisoning is from ingestion.
decode: Weedkiller ingestion, mouth ulcers, then breathlessness at 1–2 weeks
PEST-19.punch: Paraquat is lethal only when swallowed, but then a single mouthful of the 20% concentrate can kill — and there is nothing to reverse it.
fix: Skin contact is not life-threatening
True for intact skin and diluted spray; fatal poisoning has been reported after prolonged contact of the concentrate with damaged skin.

PEST-20.intro: Paraquat is not consumed when it does harm. It shuttles electrons from the cell’s reducing machinery to oxygen, again and again, making free radicals every time. The organs it injures most are those that take it up actively and hold it, and in the lung that uptake meets the highest oxygen tension in the body.
why: a

**Redox cycling generates reactive oxygen species, with mitochondrial failure.** NADPH-dependent enzymes reduce the paraquat ion to a radical; the radical gives its electron to oxygen, forming superoxide, and paraquat returns to its original state ready to go again. Each cycle makes more superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and hydroxyl radicals, damaging lipid membranes, and drains the cell’s NADPH, so its antioxidant defences fail.
b

**Active uptake by alveolar cells through the polyamine uptake system, causing alveolitis and then pulmonary fibrosis.** Paraquat resembles the natural polyamines, so type I and type II alveolar cells pump it in and concentrate it, even when plasma levels are falling. There it meets plenty of oxygen, so the redox cycle runs fastest. The acute destruction is alveolitis; the repair response that follows is fibrosis, which develops over one to three weeks.
c

**Accumulation in proximal tubular cells, causing tubular necrosis.** Paraquat is cleared almost entirely by the kidneys and is actively secreted by the proximal tubule, so these cells concentrate it. As the kidney fails, clearance falls and more paraquat is left to reach the lung.
d
**Oxygen is the substrate for free-radical formation.** Every turn of the cycle needs a molecule of oxygen, so extra oxygen accelerates the very injury that is destroying the lung.
mimic: Paraquat lung vs oxygen toxicity
Both are free-radical injuries; paraquat makes the alveoli far more vulnerable to oxygen, which is why supplemental oxygen is withheld.
traps: “Give high-flow oxygen as in every poisoning”
Oxygen feeds the redox cycle; give it only when the patient is hypoxic.
“The lung is injured because paraquat is inhaled”
It is swallowed and actively taken up by alveolar cells from the blood.
“Renal failure is a side-issue”
The kidney is the only route of elimination; when it fails, more paraquat reaches the lung.
decode: Why is oxygen withheld in paraquat poisoning?
Oxygen is the substrate for the redox cycle that forms free radicals.
Transport system concentrating paraquat in the lung
The polyamine uptake system of alveolar cells.
PEST-20.punch: Paraquat recycles itself, handing electrons to oxygen to make free radicals; the lung pumps it in and is full of oxygen, so the lung fibroses — and giving more oxygen only feeds the cycle.

PEST-21.intro: Because the redox cycle runs as long as paraquat is present, the outcome is set mainly by how much was swallowed. Grading by dose per kilogram predicts not just whether the patient dies but how: quickly from multi-organ failure, or weeks later from the lung.
why: a

**Mild: below 20 mg/kg — GI symptoms only, full recovery.** That is under about 7 mL of the 20% concentrate in an adult. The local caustic effect gives vomiting, diarrhoea and perhaps mouth ulcers, but too little reaches the lung to start fibrosis.
b

**Moderate to severe: 20–40 mg/kg — renal and hepatic failure, then pulmonary fibrosis; death in 2–3 weeks.** The kidney and liver are injured in the first days. Enough paraquat reaches the lung to start progressive fibrosis, so the patient may seem to improve and then become steadily more hypoxic. Survivors are few.
c

**Fulminant: above 40 mg/kg — multi-organ failure and shock; death in 1–4 days.** About 15 mL or more of the concentrate. The dose is so large that the heart, liver, kidneys and adrenal glands fail together, and the patient dies before fibrosis has time to develop.
mimic: Moderate vs fulminant death
Moderate dies of the lung over weeks; fulminant dies of the circulation within days.
traps: “Early recovery from the GI phase means survival”
In the 20–40 mg/kg group, fibrosis progresses over the following weeks.
“Fulminant paraquat poisoning ends in fibrosis”
Those patients die of multi-organ failure before fibrosis develops.
decode: Moderate–severe: expect progressive fibrosis, death in 2–3 weeks.
Fulminant: multi-organ failure, death in 1–4 days.
PEST-21.punch: Paraquat severity follows the dose: under 20 mg/kg the gut recovers, 20–40 mg/kg the lung fibroses over weeks, and above 40 mg/kg the whole body fails in days.

PEST-22.intro: With no antidote, the useful questions in paraquat poisoning are ‘was it paraquat?’ and ‘will this patient survive?’. A simple bedside test answers the first. The second is answered by how much paraquat is still in the plasma and how long after ingestion that level was taken, because the level falls quickly as the drug moves into the tissues and urine.
why: a

**Sodium dithionite in alkali added to urine gives a blue colour; best within 6 hours.** Dithionite reduces paraquat to its blue radical — the same reduction that drives its toxicity. Most paraquat is excreted in the first hours, so a late sample can be falsely negative; the depth of colour gives a rough guide to the amount.
b

**Severity Index of Paraquat Poisoning (SIPP) = plasma level (mg/L) × hours since ingestion; below 10, survival is likely.** A given level means more the later it is taken, because the plasma level should be falling. Multiplying by time corrects for this. Higher values predict death — first from lung fibrosis, and at very high values from circulatory failure.
c

**Other poor signs: lactate above 4, renal failure, ARDS.** A raised lactate means cellular respiration is already failing. Renal failure shuts off the only route of elimination, and early ARDS signals a large lung dose.
mimic: Paraquat vs diquat in the dithionite test
Paraquat turns blue; diquat gives green.
SIPP vs Proudfoot curve
Both use plasma level and time since ingestion; SIPP turns them into one number, Proudfoot plots them against a survival line.
traps: “A negative urine test the next day excludes paraquat”
Most is excreted early; test within about 6 hours.
“A plasma level alone predicts outcome”
It must be read against the time since ingestion.
decode: Urine turns blue with sodium dithionite
Paraquat with lactate 6 and rising creatinine
PEST-22.punch: Dithionite turns paraquat blue by the same reduction that makes it toxic, and prognosis comes from the plasma level read against time since ingestion — the SIPP — because a level that should have fallen but has not means death.

parts.q: Proudfoot curve: which levels mark 50% survival?
parts.a: About **2.0 mg/L at 4 h, 0.6 at 6 h, 0.3 at 10 h, 0.16 at 16 h and 0.1 at 24 h**; levels above the line predict death.

PEST-23.intro: Paraquat moves from the plasma into the lung and kidney within hours, and once there no treatment pulls it out. So treatment is mostly about binding what remains in the gut, keeping the kidneys excreting, and not making things worse with oxygen. Many experimental treatments have been tried; none has clearly changed survival.
why: a

**Avoid oxygen unless hypoxic; hydration; no forced emesis (caustic); wash skin and eyes; Fuller’s earth or activated charcoal early.** Oxygen feeds the redox cycle (PEST-20). Fluids keep urine flowing, because the kidney is the only route of elimination. Forcing emesis brings the corrosive back over the oesophagus and risks aspiration. Fuller’s earth (a clay) and charcoal bind paraquat in the gut, but only before it has been absorbed, which happens within hours.
b

**Experimental: immunosuppression (dexamethasone, cyclophosphamide), N-acetylcysteine, vitamins C and E, edaravone — none proven.** Immunosuppression aims to damp the alveolitis that leads to fibrosis; the antioxidants and the free-radical scavenger edaravone aim to mop up the radicals. Early small trials of steroid plus cyclophosphamide looked promising, but the largest trial (299 patients in Sri Lanka, 2018) found no significant survival benefit, and the 2021 Cochrane review rates the evidence as low certainty, with at most a small in-hospital effect and no difference at three months. None of the antioxidants has trial evidence of benefit.
c

**Haemofiltration: a meta-analysis of 3 trials showed no reduction in mortality (risk ratio 0.94).** The meta-analysis (2017: three randomised trials, 290 patients, continuous venovenous haemofiltration added to standard care) found mortality of about 58% versus 61%. Extracorporeal removal can only take paraquat out of the plasma; within hours most of it has already moved into the lung and kidney, where it is beyond reach. Haemofiltration did prolong survival, and fewer patients died of circulatory failure but more of respiratory failure — it delays death from the plasma load without stopping the lung injury already under way.
d
**False — luminescent faeces suggest yellow phosphorus.** Elemental phosphorus glows as it oxidises (PEST-15); phosphides release a gas.
e
**False — superwarfarin bleeding starts at 24–48 hours.** The circulating factors must be used up first (PEST-17).
mimic: Oxygen in paraquat vs in carbon monoxide
In CO, 100% oxygen is the treatment (TOX-13); in paraquat it feeds the injury.
traps: “Give high-flow oxygen to every poisoned patient”
In paraquat, only for hypoxia.
“Haemoperfusion or haemofiltration removes paraquat from the lung”
Only plasma paraquat is removed; tissue uptake happens within hours.
“Induce vomiting to empty the stomach”
Paraquat is caustic; use an adsorbent instead.
decode: Best early step in paraquat ingestion
Fuller’s earth or activated charcoal, fluids, no oxygen unless hypoxic.
Outcome is clear by 24–48 hours; early palliative care is appropriate.
PEST-23.punch: Paraquat leaves the plasma for the lung within hours and cannot be pulled back, so care is early binding, fluids and withholding oxygen — and when the dose is lethal, honest palliative care.

REC-01.sub: Toxicology → Cannabis & Opioids → Substance use in India
REC-01.intro: The figures come from the national survey on the magnitude of substance use in India (Ministry of Social Justice with NDDTC, AIIMS, 2019), which counted current users aged 10–75. They matter in the ICU because they predict what walks in: alcohol withdrawal and its complications far outnumber everything else, and opioids — mostly heroin — are used in India at a rate well above the world average. Children have a pattern of their own.
why: a

**Alcohol, 14.6%.** About one in seven Indians aged 10–75 is a current drinker, and a sizeable share of them are dependent. That is why alcohol withdrawal, Wernicke’s encephalopathy and alcohol-related liver and pancreatic disease are the commonest substance problems on the ward.
b

**Cannabis 2.8%, then opioids 2.1%.** Cannabis is cheap, culturally familiar (bhang) and widely available, so it comes second. Opioids come third overall, but the striking point is the comparison: at 2.1%, Indian opioid use is about three times the global figure (0.7%), and heroin has overtaken traditional opium as the commonest opioid.
c

**Inhalants.** Glue, whitener, petrol and solvent sprays are cheap, legal and easy to hide, so they are the substance of street and school-age children. The survey’s headline was that inhalants are the one class used more by children and adolescents than by adults.
mimic: Commonest substance overall vs in children
Overall it is alcohol; the class that is characteristic of children (used more by them than by adults) is inhalants.
Indian vs world opioid use
India about 2.1%, the world about 0.7% — roughly three times higher.
traps: “Cannabis is the commonest substance used in India”
Alcohol is far ahead at 14.6%; cannabis is second at 2.8%.
“Opioid use in India is below the world average”
It is about three times the global figure — 2.1% vs 0.7%.
decode: Commonest substance of abuse in India (national survey)
Substance more prevalent in children than adults
REC-01.punch: Alcohol dominates Indian substance use, cannabis and opioids follow — with opioid use three times the world rate — and inhalants are the drug of children.
fix: In children: inhalants
Inhalants are the only class used more by children than by adults (about 1.17% vs 0.58%, 2019 national survey); they are not the commonest substance in children.

REC-02.intro: Cannabis acts on the body’s own endocannabinoid system, a set of receptors that normally fine-tune neurotransmitter release. Where those receptors sit explains what the drug does: mainly brain effects — euphoria, slowed time, poor coordination, appetite — with little effect on breathing. That is why plain cannabis rarely kills and its treatment is supportive.
why: a

**Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol.** THC is the main psychoactive cannabinoid of the plant. It is highly lipid-soluble, so it is stored in fat and released slowly, which is why a chronic user stays urine-positive for weeks (TOX-02).
b

**CB1: CNS (basal ganglia, cerebellum, hypothalamus). CB2: periphery (spleen, immune cells).** CB1 receptors sit on presynaptic nerve terminals and dampen neurotransmitter release; their distribution matches the effects — basal ganglia and cerebellum (incoordination), hypothalamus (appetite and temperature), hippocampus (memory). CB2 receptors are on immune cells and modulate inflammation. CB1 is scarce in the brainstem respiratory centres, which is why cannabis alone does not stop breathing.
c

**Bhang (crushed leaves), ganja and charas (smoked), hashish (resin of flowering tops).** Bhang is made from leaves and is drunk or eaten, so its effect starts slowly and lasts longer. Ganja is the dried flowering tops; charas and hashish are concentrated resin, so they carry more THC per gram.
d

**Supportive; a short-acting benzodiazepine for agitation; exclude other drugs.** There is no antidote; the dangerous features are panic, psychosis and tachycardia, which settle with calm and a benzodiazepine. Because cannabis seldom explains coma or seizures, those features point to a co-ingestant, a synthetic cannabinoid or another cause.
mimic: Cannabis vs synthetic cannabinoids (spice, K2)
Synthetic cannabinoids are full CB1 agonists: seizures, agitated delirium, hyperthermia and AKI — and they are missed by the urine drug screen.
Cannabis vs anticholinergic
Both give tachycardia and confusion, but cannabis gives red conjunctivae with normal sweating and bowel; the anticholinergic patient is dry with urinary retention.
traps: “CB1 receptors are mainly peripheral”
CB1 is the central receptor; CB2 is on immune cells (REC-14a).
“Cannabis causes coma and respiratory depression”
Brainstem CB1 density is low, so breathing is spared; coma means look for something else.
“A negative urine screen excludes cannabinoid toxicity”
Synthetic cannabinoids are not detected by the standard immunoassay.
decode: Seizures, delirium, AKI after ‘herbal smoke’, urine screen negative
REC-02.punch: THC acts on central CB1 receptors that are scarce in the brainstem, so cannabis disturbs the mind but spares breathing — care is supportive, and anything worse means another drug.

parts.q: Synthetic cannabinoids: how do they differ from cannabis?
parts.a: Full CB1 agonists: **seizures, agitated delirium, hyperthermia, AKI**; **not detected** on urine screening; treat with **benzodiazepines** and supportive care.

parts.q: Cyclical vomiting in a chronic cannabis user, relieved by hot showers?
parts.a: **Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome** — the cure is stopping cannabis; haloperidol or topical capsaicin help acutely.

REC-03.sub: Toxicology → Cannabis & Opioids → Opioid overdose and naloxone
REC-03.intro: Opioids stimulate μ receptors in the brainstem, which blunts the response to carbon dioxide; breathing slows, then stops, and hypoxia is what kills. Naloxone is a competitive μ antagonist that displaces the opioid and restores breathing within minutes. The difficulty is that naloxone leaves the receptor sooner than most opioids do, so a patient who wakes can stop breathing again.
why: a

**Coma, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression.** μ stimulation depresses the reticular activating system (coma) and the respiratory centre (slow, shallow breathing), and releases the Edinger–Westphal nucleus from inhibition, so the pupils constrict (TOX-04). A respiratory rate below 12 in a drowsy patient with small pupils is the working definition.
b

**3,6-diacetylmorphine; 2–3 times as potent as morphine.** The two acetyl groups make heroin far more lipid-soluble, so it crosses the blood–brain barrier quickly; in blood and brain it is rapidly deacetylated to 6-monoacetylmorphine and morphine, which act on the receptor. Faster entry gives the ‘rush’ and the greater potency.
c

**0.2–0.4 mg IV or IM, repeated to a maximum of 2 mg (0.04 mg steps in the dependent).** The aim is breathing, not full wakefulness. In an opioid-dependent patient a large dose strips every receptor at once and causes abrupt withdrawal, so small steps are used and titrated to a respiratory rate of about 12 or more.
d
