**40–80 minutes (your notes also print 30–120): shorter than most opioids, so toxicity recurs.** Heroin itself is short-acting, but morphine, methadone and sustained-release preparations outlast a naloxone bolus. When the naloxone wears off the opioid still occupies the receptors, so the patient must be watched for re-sedation, not discharged on waking.
e

**Two-thirds of the effective reversal dose per hour.** The dose that woke the patient is known to work; giving two-thirds of it every hour as an infusion keeps receptor occupancy roughly steady and avoids repeated boluses. It is adjusted to breathing and to signs of withdrawal.
mimic: Opioid vs clonidine coma
Both give miosis, coma and bradycardia, but clonidine responds poorly to naloxone (TOX-04).
Naloxone pulmonary oedema vs heroin lung injury
After abrupt reversal, a catecholamine surge and gasping against a closed glottis cause non-cardiogenic oedema — one reason naloxone is titrated.
traps: “Naloxone outlasts the opioid, so one dose is enough”
It lasts 40–80 minutes, less than most opioids; re-sedation is the rule with long-acting drugs (REC-14b).
“Give 2 mg at once to any opioid overdose”
In the dependent patient that precipitates violent withdrawal, even seizures; titrate from 0.04 mg.
“Still drowsy after naloxone — give more until fully awake”
Naloxone restores breathing, not consciousness; once RR ≥12, look for a second cause (sedative, hypoglycaemia, head injury).
decode: Woke after naloxone, re-sedated an hour later
Naloxone wore off before the opioid — infusion.
Two-thirds of the reversal dose per hour.
REC-03.punch: Naloxone pushes the opioid off the μ receptor, but it leaves first — so it is titrated to breathing rather than wakefulness, and followed by an infusion or observation when the opioid will outlast it.

parts.q: Breathing restored by naloxone but patient still drowsy?
parts.a: A **second cause** — co-ingested sedative (benzodiazepine, alcohol, gabapentinoid), **hypoglycaemia**, head injury or hypoxic brain injury.

parts.q: Pulmonary oedema after naloxone: mechanism?
parts.a: **Non-cardiogenic**: catecholamine surge with negative-pressure breathing against a closed glottis; uncommon, but commoner after large, rapid doses.

fix: Naloxone to a maximum of 2 mg
2 mg is not a ceiling: up to about 10 mg is given before opioid toxicity is ruled out (more often needed with fentanyl analogues).

REC-04.intro: A body packer swallows many tightly wrapped packets of heroin or cocaine to smuggle them across a border. Each packet holds many times a lethal dose. The packer is well while the wrapping holds; if one leaks, the gut absorbs a massive dose at once — and which drug is inside decides whether there is an antidote.
why: a

**Massive toxicity from rupture of swallowed drug packets (heroin or cocaine).** The packets are made to survive transit, but gastric acid, bowel movement and time can split them. Because the gut wall absorbs freely, a single ruptured packet gives an overdose far larger than any street use. A packet that does not rupture can still obstruct the bowel.
b

**Packets may be radio-opaque.** Densely wrapped packets with air or a wax rim often show as regular oval shapes on a plain abdominal film (TOX-08). The X-ray misses some, so CT is more sensitive and is used to confirm that all packets have passed.
c

**Whole bowel irrigation for intact packets (standard teaching, not in your notes); laparotomy for a ruptured cocaine packet; naloxone infusion for heroin.** Polyethylene glycol flushes intact packets through before they break (TOX-09). Heroin leakage has a reliable antidote, so a naloxone infusion holds the patient while packets pass. Cocaine has none: continuing absorption brings seizures, hyperthermia and arrhythmia that benzodiazepines cannot outrun, so the packets must be removed surgically. Obstruction is the other indication for surgery.
mimic: Body packer vs body stuffer
A packer swallows well-made packets planned for smuggling (large dose, sealed); a stuffer hastily swallows loosely wrapped drug to evade arrest (smaller dose, leaks early).
traps: “Endoscopic removal of the packets”
Endoscopy risks tearing a packet; it is generally avoided.
“A normal abdominal X-ray excludes packets”
Plain films miss some; CT is more sensitive.
“Cocaine packer with seizures — benzodiazepines and wait for the packets to pass”
There is no antidote for continuing absorption; the packets come out at laparotomy.
decode: Traveller from an airport, asymptomatic, packets on X-ray
Body packer with seizures, hyperthermia, tachycardia
Body packer with pinpoint pupils and apnoea
REC-04.punch: A body packer is safe only while every packet holds: flush the intact ones through, cover a heroin leak with naloxone, and take a leaking cocaine packet out surgically because nothing else can stop the absorption.

table.title: What to do with a body packer
head: Situation
Management
rows: whole bowel irrigation, observe, CT to confirm clearance

REC-05.intro: Cocaine does two things at once. It blocks reuptake of noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin, so the synapses fill with catecholamine and the patient becomes hot, hypertensive and agitated; and it blocks cardiac sodium channels, as a local anaesthetic does. Most of its harm comes from intense vasoconstriction and that sympathetic storm — which is why calming the brain comes before treating the blood pressure.
why: a

**Tropane alkaloid; CNS stimulant.** Cocaine comes from the coca leaf and shares the tropane ring with atropine and scopolamine. It is an ester local anaesthetic as well as a stimulant, and that sodium-channel block explains its wide-QRS arrhythmias.
b

**Hyperthermia, seizures, myocardial infarction, aortic dissection, stroke, rhabdomyolysis and AKI.** Coronary vasospasm, increased platelet aggregation and a higher oxygen demand cause infarction even in young patients with normal arteries. Sudden surges in blood pressure tear the aorta and rupture cerebral vessels. Agitation and muscle activity generate heat, break down muscle and release myoglobin, which injures the kidney.
c

**Benzodiazepines; cooling; aggressive fluids for rhabdomyolysis.** Benzodiazepines reduce central sympathetic outflow, so the heart rate, blood pressure, agitation and heat production all fall together — they treat the cause. Cooling is active because the set point is normal (TOX-12). Fluids keep urine flowing to clear myoglobin.
d

**Avoid pure beta-blockers: unopposed alpha stimulation. Use nitrates, calcium-channel blockers or phentolamine.** Cocaine stimulates both α- and β-receptors; β₂ stimulation partly offsets the α-mediated vasoconstriction. Block β alone and α-vasoconstriction is left unopposed, worsening coronary spasm and blood pressure. Nitrates and calcium-channel blockers relax coronary spasm, and phentolamine blocks α-receptors directly.
e

**Sodium bicarbonate; lidocaine; lipid emulsion.** The wide QRS is sodium-channel block, so bicarbonate overcomes it as in a tricyclic overdose (TOX-07). Lidocaine is class Ib: it binds and leaves the channel quickly, so it is thought to compete with cocaine for the channel without deepening the block, unlike class Ia and Ic drugs; it is used if bicarbonate fails, accepting a small risk of lowering the seizure threshold. Lipid emulsion is a last-resort rescue in refractory arrest because cocaine is lipophilic.
mimic: Cocaine vs amphetamine
Both are sympathomimetic, but cocaine is short-acting and also blocks sodium channels (wide QRS); amphetamine lasts many hours.
Cocaine chest pain vs ordinary ACS
Same work-up, but benzodiazepines come first, then aspirin and nitrates — and no pure beta-blocker.
traps: “Beta-blocker for cocaine tachycardia or hypertension”
Unopposed α stimulation worsens spasm and hypertension; the exam answer is avoid (REC-14c).
“Class Ia or Ic anti-arrhythmic for cocaine VT”
They deepen sodium-channel block; bicarbonate first, lidocaine is the acceptable anti-arrhythmic.
“Labetalol is safe in cocaine toxicity because it also blocks α”
Given IV, labetalol is mainly a β-blocker (α:β roughly 1:7), so α-vasoconstriction is still left largely unopposed; nitrates, calcium-channel blockers or phentolamine are preferred.
“Paracetamol for cocaine hyperthermia”
The heat is muscular and the set point normal; cool actively and sedate.
decode: Young man, chest pain, ST elevation after cocaine — first drug
Haemoptysis and diffuse infiltrates within 48 h of smoking crack
REC-05.punch: Cocaine is a catecholamine storm plus a sodium-channel blocker: calm the brain with benzodiazepines, open the vessels without blocking β alone, and treat the wide QRS with bicarbonate.

parts.q: Cocaine STEMI: reperfusion strategy?
parts.a: **Primary PCI** (spasm, dissection and thrombus are common); fibrinolysis is the fallback, with added dissection and bleeding risk.

parts.q: Cocaine withdrawal: what does it look like?
parts.a: A **crash** — depression, hypersomnia and craving, not an autonomic storm.

REC-06.intro: Amphetamines push monoamines out of nerve terminals rather than only blocking their reuptake, so their effect is longer and stronger than cocaine’s. MDMA is the amphetamine with the biggest serotonin effect. In a crowded, hot dance venue that serotonin surge combines with exertion to drive temperature up, and with ADH release and heavy drinking to drive sodium down — those two are what kill.
why: a
**Ecstasy (tablet), Molly (crystal).** Molly is sold as the ‘pure’ crystal or powder form, though street samples are often adulterated with cathinones or other drugs.
b

**Releases and blocks reuptake of dopamine and serotonin; 5-HT2A agonist.** MDMA enters the nerve terminal through the transporter and reverses it, so serotonin (and dopamine and noradrenaline) pour out into the synapse; it also blocks reuptake. The serotonin release is far greater than with other amphetamines, which explains the empathy and closeness users seek and the serotonergic toxicity.
c

**Serotonin syndrome; also hyperthermia and hyponatraemia (standard teaching, not in your notes).** Excess serotonin gives clonus, hyperreflexia and heat (REC-11, REC-13). Hyperthermia, worsened by dancing in a hot room, drives rhabdomyolysis, DIC and multi-organ failure. Serotonin also releases ADH, and users drink large volumes of water, so a dilutional, SIADH-type hyponatraemia develops and can cause cerebral oedema and seizures — especially in young women.
d

**Parenteral benzodiazepines; nitroglycerine or nicardipine; no beta-blockers; external cooling.** Benzodiazepines lower central sympathetic drive and therefore the heat, the heart rate and the pressure together. If hypertension persists, a vasodilator is added; a beta-blocker is avoided for the same unopposed-α reason as with cocaine (REC-05). Cooling comes first if the temperature is high, because temperature predicts death.
mimic: MDMA vs cocaine
Bruxism and jaw clenching, hyponatraemia and long duration point to MDMA; cocaine is short-acting with a wide QRS.
MDMA hyponatraemia vs exercise-associated hyponatraemia
Both are dilutional; MDMA adds drug-driven ADH release (urine inappropriately concentrated).
traps: “Treat MDMA hypertension with a beta-blocker”
Unopposed α stimulation; benzodiazepine first, then a vasodilator.
“Fit at a rave — give phenytoin and normal saline”
Check sodium: seizures with severe hyponatraemia need 3% saline boluses.
“Dantrolene for MDMA hyperthermia”
Evidence is limited to case reports and it is not standard care; the heat comes from central drive and muscle activity, not a ryanodine-receptor leak — cool, sedate, paralyse above 41 °C.
decode: MDMA serotonin toxicity — cooling, benzodiazepines, paralysis.
REC-06.punch: MDMA is the serotonin amphetamine: the serotonin surge brings heat, clonus and ADH release, so temperature and sodium decide survival — cool first, sedate with benzodiazepines, and never use a beta-blocker.

parts.q: MDMA hyponatraemia with seizures: treatment?
parts.a: **3% saline, 100–150 mL boluses**; mild cases fluid restriction. It is SIADH-type (urine osmolality >100, urine Na >30) plus water loading.

REC-07.intro: Every feature of the sympathomimetic toxidrome is the fight-or-flight response turned up and left on. Cocaine, amphetamines, MDMA and cathinones flood the synapses with noradrenaline and dopamine, so each organ shows its sympathetic action. Going system by system is just going round the body and asking what adrenaline does there.
why: a

**CNS: euphoria, agitation, psychosis, seizures.** Dopamine excess in reward pathways gives euphoria; more of it gives paranoia and psychosis that looks like schizophrenia. At high levels the cortex becomes hyperexcitable and seizes, and agitation itself adds heat and acidosis.
b

**Neuromuscular: hyperreflexia, tremor.** Raised central drive and β₂ stimulation of muscle make reflexes brisk and produce tremor — but without the inducible clonus that marks serotonin toxicity (REC-12).
c

**Autonomic: hyperthermia, sweating, mydriasis.** Heat comes from muscle activity and vasoconstriction that stops the skin losing it. Sweating continues because sympathetic sweat fibres use acetylcholine and are driven, not blocked — the key difference from the anticholinergic patient (TOX-03). The pupils dilate through α₁ action on the dilator muscle.
d

**Cardiovascular: tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmia.** β₁ stimulation speeds and strengthens the heart; α₁ vasoconstriction raises the pressure. The combination raises myocardial oxygen demand while narrowing coronary supply, so ischaemia and arrhythmia follow.
e
**GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea.** These are common but non-specific; importantly, bowel sounds are present, unlike the silent bowel of anticholinergic poisoning.
mimic: Sympathomimetic vs anticholinergic
Both hot, fast and dilated; the sympathomimetic patient sweats and has bowel sounds, the anticholinergic is dry with retention.
Sympathomimetic vs serotonin syndrome
Both sweat with brisk reflexes; clonus (inducible or ocular) belongs to serotonin toxicity.
Sympathomimetic vs alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal
Look alike at the bedside and both settle with benzodiazepines; only the history (recent stopping of alcohol or sedatives) separates them.
traps: “Dilated pupils and fever — anticholinergic”
Shared with sympathomimetics; check the skin (TOX-03).
“Hyperreflexia means serotonin syndrome”
Sympathomimetics give brisk reflexes too; clonus is the serotonin sign.
decode: Paranoid psychosis after several days of a stimulant binge
REC-07.punch: The sympathomimetic toxidrome is adrenaline on every organ — hot, fast, hypertensive and dilated — and, unlike the anticholinergic, still sweating with bowel sounds present.

REC-08.intro: Most classic hallucinogens act as agonists at the 5-HT2A receptor in the cortex, which scrambles the way sensory input is filtered and gives visions, synaesthesia and a distorted sense of self. A second group — phencyclidine and ketamine — block the NMDA glutamate receptor instead and cut the mind off from the body (dissociation). The physical danger is usually small; the danger is behaviour, panic and, occasionally, heat.
why: a

**LSD: ergot-derived; synaesthesia, panic, hyperthermia.** Lysergic acid diethylamide is made from lysergic acid, found in the ergot fungus, and is active in microgram doses. Strong 5-HT2A agonism mixes the senses (seeing sounds) and can cause terrifying ‘bad trips’; with large doses mild sympathetic stimulation and hyperthermia occur.
b

**Psilocybin: magic mushrooms; active form psilocin.** Psilocybin is a prodrug: it is dephosphorylated to psilocin, the molecule that acts at 5-HT2A. The main real-world risk is eating a toxic mushroom by mistake.
c

**Mescaline: phenylethylamine (peyote).** Mescaline comes from the peyote cactus and is chemically a phenylethylamine — the same backbone as amphetamine and MDMA — which is why it carries some sympathetic effects with its visions.
d

**Phencyclidine: angel dust; nystagmus, violence.** PCP blocks NMDA receptors; that dissociation with anaesthesia to pain lets patients become violent and injure themselves without noticing. Nystagmus — horizontal, vertical or rotatory — is its bedside signature (TOX-05).
e

**Ketamine: NMDA antagonist; dissociation.** Ketamine is the shorter-acting relative of PCP: dissociation, nystagmus, raised heart rate and blood pressure, with airway reflexes and breathing usually preserved — which is why it is used as an anaesthetic.
f
**Salvia: salvinorin A.** Salvinorin A, from Salvia divinorum, is unusual in being a κ-opioid agonist rather than a serotonin or NMDA drug; it gives intense, very brief dissociation.
mimic: Classic hallucinogen vs dissociative
LSD and psilocybin (5-HT2A) alter perception with insight largely kept; PCP and ketamine (NMDA) dissociate and add nystagmus.
PCP vs sympathomimetic
Both agitated, hypertensive and violent; nystagmus points to PCP.
traps: “Activated charcoal and an antidote for hallucinogens”
There is no antidote and charcoal does not help; a quiet room and benzodiazepines are the treatment.
“Ketamine is a GABA agonist”
It is an NMDA antagonist (REC-14d).
“Psilocybin is the active molecule”
It is a prodrug; psilocin acts.
REC-08.punch: Hallucinogens split into 5-HT2A agonists that distort perception (LSD, psilocybin, mescaline) and NMDA antagonists that dissociate with nystagmus (PCP, ketamine) — neither has an antidote, so quiet and benzodiazepines are the treatment.

parts.q: An over-the-counter dissociative often combined with paracetamol?
parts.a: **Dextromethorphan** (NMDA antagonist) — check a **paracetamol level**; agitation gets benzodiazepines.

REC-09.sub: Toxicology → Hallucinogens & Sedatives → Sedative street drugs
REC-09.intro: Flunitrazepam and GHB are both used to sedate a victim without their knowledge (‘date-rape drugs’) because they are tasteless in a drink, act fast and erase memory of the events. Both enhance GABA inhibition, so the picture is sedation and amnesia — and, as with all sedative-hypnotics, the vital signs stay surprisingly normal until coma is deep.
why: a

**Rohypnol: a benzodiazepine 10 times as potent as diazepam; acts in 10–20 minutes for 4–6 hours; detected as a benzodiazepine on screening.** Flunitrazepam binds the GABA-A benzodiazepine site with high affinity, so a 1–2 mg tablet sedates strongly. Its rapid onset and anterograde amnesia are what make it a drug of assault — and sedation and amnesia often last well beyond 4–6 hours (8–12 hours or more is described); alcohol greatly deepens the sedation and respiratory depression.
b

**Gamma-hydroxybutyrate: liquid, mixed with alcohol; euphoria, amnesia, hypotonia, then sudden coma; supportive care.** GHB acts mainly on GABA-B receptors. It has a steep dose–response curve, so a little more than the euphoric dose gives coma within minutes — often with bradycardia and myoclonus — and, characteristically, the patient wakes abruptly a few hours later. Airway support is all that is needed; there is no antidote.
c

**CNS depression with near-normal vital signs and reflexes.** Sedative-hypnotics depress the cortex and reticular activating system long before they affect the brainstem centres that control breathing and circulation. So the patient is deeply asleep with a nearly normal pulse, blood pressure and breathing — unless alcohol or an opioid is added (TOX-04).
mimic: GHB vs opioid coma
GHB coma comes on suddenly and ends abruptly, often with bradycardia and myoclonus, and does not respond to naloxone.
Sedative-hypnotic vs opioid
Opioid: pinpoint pupils and a very slow respiratory rate. Sedative: variable pupils, near-normal breathing, often nystagmus.
traps: “Flumazenil to reverse a suspected Rohypnol drink”
Rarely given — seizure risk in dependence or mixed ingestion; support the airway (TOX-01).
“Profound coma means respiratory failure in a sedative overdose”
Vital signs stay near normal unless alcohol or opioids are added.
“A negative screen excludes a drink spiked with GHB”
GHB is not on the standard urine immunoassay.
decode: Sudden coma at a party, wakes abruptly after 3 hours
Amnesia after a spiked drink, benzodiazepine-like
Deep coma with normal vital signs
REC-09.punch: Flunitrazepam and GHB both deepen GABA inhibition — sedation and amnesia with near-normal vital signs — and GHB adds a sudden coma that ends as suddenly, needing only airway support.
fix: Flunitrazepam is detected as a benzodiazepine; lasts 4–6 hours
Routine urine benzodiazepine screens often miss it (specific assays needed), and sedation and amnesia often last 8–12 hours or more.

REC-10.intro: Volatile solvents — toluene, butane, propane and other hydrocarbons — are inhaled from a bag or rag (‘huffing’, ‘bagging’). They behave like inhaled anaesthetics: fat-soluble, taken up and cleared through the lungs within minutes. The acute danger is not the intoxication but the heart; the chronic danger is to every lipid-rich tissue, especially the brain.
why: a

**Glue, lighter refills, spray deodorants; street children.** These products are cheap, legal and sold everywhere, so they are the drug of the poorest and youngest users (REC-01). Toluene is the usual solvent in glue; butane and propane fill lighters and aerosol propellants.
b

**Sudden sniffing death syndrome: arrhythmia (myocardium sensitised to catecholamines).** Halogenated and hydrocarbon solvents make the myocardium excitable, so a surge of adrenaline — a fright, being chased or startled, sudden exertion — triggers ventricular fibrillation. Hypoxia from rebreathing in a bag adds to it. This is why the user should be approached calmly, and adrenaline is used with great care.
c

**Neurological, lung, liver and kidney damage.** Solvents dissolve into myelin: chronic toluene use gives white-matter loss (leukoencephalopathy), cerebellar ataxia and dementia. Toluene also causes distal renal tubular acidosis with hypokalaemia. Other solvents have their own targets — n-hexane causes peripheral neuropathy, and chlorinated solvents injure the liver.
mimic: Solvent coma vs heroin coma
Solvent coma clears within minutes of removal from the vapour; heroin coma lasts hours and responds to naloxone.
Toluene vs other causes of hypokalaemic acidosis
Toluene gives a normal anion gap acidosis from distal RTA, with very low potassium and weakness.
traps: “Sudden death in huffing is from asphyxia alone”
The main mechanism is catecholamine-sensitised VF, often triggered by fright or exertion.
“Give adrenaline freely to a solvent abuser in arrest”
The myocardium is sensitised to catecholamines; adrenaline may perpetuate VF — β-blockade has been used for refractory arrhythmia.
decode: Teenager collapses while running from police after sniffing glue
Chronic glue sniffer with weakness, hypokalaemia, normal anion gap acidosis
Solvent abuser, GCS 3 recovering to 15 within minutes
Volatile solvent cleared through the lungs.
REC-10.punch: Solvents are cheap anaesthetic vapours: they wear off in minutes, but they sensitise the heart to adrenaline — so fright can cause fatal VF — and with chronic use they dissolve the brain’s myelin.

REC-11.sub: Toxicology → Hyperthermic Toxidromes → Serotonin syndrome vs NMS
REC-11.intro: Both syndromes give a hot, confused, rigid patient on psychiatric drugs, and both can kill through hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis. But they arise from opposite neurochemistry: serotonin syndrome is too much serotonin stimulation, NMS is too little dopamine action. Too much serotonin excites — fast onset, clonus, brisk reflexes; too little dopamine freezes — slow onset, rigidity, slow reflexes.
why: a

**Cause: serotonin syndrome — excess serotonin, usually two serotonergic drugs; NMS — dopamine blockade, or stopping a dopamine agonist.** Serotonin syndrome usually follows adding a second serotonergic drug (TOX-05). NMS follows a dopamine D₂ antagonist — antipsychotics, metoclopramide — or abrupt withdrawal of levodopa in Parkinson’s disease, which removes dopamine action in the same way.
b

**Onset: serotonin syndrome under 12 hours; NMS 1–3 days.** Serotonin excess is a direct pharmacological effect, so it appears within hours of the dose change. NMS develops gradually as dopamine block in the hypothalamus and basal ganglia builds up, over days.
c
**Pupils: serotonin syndrome dilated; NMS normal.** Serotonin excess drives the sympathetic system and dilates the pupil; dopamine block has no such effect.
d

**Tone: serotonin syndrome increased, in the legs; NMS lead-pipe rigidity.** Serotonin excitation of spinal motor neurones raises tone mostly in the lower limbs. Loss of dopamine in the basal ganglia produces generalised parkinsonian ‘lead-pipe’ rigidity, uniform throughout the range of movement.
e

**Reflexes: serotonin syndrome hyperreflexia and clonus; NMS bradyreflexia.** This is the most reliable discriminator: clonus means serotonin. In NMS the rigid muscle and slowed motor system give sluggish reflexes.
f
**Bowel: serotonin syndrome hyperactive; NMS normal.** Most of the body’s serotonin is in the gut, where it drives motility, so serotonin excess gives diarrhoea and loud bowel sounds.
g

**Treatment: serotonin syndrome — cyproheptadine; NMS — bromocriptine, dantrolene.** Both start with stopping the drug, benzodiazepines and cooling. Cyproheptadine blocks 5-HT2A receptors (REC-13). Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist that replaces the missing dopamine action; dantrolene relaxes skeletal muscle by blocking calcium release, reducing heat production.
mimic: NMS vs malignant hyperthermia
Both rigid and hot with high CK; MH happens in theatre after a volatile agent or suxamethonium, with rising ETCO₂.
Serotonin syndrome vs anticholinergic
Both hot with dilated pupils; the anticholinergic patient is dry with a silent bowel and no clonus.
traps: “NMS shows hyperreflexia and clonus”
NMS gives slow reflexes; clonus is serotonin (REC-14e).
“Bromocriptine for serotonin syndrome”
A dopamine agonist can worsen serotonin toxicity; it is for NMS.
“Haloperidol to sedate the agitated patient”
In NMS it is the cause, and in serotonin syndrome it does not treat the serotonin excess and may add dopamine-block rigidity. Use benzodiazepines.
decode: Schizophrenic on haloperidol for 3 days, rigid, CK 20 000, temperature 40 °C
On sertraline, given tramadol, sweating, clonus within hours
Parkinson’s patient, levodopa stopped, rigid and febrile
REC-11.punch: Serotonin syndrome is excess serotonin — fast, twitchy, clonus and dilated pupils within hours; NMS is lost dopamine — slow, stiff, lead-pipe rigidity with slow reflexes over days.

REC-12.sub: Toxicology → Hyperthermic Toxidromes → The five hyperthermic toxidromes
REC-12.intro: Five drug-related syndromes can push the temperature to lethal levels. In all of them the heat comes from the body producing or holding heat — muscle activity, hypermetabolism or lost sweating — not from a raised hypothalamic set point, so antipyretics do nothing and every one is cooled actively. What separates them is one bedside sign each, and that sign decides the specific treatment.
why: a

**Sympathomimetic: sweaty, extreme hypertension — benzodiazepines.** Catecholamine excess raises heat production and blood pressure while sweating continues (REC-07). Benzodiazepines lower central sympathetic drive and so treat both.
b

**Anticholinergic: dry, non-reactive pupils, retention, absent bowel sounds — physostigmine (severe).** Muscarinic block stops sweating, so heat cannot be lost; it also paralyses the pupil, the bladder and the gut (TOX-03). Physostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase and crosses into the brain, so it reverses both the delirium and the peripheral signs; it is kept for severe cases and avoided when the ECG shows conduction delay.
c
**Serotonin: clonus, hyperreflexia — cyproheptadine.** Spinal 5-HT2A stimulation gives clonus, which no other toxidrome here produces (REC-13).
d
**NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, slow reflexes — bromocriptine.** Dopamine block causes the rigidity and impairs central heat regulation; bromocriptine replaces dopamine action (REC-11).
e

**Malignant hyperthermia: rising CO₂, rigor despite relaxant; temperature often above 42 °C — dantrolene.** In susceptible patients a volatile agent or suxamethonium opens the abnormal ryanodine receptor, calcium floods the muscle cytoplasm, and the muscles contract and burn energy uncontrollably. That hypermetabolism first shows as a rising end-tidal CO₂ and tachycardia; temperature rises later. Dantrolene blocks the ryanodine receptor and stops the calcium release — which is why it is the specific cure here, where the problem is in the muscle itself, and at most an adjunct in the other toxidromes.
mimic: Sympathomimetic vs anticholinergic
The skin: wet vs dry.
Serotonin vs NMS
Clonus and hours vs rigidity and days.
Malignant hyperthermia vs NMS
MH: minutes to hours in theatre after a trigger; NMS: days after an antipsychotic.
traps: “Paracetamol for toxic hyperthermia (your notes list it under cocaine)”
The set point is normal; all five are cooled actively.
“Dantrolene for cocaine or MDMA hyperthermia”
Only case reports support it, and it is not standard care; the heat is central and muscular drive, not a ryanodine-receptor leak. Cool, sedate, paralyse above 41 °C.
“Physostigmine for any agitated, dry patient”
Avoid with QRS widening or suspected tricyclic — it can cause bradyasystole; also asthma and conduction defects.
decode: Rising ETCO₂, tachycardia, masseter rigidity under sevoflurane
REC-12.punch: Five syndromes, one heat mechanism — muscle and lost cooling, never the thermostat — so all are cooled actively, and the giveaway sign (wet, dry, clonus, lead-pipe, rising CO₂) picks the specific drug.

parts.q: Malignant hyperthermia: dantrolene dose?
parts.a: **2.5 mg/kg IV**, repeated every 5–10 minutes until the crisis settles; usual upper limit about **10 mg/kg**, though more is occasionally needed.

parts.q: Physostigmine contraindications?
parts.a: **Wide QRS or AV block (and suspected tricyclic overdose)**, asthma or reactive airways disease, and mechanical bowel or bladder obstruction.

parts.q: Physostigmine: adult dose?
parts.a: **0.5–2 mg IV slowly over at least 5 minutes** (no faster than about 1 mg/min), repeated if needed; child 0.02 mg/kg. Atropine must be at hand.

REC-13.sub: Toxicology → Hyperthermic Toxidromes → Serotonin syndrome: diagnosis and treatment
REC-13.intro: Serotonin syndrome has no laboratory test; it is a clinical diagnosis made at the bedside in a patient exposed to a serotonergic drug. Its severity ranges from tremor and a little sweating to a temperature above 41 °C with rigidity. Treatment rests mostly on removing the drug and controlling heat and agitation; the specific antidote is a helper rather than a cure.
why: a

**Altered mental status, autonomic hyperactivity, neuromuscular abnormality.** Serotonin excess acts in three places: the brain (agitation, confusion), the autonomic system (sweating, tachycardia, mydriasis, diarrhoea, heat) and the spinal cord (tremor, hyperreflexia, clonus). The neuromuscular part is the most specific.
b

**Hunter criteria (sensitivity 84%, specificity 97%); Sternbach (75%, 96%).** The Hunter criteria require a serotonergic drug plus one of: spontaneous clonus; inducible clonus with agitation or sweating; ocular clonus with agitation or sweating; tremor with hyperreflexia; or hypertonia with temperature above 38 °C and ocular or inducible clonus. Because they are built on clonus, they are more accurate than the older Sternbach criteria, which counted non-specific features that overlap with NMS and sympathomimetic toxicity.
c

**Serotonin (5-HT2A) antagonist: 2 mg per dose to a maximum of 12 mg; maintenance 8 mg every 6 hours. Usual regimen: 12 mg, then 2 mg every 2 hours (standard teaching, not in your notes).** Cyproheptadine is a first-generation antihistamine that also blocks 5-HT2A (and 5-HT1A) receptors. The larger initial dose is chosen because 12–32 mg over 24 hours is estimated to bind 85–95% of serotonin receptors; the notes’ ‘maximum of 12 mg’ does not fit the standard regimen. It exists only as an oral preparation, so in a sedated patient it is crushed and given by nasogastric tube.
d

**Symptom relief only; no proven effect on outcome.** There are no controlled trials; case series show it eases symptoms. Survival depends on stopping the drug, benzodiazepines, active cooling and, above 41 °C, paralysis with a non-depolarising relaxant and ventilation, which stops the muscle heat at its source.
mimic: Hunter vs Sternbach
Hunter rests on clonus and is more specific; Sternbach counts broader features and catches NMS and stimulant toxicity by mistake.
traps: “Cyproheptadine is the mainstay and improves survival”
It relieves symptoms only; supportive care, cooling and paralysis save life.
“Paralyse the hyperthermic patient with suxamethonium”
Use a non-depolarising agent — rhabdomyolysis raises potassium, which suxamethonium worsens.
“Give IV cyproheptadine”
It is oral only — crushed via nasogastric tube.
decode: Best diagnostic criteria for serotonin syndrome
Temperature 41.5 °C, rigid, on SSRI and linezolid
REC-13.punch: Serotonin syndrome is diagnosed by clonus (Hunter criteria) and survived by removing the drug and stopping the heat — cyproheptadine eases the symptoms but has never been shown to change the outcome.
fix: Cyproheptadine 2 mg per dose to a maximum of 12 mg
Standard regimen (Boyer & Shannon, NEJM 2005): 12 mg first, then 2 mg every 2 hours while symptoms persist, then 8 mg 6-hourly — about 12–32 mg a day.

REC-14.intro: This card tests the deck’s key distinctions. Each statement turns on one mechanism from an earlier card; the reason for each answer is the physiology met there.
why: a
**False — CB1 is central; CB2 is peripheral.** CB1 receptors sit on brain nerve terminals (basal ganglia, cerebellum, hypothalamus); CB2 is on immune cells (REC-02).
b
**False — naloxone lasts 40–80 minutes.** That is shorter than most opioids, so sedation recurs as it wears off (REC-03).
c
**False — avoid beta-blockers; give benzodiazepines.** Blocking β alone leaves α-vasoconstriction unopposed; benzodiazepines reduce the sympathetic drive itself (REC-05).
d
**True — ketamine is an NMDA antagonist,** which gives its dissociation and nystagmus (REC-08).
e
**False — hyperreflexia and clonus are serotonin syndrome.** NMS gives lead-pipe rigidity with slow reflexes (REC-11).
f
**True — malignant hyperthermia is treated with dantrolene,** which blocks calcium release from the abnormal ryanodine receptor (REC-12).
g
**False — anticholinergic skin is dry.** Sweat glands work through muscarinic receptors (TOX-03).
h
**True — serotonin syndrome begins within 12 hours** of the drug change, unlike NMS, which takes days (REC-11).
traps: “Naloxone wakes the patient for good”
It wears off before most opioids.
“Clonus can occur in NMS”
Clonus is the serotonin sign; NMS is slow and stiff.
decode: Check the reflexes and the onset: clonus and hours mean serotonin, rigidity and days mean NMS.
REC-14.punch: Every statement here turns on a mechanism from the deck — where CB1 sits, how long naloxone lasts, unopposed α, clonus versus rigidity, and the sweat gland’s muscarinic receptor.

REC-15.sub: Toxicology → Hyperthermic Toxidromes → Temperature, onset and reflexes
REC-15.intro: Once the skin and the giveaway sign are known (REC-12), three more features sort the hyperthermic toxidromes: how hot, how fast and what the reflexes do. The drug-induced syndromes that act directly — sympathomimetic, anticholinergic, serotonin — appear within hours; NMS needs days; malignant hyperthermia is the hottest because the muscle itself is out of control.
why: a
**Sympathomimetic: above 38 °C, under 12 hours, brisk reflexes.** Catecholamine excess is immediate, and central excitation makes reflexes brisk without clonus (REC-07).
b

**Anticholinergic: above 38 °C, under 12 hours, normal reflexes.** The drug blocks muscarinic receptors, which do not run the spinal reflex arc, so reflexes stay normal; the heat comes from absent sweating and agitation.
c

**Serotonin: above 38 °C, under 12 hours, clonus (ocular too).** Serotonin acts on spinal motor neurones, giving hyperreflexia and inducible, spontaneous or ocular clonus — slow, side-to-side eye movements (REC-13).
d
**NMS: 39–42 °C, 1–3 days, slow reflexes.** Dopamine block builds up over days; rigid muscle generates heat and blunts the reflexes (REC-11).
e

**Malignant hyperthermia: often above 42 °C, 30 minutes to 24 hours, hyporeflexia.** Uncontrolled calcium release keeps every muscle fibre contracting, so heat production is enormous and temperature can climb by 1 °C or more every 5 minutes in a fulminant case. It usually starts in theatre during or soon after exposure to the trigger; in the anaesthetised, relaxant-given patient reflexes are depressed.
mimic: Malignant hyperthermia vs NMS
Both rigid with high CK; MH follows a trigger within the anaesthetic, NMS takes days after an antipsychotic.
traps: “Temperature is the first sign of malignant hyperthermia”
A rising ETCO₂ and tachycardia come first; the temperature rises later.
“Propofol or rocuronium can trigger malignant hyperthermia”
Only volatile agents and suxamethonium trigger it; propofol, opioids, ketamine and non-depolarising relaxants are safe.
“Nitrous oxide is a trigger”
It is the exception — not a trigger.
REC-15.punch: Hours and brisk reflexes or clonus mean a drug acting directly (sympathomimetic, serotonin); days and slow reflexes mean NMS; the hottest of all, in theatre, is malignant hyperthermia, where the muscle itself burns.

SNAKE-01.sub: Toxicology → Snakes & Venom → The size of the problem
SNAKE-01.intro: Snakebite in India is a rural, night-time, farm-work injury, and most victims never reach a doctor in time. Most bites turn out harmless, either because the snake was not venomous or because a venomous snake injected nothing. The numbers matter clinically: they explain why every bite is observed rather than treated blindly, and why antivenom must reach the primary health centre rather than wait in the city.
why: a

**35,000–50,000 deaths per year (WHO), the highest in the world.** India has a dense rural population working barefoot in fields, sleeping on the floor, and living among the four commonest dangerous species. Because many deaths happen at home and are never registered, every count is an underestimate: the Indian Standard Treatment Guidelines (2017) estimate about 45,900 deaths a year, and the household-survey Million Death Study about 58,000.
b

**70% of bites are non-venomous, and 50% of venomous bites are dry.** A snake controls whether it injects venom, and a defensive strike often delivers none. This is why the bite alone is never an indication for antivenom (SNAKE-12): treatment waits for evidence of envenoming.
c

**About 34% of proven bites develop systemic envenoming.** Even when the snake is venomous, only a minority inject enough venom to reach the circulation and cause bleeding, paralysis, shock or kidney injury. The rest have no signs or local signs only, which is why every bite is watched for 24 hours (SNAKE-09) before it is called harmless.
d

**Most deaths occur before reaching hospital.** Neurotoxic bites can stop breathing within hours, and delay is lengthened by distance, night-time bites, and time lost with traditional healers and harmful first aid. Once a patient is in hospital with antivenom and a ventilator, most survive.
mimic: Dry bite vs delayed envenoming
A dry bite stays normal for 24 hours. Krait envenoming can look like nothing for several hours before ptosis appears — hence the full observation period.
traps: “Every snakebite needs antivenom”
Most bites are non-venomous or dry; antivenom is given only for signs of envenoming.
“No symptoms at 1 hour, so it was a dry bite”
Krait paralysis and viper coagulopathy can appear hours later; observe for at least 24 hours.
“Most deaths occur in hospital from antivenom reactions”
Most die before reaching hospital, from untreated envenoming.
decode: Snakebite deaths in India per year
Proportion of venomous bites that are dry
Where do most snakebite deaths occur?
SNAKE-01.punch: Most bites never inject venom, so the bite is watched, not treated — but those that do envenom kill mostly on the way to hospital, so speed of transport and antivenom near the patient save lives.
fix: 35,000–50,000 deaths a year
The Indian guideline 2017 estimates about 45,900 a year; the Million Death Study (2020) about 58,000 a year.

SNAKE-02.sub: Toxicology → Snakes & Venom → Families and the big four
SNAKE-02.intro: Venomous snakes fall into families whose venoms do broadly different things: elapids mainly paralyse, vipers mainly disturb clotting and damage tissue. In India four species cause most deaths, and the national antivenom is raised against exactly those four. A snake outside that list may envenom a patient whom the antivenom cannot help.
why: a

**Elapidae — cobras, kraits (also king cobra, coral snakes): neurotoxic.** Elapids have short fixed front fangs and venoms rich in small neurotoxins that block the neuromuscular junction, so the danger is descending paralysis and respiratory failure (SNAKE-04, 07).
b

**Viperidae — true vipers (Russell’s, saw-scaled) and pit vipers (hump-nosed, Malayan): haemotoxic.** Vipers have long, hinged fangs and venoms full of enzymes that consume clotting factors and damage vessel walls, so they cause local swelling, bleeding, shock and kidney injury. Pit vipers carry a heat-sensing pit between eye and nostril.
c

**Hydrophidae — sea snakes: myotoxic.** Their venom breaks down skeletal muscle, giving muscle pain, myoglobinuria and kidney injury; sea snake venom is also neurotoxic. The bite itself is usually painless, with little local reaction.
d

**Common cobra (Naja naja), common krait (Bungarus caeruleus), Russell’s viper (Daboia russelii), saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus).** These four are widespread, live close to people and cause most bites and deaths, so Indian polyvalent antivenom is made by immunising horses with their venoms. Its antibodies recognise these venoms and not others, which is why a hump-nosed pit viper bite does not respond.
mimic: Russell’s viper vs hump-nosed pit viper
Both give local swelling, coagulopathy and kidney injury; only Russell’s viper is covered by Indian antivenom.
Cobra vs king cobra
Both elapids with local necrosis and paralysis; the king cobra is not one of the big four and is not covered by the polyvalent antivenom.
traps: “Polyvalent antivenom covers all Indian venomous snakes”
It covers only the big four; hump-nosed pit viper and king cobra are not covered.
“The krait is a viper because it bites at night”
The krait is an elapid: neurotoxic, with almost no local signs.
decode: Which snake is NOT one of the big four?
Hump-nosed pit viper or king cobra.
Viper bite with coagulopathy not responding to antivenom
Sea snake bite, muscle pain, dark urine
SNAKE-02.punch: Elapids paralyse and vipers make the blood unclottable; Indian antivenom is raised against only the big four, so a snake outside that list may envenom a patient the antivenom cannot help.
fix: Sea snakes: Hydrophidae, myotoxic
Sea snakes are now classed within Elapidae, and their venom is neurotoxic as well as myotoxic.

SNAKE-03.sub: Toxicology → Snakes & Venom → What the venom contains
SNAKE-03.intro: Venom is modified saliva, and more than 90% of its dry weight is protein — enzymes and small toxins, each with its own target. The clinical picture of a bite is simply the sum of what each component does. Knowing the components explains why vipers bleed, why cobras necrose and why kraits paralyse without a mark on the skin.
why: a

**Metalloproteinases damage the endothelial basement membrane: capillary leak, bleeding, shock.** These zinc-dependent enzymes digest the collagen and matrix that hold capillary walls together. Red cells and plasma escape through the damaged wall, giving local swelling and blistering, bleeding from gums and wounds, and hypovolaemic shock.
b

**Procoagulant enzymes activate clotting: consumption coagulopathy (DIC-like).** Russell’s viper venom activates factors X and V, and saw-scaled viper venom activates prothrombin. Clotting is triggered throughout the blood until fibrinogen and factors are used up, and the blood becomes unclottable — the basis of the 20-minute clotting test (SNAKE-09). It is called DIC-like because it is consumption by venom, not sepsis or tissue factor.
c

**Phospholipase A₂: myotoxicity, presynaptic neurotoxicity, mitochondrial damage.** This enzyme breaks down membrane phospholipids. In muscle it causes rhabdomyolysis; at the motor nerve terminal it destroys the terminal itself (β-bungarotoxin of the krait is a phospholipase A₂), which is why krait paralysis lasts and does not respond to neostigmine (SNAKE-04).
d

**Hyaluronidase: the spreading factor, with tissue destruction.** It breaks down hyaluronic acid in the connective tissue, opening a path for the other toxins to spread from the bite. The necrosis itself comes mainly from the enzymes and cytotoxins that hyaluronidase lets through.
e

**Polypeptide neurotoxins block the neuromuscular junction.** These small toxins (the α-neurotoxins of cobras) bind the postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptor and stop acetylcholine from acting. The nerve terminal is intact, so more acetylcholine — neostigmine — can compete them off.
mimic: Presynaptic vs postsynaptic neurotoxin
Presynaptic (phospholipase A₂, krait) destroys the nerve terminal; postsynaptic (α-neurotoxin, cobra) blocks the receptor and can be overcome by more acetylcholine.
Venom coagulopathy vs septic DIC
Venom consumes factors directly and is reversed by antivenom; septic DIC follows tissue factor release and is treated by treating the infection.
traps: “Give FFP to correct the venom coagulopathy”
Free venom consumes the new factors too; antivenom first, FFP only afterwards (SNAKE-16).
“Venom is mainly lipid”
More than 90% of it is protein, which is why horse antibodies can neutralise it.
decode: Procoagulant enzymes (factor X, V and prothrombin activators).
SNAKE-03.punch: Each venom protein has one target — the vessel wall, the clotting cascade, the cell membrane, the connective tissue or the acetylcholine receptor — and the bite’s picture is their sum.
fix: Hyaluronidase: tissue destruction
Hyaluronidase is the spreading factor; the tissue destruction comes mainly from metalloproteinases, phospholipase A₂ and cytotoxins.

SNAKE-04.sub: Toxicology → Snakes & Venom → Cobra vs krait neurotoxicity
SNAKE-04.intro: Cobras and kraits both paralyse, from the eyelids downwards, but they attack the neuromuscular junction from opposite sides. The cobra blocks the receptor on the muscle; the krait destroys the nerve terminal that releases acetylcholine. That one difference explains the local signs, the timing, the response to neostigmine and the length of ventilation.
why: a

**Toxin site: cobra postsynaptic (α-neurotoxin); krait presynaptic (β-bungarotoxin).** The α-neurotoxin sits on the nicotinic receptor like a competitive blocker. β-bungarotoxin is a phospholipase A₂ that enters the nerve terminal, first causing a burst of release and then exhausting and destroying it.
b

**Local reaction: cobra swelling and necrosis; krait virtually painless, none.** Cobra venom contains cytotoxins that kill tissue at the bite, so the limb is painful and swollen and may necrose. Krait venom has almost no local toxins and the fangs are small, so the bite may not even be noticed.
c

**Onset: cobra early, within 30 minutes; krait delayed, with prolonged paralysis.** A receptor block acts as soon as toxin reaches the junction. Presynaptic damage takes hours to show, and recovery needs a new nerve terminal to grow, so paralysis can last days to weeks.
d

**Neostigmine: cobra responds; krait does not.** Neostigmine raises acetylcholine in the cleft, which competes the α-neurotoxin off the receptor. With a destroyed terminal there is no acetylcholine to increase (SNAKE-10).
e

**Typical story: cobra — painful swollen bite; krait — bitten asleep on the floor at night, with abdominal pain.** Kraits hunt at night and enter houses, so the victim is bitten while sleeping and wakes with abdominal pain, then ptosis by morning, with no mark to explain it.
mimic: Krait bite vs Guillain–Barré or stroke
Sudden ptosis and bulbar palsy at dawn in a rural patient who slept on the floor, with no bite mark, is krait until proven otherwise.
traps: “No bite mark and no swelling, so not envenomed”
Krait bites are painless and leave little trace; watch for ptosis.
“Neostigmine failed, so antivenom is useless”
Antivenom is still given in krait bites to neutralise venom still circulating, though it cannot repair terminals already damaged.
“SpO₂ is normal on oxygen, so the paralysed patient is safe”
Oxygen hides a rising CO₂; ventilatory failure needs intubation, not more oxygen.
decode: Woke at night with abdominal pain, ptosis by morning, no local swelling
Painful swollen bite, then ptosis within an hour, improves with neostigmine
SNAKE-04.punch: The cobra blocks the receptor, so more acetylcholine wins and recovery is quick; the krait destroys the terminal, so neostigmine has nothing to work with and the patient needs the ventilator until the nerve regrows.

parts.q: Krait bite: when to intubate?
parts.a: **Early** — for bulbar palsy with pooled secretions, neck-flexor weakness, paradoxical breathing, a falling single-breath count, or a **rising PaCO₂**. Oxygen alone masks hypoventilation.

SNAKE-05.sub: Toxicology → Clinical Syndromes → WHO syndromic approach
SNAKE-05.intro: Most patients never see the snake, or bring a description that cannot be trusted. The WHO approach turns the question round: instead of identifying the snake to predict the illness, it reads the illness to name the snake. Three questions do most of the work — is there local swelling, is the blood clotting, and is there paralysis?
why: a
**Syndrome 1 — local envenoming with bleeding: Viperidae.** Swelling plus incoagulable blood means a viper, because procoagulant and haemorrhagic enzymes are the vipers’ hallmark (SNAKE-03).
b

**Syndrome 2 — as syndrome 1 plus shock or AKI, conjunctival oedema, pituitary failure; or plus ptosis and dark urine: Russell’s viper.** Russell’s venom adds vasodilating and nephrotoxic effects; in Myanmar it also causes chemosis and infarction of the anterior pituitary. In South India and Sri Lanka it carries a presynaptic phospholipase A₂, giving ptosis, and haemolysis or rhabdomyolysis turns the urine dark.
c

**Syndrome 3 — local envenoming with paralysis: cobra.** Only cobras combine cytotoxic necrosis at the bite with neurotoxic paralysis; WHO lists cobra or king cobra here, and the king cobra is not one of the big four.
d
**Syndrome 4 — paralysis with minimal local signs: krait (on land, asleep) or sea snake (in water).** Both venoms are neurotoxic with almost no local toxins; the place of the bite separates them.
e

**Syndrome 5 — paralysis with dark urine and AKI: Russell’s viper; sea snake.** Paralysis and kidney injury together mean a venom that is both neurotoxic and myotoxic or haemolytic, so muscle or red cells break down and the pigment injures the tubules. The clotting test separates the two: a land bite with incoagulable blood is Russell’s viper (South India, Sri Lanka), a sea bite with normal clotting is a sea snake. WHO also lists kraits of Bangladesh and Thailand here, but not the Indian common krait.
mimic: Syndrome 3 vs 4
Both paralyse; local swelling and necrosis mean cobra, a clean bite site means krait.
traps: “Wait for the snake to be identified before giving antivenom”
The syndrome is enough; polyvalent antivenom covers all four, so the species need not be known.
“Ptosis rules out a viper”
Russell’s viper in South India and Sri Lanka can cause ptosis, with coagulopathy and dark urine.
decode: Ptosis, no swelling, bitten asleep on the floor
SNAKE-05.punch: Read the patient, not the snake: swelling with bleeding is a viper, swelling with paralysis a cobra, paralysis on a clean bite a krait — and Russell’s viper adds shock, kidney injury and sometimes ptosis.

SNAKE-06.sub: Toxicology → Clinical Syndromes → Features by species
SNAKE-06.intro: This table is the syndromic approach laid out snake by snake. Each column is the venom’s chemistry seen at the bedside: cytotoxins give local damage, neurotoxins give paralysis, procoagulants give coagulopathy, and the nephrotoxic Russell’s venom gives kidney failure. Only one box separates cobra from krait in the treatment column — neostigmine.
why: a

**Local damage: cobra yes, krait no, Russell’s yes, saw-scaled yes.** Cobra cytotoxins and viper metalloproteinases destroy tissue at the bite. The krait’s venom has almost none, so a clean bite site with paralysis points to a krait.
b

**Ptosis and paralysis: cobra yes, krait yes, Russell’s sometimes, saw-scaled no.** The elapids paralyse; Russell’s viper does so only in some regions (presynaptic phospholipase A₂). The saw-scaled viper is purely haemotoxic.
c

**Coagulopathy: cobra no, krait no (may occur), Russell’s yes, saw-scaled yes.** Viper procoagulants consume clotting factors (SNAKE-03), so a positive 20WBCT points to a viper and away from the elapids.
d

**Renal failure: only Russell’s viper.** Russell’s venom injures the kidney directly and through haemolysis, rhabdomyolysis, shock and DIC, producing acute tubular necrosis (SNAKE-07). The saw-scaled viper bleeds but seldom damages the kidney.
e
**Neostigmine: only the cobra.** Its postsynaptic block can be overcome by more acetylcholine; the krait and Russell’s viper act presynaptically (SNAKE-10).
f
**Antivenom: all four.** Polyvalent antivenom is raised against each of the big four, so all respond — unlike the hump-nosed pit viper, which looks like a Russell’s bite but is not covered.
mimic: Russell’s vs saw-scaled viper
Both cause swelling and coagulopathy; kidney failure (and ptosis in some regions) points to Russell’s.
Russell’s vs hump-nosed pit viper
Same picture of local damage, coagulopathy and AKI; hump-nosed does not respond to Indian antivenom.
traps: “Coagulopathy can be a cobra bite”
Indian cobra venom does not cause coagulopathy; a positive 20WBCT means a viper.
“Saw-scaled viper causes paralysis”
It is purely haemotoxic.
“Neostigmine helps any neurotoxic bite”
Only postsynaptic (cobra) paralysis responds.
decode: Viper picture, no response to adequate antivenom
SNAKE-06.punch: Every box follows from the venom: cytotoxins give local damage, procoagulants give bleeding, neurotoxins give paralysis — and only the cobra’s postsynaptic block lets neostigmine work.

SNAKE-07.sub: Toxicology → Clinical Syndromes → What kills, and the brain-death trap
SNAKE-07.intro: Systemic envenoming kills in two different ways. Vipers make the blood unclottable and the vessels leaky, so the patient bleeds where it does most harm and the kidneys fail. Elapids paralyse from the head down until the breathing muscles stop. A fully paralysed patient can look dead while wide awake — the most dangerous misjudgement in the snakebite ward.
why: a

**Viper bite deaths: intracranial bleeding, anterior pituitary haemorrhage, multi-organ failure.** Incoagulable blood plus vessel damage lets a small bleed in the brain expand. Russell’s venom can cause haemorrhagic infarction of the anterior pituitary: acutely shock and hypoglycaemia from adrenal insufficiency, and months to years later chronic hypopituitarism (loss of body hair, amenorrhoea or testicular atrophy, hypothyroidism). Shock, AKI and DIC together give multi-organ failure.
b

**Neurotoxic paralysis is descending: ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, bulbar weakness, then respiratory muscles.** The small, fast-firing motor units of the eye and face have the least safety margin at the neuromuscular junction, so they fail first. Bulbar weakness then threatens the airway, and the diaphragm fails last.
c

**Locked-in state mimics brain death: fixed dilated pupils and no movement, yet conscious. Never diagnose brain death.** Venom blocks the neuromuscular junction, including the eye muscles and the iris, but not the brain. The patient can hear everything, so is sedated and spoken to, and brainstem death testing is invalid until the toxin has gone.
d

**Acute tubular necrosis is the commonest renal lesion.** Shock, haemoglobin and myoglobin pigments, microthrombi from consumption coagulopathy and direct venom toxicity all injure the tubular cells. Cortical necrosis is less common and carries a worse outlook.
mimic: Locked-in envenoming vs brain death
Both: fixed pupils, no movement, apnoea. Envenoming is a junction block in a conscious brain — the EEG is active and recovery is expected.
traps: “Fixed dilated pupils in a krait bite mean brain death”
Paralysis of the iris and every muscle mimics it; never certify brain death in neurotoxic envenoming.
“Russell’s viper AKI will settle with fluids”
Pigment, DIC and direct toxicity rarely reverse on fluid alone; repeat antivenom if still incoagulable and start renal replacement early.
“Steroids help venom AKI”
They have no role.
decode: Viper bite, sudden headache and coma
Recovered from Russell’s bite, later amenorrhoea and hypotension
Ventilated krait patient, fixed pupils, no movement
SNAKE-07.punch: Vipers kill by bleeding and kidney failure, elapids by descending paralysis — and a paralysed patient can look brain-dead while fully aware, so brain death is never diagnosed in envenoming.

parts.q: Russell’s viper, oliguric AKI, blood still incoagulable: management?
parts.a: **Repeat antivenom** (venom still active) **and early renal replacement therapy**; FFP only after antivenom; no steroids.

SNAKE-08.sub: Toxicology → First Aid & Tests → First aid
SNAKE-08.intro: First aid for a snakebite has two aims: slow the spread of venom through the lymphatics, and get the patient to antivenom quickly. Venom travels mainly through lymph, which moves when the muscles of the limb contract. Most traditional measures do neither and add harm, especially in viper bites where the tissue is already being destroyed.
why: a

**Do: reassure, immobilise the limb like a fracture, carry the patient (no walking), get to hospital.** Fear raises heart rate and makes the patient run; immobility stops the muscle pump that drives lymph and venom towards the circulation. Walking does the opposite. The definitive treatment is antivenom, so transport is the most important step.
b

**Do not: tourniquet, cutting or sucking, ice, electric shock.** A tight tourniquet traps venom in an ischaemic limb, worsening necrosis and gangrene, and releases it in a bolus when removed. Cutting causes bleeding in a coagulopathic patient and infection; suction removes no useful venom; ice and electric shock damage tissue and achieve nothing.
c

**Pressure immobilisation is controversial; only for purely neurotoxic bites, and not so tight as to stop perfusion.** A firm crepe bandage compresses the lymphatics and slows spread, which matters most for elapid venom that kills by paralysis and does little local damage. The worry in viper bites, which are most Indian bites, is that holding a tissue-destroying venom in the limb may worsen local necrosis. WHO 2016 favours pressure-pad immobilisation for suspected elapid bites, and the Indian Standard Treatment Guidelines (2017) allow a crepe bandage only when applied by trained staff and the hospital is 30 minutes to 3 hours away.
mimic: Pressure immobilisation vs tourniquet
The bandage compresses lymphatics but keeps the arterial supply; a tourniquet stops blood flow and causes ischaemia.
traps: “Apply a pressure-immobilisation bandage to every snakebite”
It comes from Australian elapid practice; in India most bites are vipers, so the default is splinting without a tight bandage, and a crepe bandage is left to trained staff.
“Remove the tourniquet at once”

Sudden release can flood the circulation with venom; remove it only once antivenom has started and resuscitation is ready — check the distal pulse, apply a proximal cuff, remove the tourniquet, then deflate slowly.
“Incise and suck the wound”
It removes nothing useful and causes bleeding and infection.
decode: First aid in an Indian snakebite
Reassure, immobilise, carry to hospital — no tourniquet.
Patient arrives with a tight tourniquet
Check pulse, proximal cuff, remove tourniquet, slow deflation, antivenom ready.
SNAKE-08.punch: Keep the limb still so the lymph — and the venom — stops moving, and move the patient to antivenom instead; everything that cuts, ties or freezes the limb only adds injury.

SNAKE-09.sub: Toxicology → First Aid & Tests → 20-minute whole blood clotting test
SNAKE-09.intro: Viper venom consumes fibrinogen and clotting factors until the blood cannot clot. The 20-minute whole blood clotting test checks this at the bedside with only a glass tube and a clock, so a peripheral health centre can decide on antivenom without a laboratory. It relies on glass activating the contact pathway of coagulation.
why: a

**A few mL of venous blood in a new, clean, dry glass tube, left undisturbed for 20 minutes, then tilted.** The glass surface activates factor XII and starts the intrinsic pathway; normal blood forms a firm clot well within 20 minutes. Disturbing the tube early breaks a forming clot and gives a false result.
b

**Still liquid = coagulopathy = viper bite, and an indication for antivenom.** If fibrinogen has been consumed, no clot can form however long you wait. Indian cobras and kraits do not cause coagulopathy, so an unclotted tube points to a viper.
c

**Plastic tubes, or glass washed with detergent, give false results.** Plastic does not activate the contact pathway, so normal blood stays liquid — a false positive. Detergent coats the glass and has the same effect.
d

**Every 30 minutes for 3 hours, then hourly; and 6 hours after antivenom. Observe every bite for at least 24 hours.** Coagulopathy can appear hours after the bite, so a single normal test excludes nothing. After antivenom the liver needs about 6 hours to make new clotting factors, so testing sooner would mislead (SNAKE-13).
mimic: 20WBCT vs PT/INR
Both detect venom coagulopathy; 20WBCT needs no laboratory, and PT or INR (INR >1.2) is used where available (SNAKE-12).
traps: “Use any clean tube — plastic is fine”
Plastic does not activate clotting; only new, clean, dry glass.
“Repeat the test 1 hour after antivenom”
The liver needs about 6 hours to restore clotting factors.
“Normal test on arrival — discharge”
Repeat for 3 hours, then hourly; observe 24 hours.
SNAKE-09.punch: Glass starts clotting, so normal blood clots within 20 minutes; liquid blood means the venom has used up the factors — and because the liver needs 6 hours to replace them, that is when the test is repeated.
fix: 20WBCT every 30 min for 3 h, then hourly
That is the 2009 protocol. Indian guideline 2017: 6 hours after the loading dose of ASV, and in suspected bites hourly for 3 h, then 6-hourly up to 24 h.

SNAKE-10.sub: Toxicology → First Aid & Tests → Neostigmine test
SNAKE-10.intro: A neurotoxic bite paralyses by stopping acetylcholine from acting on muscle. If the block is on the receptor, raising acetylcholine with an anticholinesterase can overcome it. The neostigmine test is a trial of exactly that — and its result tells you whether the drug can be continued as treatment.
why: a
**In any neurotoxic envenoming.** The snake is often unknown, and some patients respond who would not be predicted to, so every patient with ptosis or paralysis is tested.
b

**Atropine 0.6 mg IV first, then neostigmine 0.5–2 mg IM (children 50 µg/kg and 0.04 mg/kg).** Neostigmine raises acetylcholine at every synapse, including muscarinic ones, causing bradycardia, bronchorrhoea and salivation. Atropine first blocks those muscarinic effects while leaving the nicotinic junction free to benefit. The response is judged at one hour: the Indian guideline calls the test positive if ptosis recovers by 50% or more, with eye movements and the single-breath count as further measures.
c

**If it works, repeat every half hour for 3 hours, then hourly.** A response proves the block is postsynaptic and can be overcome. Neostigmine lasts only a few hours, so it is repeated, with atropine, to hold the improvement while antivenom works.
d
**It fails in krait (and Russell’s viper) bites: presynaptic toxins.** Their phospholipase A₂ destroys the nerve terminal, so there is no acetylcholine release for neostigmine to amplify.
mimic: Neostigmine here vs in organophosphate poisoning
Here we raise acetylcholine to beat a receptor block; in organophosphate poisoning acetylcholine is already in excess and atropine is the treatment.
traps: “Neostigmine replaces antivenom in cobra bites”
It only buys time; antivenom is still given.
“Give neostigmine without atropine”
Muscarinic effects — bradycardia and secretions — follow; atropine first.
“A negative test means no envenoming”
It means a presynaptic toxin, as in krait; the patient may still need ventilation.
decode: What counts as a positive test?
50% or more recovery of ptosis at 1 hour.
SNAKE-10.punch: Neostigmine can only add acetylcholine, so it helps only where the nerve terminal is intact and the receptor is blocked — the cobra — and atropine goes first to stop the muscarinic side effects.
fix: Neostigmine 0.5–2 mg IM

Indian guideline 2017: atropine 0.6 mg, then neostigmine 1.5 mg IV; then 0.5 mg with atropine every 30 min for 5 doses (child: atropine 0.05 mg/kg, neostigmine 0.04 mg/kg, repeat 0.01 mg/kg). Positive test: ≥50% recovery of ptosis at 1 hour. WHO gives neostigmine IM (about 0.02 mg/kg).

SNAKE-11.intro: Antivenom is made by immunising horses with venom and purifying their antibodies. Because it is a foreign protein, a minority of patients react to it, and the rules on test doses and premedication come from trials of how to predict and prevent those reactions. Its storage rules matter because it must be kept at rural centres without a cold chain.
why: a

**Polyvalent equine immunoglobulin against the big four.** Horses are immunised with the venoms of cobra, krait, Russell’s viper and saw-scaled viper, so one product covers all four and the snake need not be identified. Each vial is standardised by how much of each venom it neutralises.
b

**Liquid: 2 years at 2–8 °C. Lyophilised: 5 years below 25 °C.** Liquid protein degrades unless refrigerated. Freeze-dried powder is stable at room temperature, which makes it the practical form for rural centres; it is reconstituted before use.
c

**No test dose: it does not predict reactions.** Most early reactions are not IgE-mediated but complement activation by the foreign protein, so a small skin or IV test dose neither predicts nor prevents them, and it delays treatment.
d

**Subcutaneous adrenaline 0.25–0.3 mg is the only premedication with evidence; antihistamines, steroids and slower infusion have no role.** In a large Sri Lankan trial (de Silva, PLoS Med 2011) low-dose SC adrenaline reduced severe early reactions, while promethazine and hydrocortisone did not. Low-dose adrenaline narrows the leaky vessels and stabilises mast cells before the protein arrives. WHO 2016 recommends it routinely unless the antivenom is known to cause few reactions, and the Indian guideline (2017) advises it before ASV except in known hypertensives; drugs for anaphylaxis are still drawn up for every infusion (SNAKE-15).
mimic: Test dose for antivenom vs antibiotics
Neither is recommended; for antivenom it fails because most reactions are not IgE-mediated.
traps: “Give a test dose first”
It does not predict reactions and wastes time.
“Premedicate everyone with hydrocortisone and chlorphenamine”
No evidence; only low-dose SC adrenaline has shown benefit, and it is now advised routinely.
“A past horse-serum reaction is a contraindication”
No absolute contraindication; give it with resuscitation drugs ready.
decode: Shelf life of lyophilised Indian ASV
Is a sensitivity test dose required?
SNAKE-11.punch: Antivenom is horse antibody against the big four; because its reactions are mostly not allergic, a test dose predicts nothing, and only low-dose adrenaline has been shown to prevent them.

parts.q: How much venom does one vial neutralise, and why start with 10?
parts.a: Each mL neutralises **0.6 mg** of cobra and Russell’s venom (0.45 mg krait and saw-scaled), so a 10 mL vial ≈ **6 mg**. A Russell’s viper injects about **63 mg** on average — hence **10 vials** (~60 mg), and the same dose in children.

fix: Premedication not stated as routine
SC adrenaline 0.25 mg is now advised routinely before ASV (WHO SEARO 2016; Indian 2017 except known hypertensives). Freeze-dried ASV keeps 3–5 years.

SNAKE-12.sub: Toxicology → Antivenom & Complications → Indications for antivenom
SNAKE-12.intro: Antivenom is scarce, costly and can cause reactions, while half of venomous bites are dry. So it is given for evidence that venom has reached the circulation or is spreading dangerously in the limb — never for the bite itself. Once that evidence is there, no reaction risk outweighs it.
why: a

**Systemic: coagulopathy (20WBCT positive, INR >1.2 or PT 4–5 s over normal, spontaneous bleeding); neurotoxicity (ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, paralysis); shock, arrhythmia; AKI, rhabdomyolysis, haemolysis.** Each sign means circulating venom acting on a distant organ. Antivenom neutralises venom that is still free, so it stops further damage — which is why it is still given to a late presenter with systemic signs.
b

**Local: swelling of more than half the limb; rapidly extending swelling; swelling after a bite on a digit; a tender regional lymph node.** These mark a large venom load spreading through the tissue and lymphatics. A finger has little room to swell, so even modest swelling threatens necrosis and loss of the digit.
c
**Local swelling alone is not an indication.** Minor swelling occurs in many bites and settles without antivenom; treating it exposes the patient to reactions without benefit.
mimic: Minor local swelling vs local envenoming
Swelling confined near the bite is observed; swelling beyond half the limb, rapid spread or a tender node is treated.
traps: “Krait patient already ventilated at 48 hours — antivenom is too late”
Free venom may remain; antivenom is still given if envenomed, though it cannot undo toxin already bound.
“Asthma or a previous serum reaction is a contraindication”
There is no absolute contraindication; untreated envenoming is deadlier — have adrenaline ready.
“Egg allergy contraindicates antivenom”
Irrelevant — antivenom is horse protein, not egg-based.
decode: Bite with mild swelling at the site, 20WBCT normal
Bite on a finger with swelling
SNAKE-12.punch: Antivenom treats venom, not the bite: give it for any systemic sign or dangerous local spread, withhold it for local swelling alone — and once indicated, no allergy history stops it.

table.title: Give antivenom when
head: Domain
Sign
rows: >half the limb, rapid spread, digit, tender node

SNAKE-13.intro: Antivenom neutralises venom molecule for molecule, so the dose is set by how much venom the snake injected, not by the size of the patient. It cannot repair damage already done: in haemotoxic bites the liver must remake the clotting factors, and in neurotoxic bites only free venom can be caught. Those two facts decide when, and whether, to repeat.
why: a

**10 vials, by IV infusion over 1 hour (or slow IV at 2 mL/min).** Ten vials neutralise roughly the average venom load of a Russell’s viper bite (SNAKE-11); the older national protocol allows 8–10. The whole dose goes in quickly so free venom is caught early; IM injection is never used, because absorption is too slow and causes haematomas. Indian studies found that larger initial doses add cost and reactions without better outcomes, and the 2017 guideline states that low-dose infusion is as effective as high-dose bolus therapy (expert consensus).
b

**No reduction in children: the snake injects the same venom.** The dose matches the venom, not the body weight, and a child receives a larger dose of venom per kilogram, so the need is if anything greater.
c

**Haemotoxic: repeat 20WBCT at 6 hours; if still incoagulable, another 5–10 vials, 6-hourly.** After venom is neutralised the liver needs about 6 hours to make new clotting factors, so a test sooner would be misleading. Blood still liquid at 6 hours means venom is still active.
d

**Neurotoxic: if no better or worse after 1–2 hours, a second 10 vials; then stop (maximum 20) and ventilate.** Antivenom catches only circulating toxin; toxin already bound, and terminals already destroyed, are beyond it. If 20 vials have not helped, more adds reaction risk without benefit — the patient needs ventilation and time.
e

**Late presenters: haemotoxic — antivenom if coagulopathy persists; neurotoxic — one dose of 8–10 vials, then support.** Persistent coagulopathy proves free venom is still present. In a late neurotoxic case most toxin is already bound, so one dose mops up the rest.
mimic: Haemotoxic vs neurotoxic repeat timing
Haemotoxic waits 6 hours for the liver; neurotoxic is judged at 1–2 hours by the paralysis.
traps: “Halve the dose in children”
Same dose — the venom load is the same.
“Keep giving antivenom until the krait patient breathes”
Stop at 20 vials; recovery needs nerve terminals to regrow, so ventilate.
“Repeat 20WBCT at 1 hour after antivenom”
At 6 hours — the liver needs that long to restore factors.
decode: Initial ASV dose in a 20 kg child with a viper bite
Blood still incoagulable 6 hours after ASV
SNAKE-13.punch: The dose is set by the venom, not the patient, so children get the full 10 vials; repeat at 6 hours in haemotoxic bites because the liver needs that long, and stop at 20 in neurotoxic bites because bound toxin cannot be reached.

parts.q: Is 10 vials a universal rule?
parts.a: No — it is the Indian polyvalent rule. **CroFab** for North American pit vipers starts at **4–6 vials**. The constant is that **children get the adult dose**.

fix: Repeat 5–10 vials 6-hourly

Indian guideline 2017: neurotoxic — 10 vials over 30 min, another 10 at 1 h if no better (maximum 20). Haemotoxic low-dose — 10 vials (Russell’s) or 6 (saw-scaled), then 2 vials 6-hourly; high-dose — 10, then 6 vials 6-hourly.

SNAKE-14.sub: Toxicology → Antivenom & Complications → Expected response to antivenom
SNAKE-14.intro: Antivenom works by binding free venom, so anything caused directly by circulating venom improves fast. Anything that needs the body to rebuild — clotting factors, damaged tissue — takes hours. Knowing the expected time course tells you whether the dose was enough or a repeat is needed.
why: a

**Spontaneous bleeding stops in 15–30 minutes.** Once the haemorrhagins and procoagulants are bound, vessel damage and factor consumption stop at once, and platelets plug the small leaks, even before the factor levels recover.
b

**Blood pressure normalises in 30–60 minutes.** Venom-induced vasodilatation and myocardial depression stop when the toxin is neutralised; fluid lost through leaky capillaries may still need replacing.
c

**Blood becomes coagulable in 3–9 hours.** Neutralising venom stops consumption, but the liver must make new fibrinogen and factors, which takes hours — the reason the 20WBCT is repeated at 6 hours (SNAKE-09, 13).
d
**Haemolysis and rhabdomyolysis stop within a few hours.** The membrane-damaging enzymes are bound, so no new cells break, and the dark urine clears as the pigment is excreted.
e

**Postsynaptic paralysis improves from 30 minutes.** Antivenom pulls α-neurotoxin off the receptor, so cobra paralysis can begin to lift early. Presynaptic krait paralysis does not improve this way, because the nerve terminal must regrow.
mimic: Bleeding stops vs blood clots again
Bleeding stops in under 30 minutes; the 20WBCT normalises only after 3–9 hours. A still-liquid test at 1 hour is expected, not a failure.
traps: “20WBCT still positive at 2 hours — repeat the antivenom”
Clotting takes 3–9 hours to return; reassess at 6 hours.
“Krait paralysis should lift within an hour of antivenom”
Only postsynaptic paralysis responds early; presynaptic recovery takes days.
decode: Bleeding gums stop how soon after ASV?
Time for blood to become coagulable
SNAKE-14.punch: Whatever free venom causes stops within minutes of antivenom; whatever the body must rebuild takes hours — so bleeding stops in half an hour but clotting returns only after the liver has had about 6 hours.

SNAKE-15.sub: Toxicology → Antivenom & Complications → Reactions to antivenom
SNAKE-15.intro: Antivenom is foreign horse protein, and the body can react to it in three ways at three different times. Early reactions come from complement and mast-cell activation by the protein; pyrogenic reactions from bacterial endotoxin contaminating the product; serum sickness from immune complexes once the body makes antibodies against horse protein about a week later. The timing tells you which one you face.
why: a

**Early anaphylactic, 10–180 minutes: urticaria, bronchospasm, shock — stop; chlorphenamine 10 mg + hydrocortisone 100 mg IV; IM adrenaline if severe; restart slowly after 10–15 minutes.** The infusion is stopped to remove the trigger. Adrenaline is the drug that reverses bronchospasm and vasodilatation; current WHO guidance gives IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (child 0.01 mg/kg) at the first sign, with chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone as slower adjuncts. Antivenom is then restarted slowly, because the envenoming still needs treating.
b

**Pyrogenic, 1–2 hours: fever, rigors, hypotension (endotoxin) — antipyretic, fluids.** Endotoxin in the product triggers cytokine release, so the patient has rigors and vasodilatation. Physical cooling, an antipyretic and fluids are enough.
c

**Serum sickness, 1–12 days: fever, arthralgia, urticaria, nephritis — oral prednisolone, antihistamine.** The patient makes antibodies to horse protein, which form immune complexes with the antivenom still circulating; these deposit in joints, skin and glomeruli. Steroids suppress the inflammation, and antihistamine relieves the itch.
mimic: Pyrogenic reaction vs anaphylaxis
Both can drop the blood pressure; rigors and fever without urticaria or wheeze point to endotoxin.
traps: “Antihistamine and hydrocortisone first, adrenaline only if severe”
Adrenaline IM 0.5 mg comes first; the others are slow adjuncts.
“After a reaction, antivenom is abandoned”
It is restarted slowly once the reaction settles — the envenoming is the greater danger.
“Fever and joint pain a week later is a new infection”
Serum sickness — oral prednisolone.
decode: Wheeze and hypotension 20 minutes into ASV
Stop; IM adrenaline 0.5 mg; then chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone.
Arthralgia, rash and proteinuria 7 days later
SNAKE-15.punch: The timing names the reaction — minutes for anaphylaxis, an hour or two for endotoxin, a week for immune complexes — and in anaphylaxis adrenaline comes first, after which the antivenom is restarted.
